American chipmaker Nvidia has announced minority investments in four French technology companies, including the medical appointment platform Doctolib, as it expands its presence in Europe’s fast-growing artificial intelligence sector.

Ukraine’s Starlink disruptions expose European reliance on US tech. Ukraine has reported disruptions to drones relying on Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet network, as well as the United States-operated early warning system supposed to alert it to Russian missile attacks. The problems expose Europe's dependence on US technology, with no homegrown alternatives immediately available.

Belgian police raid Tshisekedi family properties in DRC mining investigation. Police have searched several properties in Belgium belonging to family members of Democratic Republic of Congo's President Félix Tshisekedi, as part of an investigation into suspected personal enrichment from the country’s mining sector.

France’s emissions falling faster in 2026 but still over climate target. France’s greenhouse gas emissions are expected to fall by 2.8 percent in 2026, slightly more than last year – but the pace of decarbonisation remains well below what is needed to meet the country’s climate targets.

Zelensky rallies European allies after defying Trump over Russia strikes. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky is seeking to rally European allies at a Brussels summit on Friday after saying Kyiv would no longer abide by US President Donald Trump's demands not to strike Russian oil refineries.

Challenge to HIV restrictions in French armed forces goes before top court. Several organisations have brought a case before France’s highest court to challenge the continued exclusion of people living with HIV from certain posts in the armed forces, gendarmerie and fire services.

Trial of French IS returnee highlights a growing focus on the women who came back. Courts are increasingly turning their attention to the women who joined the Islamic State armed group in Syria and Iraq, and then returned to France. The latest case opened Wednesday: that of Radia Tahar Aouidate, was one of 23 members of her family to travel to Syria, under the influence of her brother.

Infantino offers apology but 'no answers' at Fifa meeting over World Cup plan. Fifa president Gianni Infantino gave "no satisfactory answers" when grilled Thursday during a meeting to discuss his attempts to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, senior members of football's global governing body said, but he did offer an apology for the failed project.

Nineteen injured as minibus crashes into Channel Tunnel shuttle train. A minibus carrying truck drivers crashed into a freight train at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel injuring 19 people, French authorities said.

Somalia sets date for May presidential election amid ongoing Islamist insurgency. Somalia's election commission has announced it will hold parliamentary and presidential polls in April and May next year, but critics say the decision will lead to more conflict in a deeply fragmented country facing a long-running Islamist insurgency.

School students called to join Yellow Vests and unions for mass French protest. Following an unsuccessful meeting with France's education minister on Thursday, protesting high school pupils across the country say they will not let up the pressure on the government. The Yellow Vests movement has called on the students to join them at a nationwide demonstration on Saturday over working conditions and the cost of living.

Mayors urge France to recognise 1961 Paris massacre of Algerians as state crime. On the eve of the 65th anniversary of the massacre of Algerian protesters in Paris, French mayors are calling for the events of 17 October, 1961 to be officially recognised as a state crime.

France and Germany strike deal to boost Europe's struggling car industry. France and Germany have agreed a deal to safeguard Europe's automobile industry and stave off fierce competition from Chinese electric car companies. The agreement also opens the door for the United Kingdom to be treated as a trusted partner under "Made in EU" rules.

Madagascar marks one year since uprising as Russia’s influence grows. Madagascar marks one year on Saturday since military leader Michael Randrianirina took power following weeks of youth-led protests that brought down elected president Andry Rajoelina. Over the past year, Russian influence has grown through closer military ties and weapons deliveries, while researchers have identified Moscow’s interest in a strategic Indian Ocean port. Many of the political reforms demanded by protesters, however, remain unfinished.

Pacific nations await climate billions, as fossil fuel divide looms over Cop31. Ahead of next month’s United Nations Cop31 climate summit, as a strengthening El Niño drives Pacific sea temperatures towards record levels, more than $5 billion promised to the region remains unpaid. Cop31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia are pushing to speed up the switch to electric transport, heating and industry, but participating countries are divided over how to wind down the use of coal, oil and gas.

Thousands expected to take part in day of action across France. Tens of thousands of people are expected to demonstrate across France on Saturday, as students, trade unionists and activists from the Yellow Vest movement join forces to demonstrate against the high cost of living and poor conditions in schools.

France's new sexual violence bill 'fails to tackle root causes', campaigners warn. A sweeping package of reforms, passed unanimously by the lower house of parliament this week, aims to overhaul how France investigates and prosecutes sexual violence. Yet campaigners say the legislation does not do enough to prevent abuse, while protection for some of the most vulnerable victims is lacking.

Journaliste arrêté en Russie: le Japon victime de la «diplomatie des otages». Nouveau coup de froid diplomatique entre Tokyo et Moscou. En début de semaine, la Russie a annoncé l'arrestation pour espionnage d'un journaliste japonais sur l'île de Sakhaline, au large de la Sibérie et surtout au nord de l'archipel nippon.

Prix Découvertes RFI 2027: inscrivez-vous !. Le Prix Découvertes RFI lance sa nouvelle édition ! Appel à tous les artistes qui veulent se faire entendre dans le monde entier et développer leur carrière à l'international. Les candidatures sont ouvertes jusqu'au 22 novembre 2026.

Dix ans de santé numérique en Afrique de l'Ouest: «Il faut digitaliser notre système de soin». L'Observatoire de la e-santé dans les pays du sud (Odess) fêtait ses 10 ans ce 15 octobre 2026. Son rôle : repérer, documenter et accompagner les projets de santé numérique sur les continents africain et asiatique. En dépit de progrès technologiques indéniables et face à l'arrivée rapide de l'intelligence artificielle, les avancées proposées sont parfois déconnectées des besoins réels des patients et des professionnels de santé. Entretien avec Cheikh Oumar Bagayoko, professeur à l'université de Bamako et directeur de Digi-santé Mali.

En Inde, les initiatives en santé numérique ont entraîné «une hausse de 12% de vaccination chez les bébés». À l'occasion de ses 10 ans, l'Observatoire de la e-santé dans les pays du sud (Odess) a récompensé l'ONG Khushi Baby, programme d'amélioration de la santé maternelle et infantile au Rajasthan (Ouest). Accompagnée par l'Odess depuis 2017, la plateforme Khushi Baby est désormais utilisée par 85 000 agents de santé communautaires et 60 000 patients. Ruchit Nagar, médecin et cofondateur de la plateforme, revient sur son bilan.

Benjamin Stora: le massacre du 17 octobre 1961, «doit être reconnu dans les manuels scolaires». « La reconnaissance pleine et entière du massacre du 17 octobre 1961 comme un crime d’État » et « l'inscription du 17 octobre au calendrier officiel des journées nationales et cérémonies officielles ». C’est ce que demandent aujourd’hui une trentaine de maires, 65 ans après le massacre des Algériens. Ce jour-là, près de 25 000 Algériens se sont rassemblés à Paris, à l’appel du FLN pour contester un couvre-feu discriminatoire du 5 octobre, sous l’autorité du préfet Maurice Papon. Un couvre-feu, qui ne visait que les Français musulmans d’Algérie. Une manifestation pacifiste, et pourtant une répression sanglante : plus de 12 000 arrestations, au moins 150 Algériens tués, par balle, jetés dans la Seine. 65 ans après, où en est l’ouverture des archives ? « Des faits inexcusables pour la République », selon Emmanuel Macron, mais toujours pas de reconnaissance de crime d'État.

Manana Cissé, légende vivante des Ballets africains de Guinée. À près de 80 ans, Manana Cissé raconte toujours avec fierté son légendaire mouvement de danse ultra-rapide, impossible à saisir en photo. Née en 1947 à Boké, en Guinée, elle a rejoint les prestigieux Ballets africains à l’âge de douze ans. Aujourd’hui, elle est directrice artistique de cette troupe mythique, jadis figure de proue du renouveau culturel guinéen. Dans une interview exclusive, la grande dame de la danse évoque son parcours, son engagement auprès d’Ahmed Sékou Touré, l’héritage de Keita Fodéba et la nouvelle dynamique insufflée aux Ballets africains par le spectacle « Mansa Moussa, roi d’or ».

L'Irak a perdu 60 milliards de dollars à cause du blocus du détroit d'Ormuz. L'Irak a perdu 60 milliards de dollars depuis fin février. En conséquence de la guerre au Moyen-Orient et du blocus du détroit d'Ormuz par l'Iran. Le pétrole est la richesse de l'Irak et il est devenu très difficile de l'exporter.

Pierre Moscovici: «L'extrême droite veut réduire l'UE à une union de nations, cible des prédateurs». Cette semaine, Caroline De Camaret reçoit Pierre Moscovici, membre français de la Cour des comptes européenne. Depuis 1977, la Cour des comptes agit comme un auditeur externe de l’Union européenne, examinant la gestion financière et le budget de l’UE. Ancien député européen, Pierre Moscovici fut aussi ministre des Affaires européennes puis de l'Économie, avant de devenir commissaire européen aux affaires économiques et financières, président de la Cour des comptes française et, finalement, membre de la Cour des comptes européenne à Luxembourg.

Italie: à Rome, l'école publique Di Donato se bat contre un décret-loi du gouvernement Meloni. À quelques mois des élections générales en Italie, un décret-loi adopté par le gouvernement Meloni impose notamment l'interdiction du port du voile dans les établissements scolaires ou bien des limites d'élèves étrangers. Au cœur de l'Esquilin, le quartier le plus cosmopolite de Rome, enseignants et parents d'élèves de l’école Di Donato font front commun contre ce décret-loi.

Tous les candidats au poste de chef de l'ONU essuient un veto lors d'un vote indicatif au Conseil de sécurité. Tous les candidats au poste de secrétaire général de l'ONU se sont vu opposer, vendredi 16 octobre, un veto par les membres permanents du Conseil de sécurité, a-t-on appris de source diplomatique. Au terme de ce vote indicatif, aucun des sept candidats n'a réussi à échapper à un veto des cinq grandes puissances qui disposent de ce droit, ouvrant la voie à d'éventuelles nouvelles candidatures.

Un Conseil européen divisé sur le budget et les migrations, mais uni sur l'Ukraine. Quand un Conseil européen se termine plus tard que prévu, ce n'est jamais bon signe et c'est ce qu'il s'est passé ce soir à Bruxelles. Les 27 dirigeants de l'Union européenne ont quitté ce vendredi 16 octobre le sommet il y a un peu plus d'une heure. Ils se sont divisés sur les migrations.

Certains pays interdisent aux personnes sourdes et malentendantes de conduire. Le numéro 114 fête son anniversaire : le 114, c'est l’appel d’urgence en France pour les personnes sourdes et malentendantes. Depuis 15 ans, ce système reçoit les urgences sous forme de texte ou de connexions vidéo. Un numéro utile qui peut sauver des vies sur les routes ou dans les transports. Les personnes sourdes conduisent, mais pas dans tous les pays.

Au Pakistan, l'avenir est incertain pour les étudiants afghans en médecine. Du jour au lendemain, en pleine année universitaire, des centaines d’étudiants afghans en médecine au Pakistan se retrouvent menacés de devoir interrompre leurs études et de rentrer en Afghanistan.

France: le président du Conseil constitutionnel Richard Ferrand s'attire les foudres du RN. Les députés RN et UDR ont saisi le Conseil constitutionnel pour obtenir la démission de son chef Richard Ferrand, dont Marine Le Pen demandait le départ après que ce dernier a déclaré publiquement qu’on ne pouvait réformer la Constitution par référendum qu’avec l’accord du Parlement (article 89), contrairement à ce que pense le parti d’extrême droite.

80 ans du Rassemblement démocratique africain (RDA): la radicalité du PDG, section guinéenne du RDA [1/2]. Il y a 80 ans, du 18 au 21 octobre 1946, se tenait le congrès de Bamako, au cours duquel naissait le Rassemblement démocratique africain (RDA), le premier grand mouvement politique panafricain et anticolonialiste. En Guinée, une délégation de leaders politiques guinéens a participé au congrès de Bamako. Peu de temps après, ces responsables ont fondé la section guinéenne du RDA, le Parti démocratique de Guinée (PDG), qui a mené le pays à l’indépendance en 1958. Le fils d’un des acteurs majeurs de l’époque, Mamadou Traoré, dit Ray Autra, nous fait le récit de cette histoire.

États-Unis: Katie Zacharia, la nouvelle porte-parole de Trump, poussée vers la sortie après cinq jours. La porte-parole de la Maison Blanche Katie Zacharia, nommée il y a une semaine par Donald Trump et en poste depuis lundi, a pris la porte vendredi, devenant ainsi la plus éphémère « Press Secretary » de l'histoire récente. Un haut responsable américain a indiqué à l'AFP qu'une information de la chaîne Fox News, selon laquelle cette juriste de 41 ans quittait officiellement son poste, était exacte.

Sénégal: à Dakar, une marche contre les féminicides après la mort d'une femme attaquée à l'acide. Au Sénégal, une nouvelle marche a eu lieu vendredi 16 octobre 2026 pour dire stop aux féminicides. Le 1er octobre, une femme de 40 ans a succombé à ses blessures après avoir été aspergée d'acide par son ex-compagnon à Dakar. Plus de 200 habitants de son quartier ont marché jusqu'à la préfecture de Grand Dakar pour demander justice et l'arrestation du suspect, toujours en fuite.

Éthiopie: le gouvernement fédéral installe une administration intérimaire au Tigré pour six mois. En Éthiopie, c'est désormais officiel : le gouvernement fédéral reprend le contrôle administratif du Tigré. Il a annoncé vendredi 16 octobre la mise en place d'une administration intérimaire pour six mois. Les autorités fédérales reprennent ainsi formellement l'administration de cette région, jusqu'ici dirigée par les rebelles du Front de libération du peuple du Tigré (TPLF). Après plusieurs semaines de combats contre l'armée fédérale, les troupes du TPLF ont été repoussées vers le nord et ont perdu le contrôle des grandes villes de la région.

États-Unis: Donald Trump exempte la Russie de nouvelles sanctions adoptées par le Congrès. Le président américain Donald Trump a annoncé, vendredi 16 octobre 2026, la levée de plusieurs sanctions, restrictions et droits de douane visant la Russie, prévus dans le cadre d'une loi promulguée le mois dernier, avant même leur entrée en vigueur.

Steve Rosenberg, BBC Moscou: «Travailler en Russie, c’est comme être plongeur en eaux profondes». Depuis plus de 30 ans, Steve Rosenberg est le correspondant de la BBC à Moscou. En visite en France pour le prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandie des correspondants de guerre, il a accordé un long entretien à L’atelier des médias de RFI pour raconter son quotidien de journaliste étranger en Russie. Il y explique pourquoi il fait le choix de rester en Russie, malgré un environnement de plus en plus hostile aux médias.

Midterms 2026: quels sont les scrutins qui attendent les Américains ce 3 novembre?. Le 3 novembre prochain, les Américains ne voteront pas seulement pour renouveler une partie du Congrès. Gouverneurs, élus locaux, référendums… Les élections de mi-mandat se jouent aussi à l’échelle des États. Tour d’horizon de ce que les électeurs trouveront sur leur bulletin de vote.

«Je n'abandonnerai jamais de documenter l'invasion russe en Ukraine», promet le photographe Adrien Vautier. Dans le cadre du Prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandie, l'exposition photo « Si tu traverses l'hiver » d’Adrien Vautier en Ukraine est affichée dans les rues de la ville normande. Présent depuis les premiers jours de l’agression russe en 2022, il tente de synthétiser ce qu’il a pu observer tant sur le front que dans une vie quotidienne à l’arrière marquée par la guerre.

DIRECT - Journée de mobilisation commune en France: premières actions à Rennes, Lyon et Marseille. Des centaines d'actions, de blocages et de rassemblements sont prévus ce samedi 17 octobre partout en France. Anciens « gilets jaunes », lycéens, étudiants, militants du climat et agriculteurs entendent faire converger leurs colères contre la vie chère, le manque de moyens dans l'éducation et la dégradation des services publics. À six mois de l'élection présidentielle, l'ampleur de cette mobilisation aux revendications protéiformes reste difficile à prévoir.

Maroc: un système inédit de surveillance de voix dissidentes révélé par Amnesty. Après des années d’enquête, l’ONG de défense des droits de l’homme sort un rapport inédit sur le fonctionnement du système de surveillance marocain pour réprimer des militants de la liberté d’expression et des journalistes.

An Underwater Shadow War Is Raging. A new book examines a hugely consequential conflict happening mostly out of sight.
Israeli Settlers Launch a Coordinated Attack in the West Bank. Netanyahu vowed to investigate the incident but stopped short of condemning settler violence.

Iran hardliners back threats to strike Persian Gulf digital infrastructure. Iranian hardliners have backed security chief Mohsen Rezaei’s threat to strike data centers, undersea internet cables and artificial intelligence facilities in the Persian Gulf if the United States and Israel resume hostilities.

US military support against Houthis risks widening Iran war, expert says. Washington could support the Saudi campaign against the Houthis at little direct cost by lifting political objections to its operations, but deeper military involvement risks appearing to widen the Iran war, senior Middle East analyst Ryan Bohl told Iran International.

UKMTO warnings show 12 commercial ships attacked in one week. Twelve attacks on commercial vessels were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf between October 5 and 11, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) warnings.

Iran officials hinted at land incursions if US resumes strikes - WSJ. Some Iranian officials have privately suggested Tehran could send forces into neighbouring countries if the United States launches new strikes, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the warnings.

‘Best advertisement for Starlink’ Iranians mock threat to subsea cables. The Islamic Republic’s threats to target undersea internet cables in the Persian Gulf drew mockery and criticism from readers who told Iran International that such attacks could deepen Iran’s isolation and damage its own connectivity.

Iran says six killed as armed clashes intensify in southeast. The Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that five members of an alleged kidnapping cell and one of its personnel were killed near Zahedan, while separate reports said more than 20 members of an Iran-backed militia were killed or wounded in the area.

Gunfire heard as county-naming protest turns violent in central Iran. A protest over the name of a newly created county in central Iran turned violent after security forces moved to disperse demonstrators, with videos sent to Iran International capturing gunfire, tear gas and injured protesters.

Amnesty urges global action after Iran executes five protest-linked prisoners in one week. Amnesty International on Tuesday condemned Iran’s execution of five men in cases linked to the January protests within one week and called for coordinated international pressure on Tehran to halt further executions.

Houthi airport strikes carry echoes of Iran’s aviation threats, experts say. The deadly attacks on Riyadh’s main airport mirror Iranian warnings to disrupt regional air travel in response to US sanctions, analysts say, while serving the Houthis’ own goal of pressuring Saudi Arabia over its support for rival forces in Yemen.

State TV calls Iran’s northern sea by its English name, citing Israeli agenda. Iranian state television has begun referring to the country’s northern sea as Caspian in Persian, a departure from the customary Khazar, after airing claims that the older familiar name serves alleged Israeli ambitions in the Caucasus.

Iran faces worse economic outlook than war-hit Mideast rivals, IMF says. The International Monetary Fund forecast Tuesday that Iran’s economy would shrink 7.6% in 2026, a worse outlook than for its main Middle Eastern rivals amid the war, with Saudi Arabia and the UAE facing smaller contractions and Israel and Turkey expected to grow.

Tehran raises the stakes, betting Washington will blink. Despite signs of movement in negotiations with Washington, Tehran is showing little inclination to ease military pressure, pursuing diplomacy while signaling that renewed US attacks could trigger a broader regional response.

Iranians' support for US pressure masks divisions over its cost. Nearly three-quarters of respondents to an Iran International Instagram poll backed continued US pressure on the Islamic Republic, while thousands of comments revealed deep divisions over its economic cost and whether it could bring political change.

Iran names new commander for renamed Quds Force assassination unit. The Quds Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has appointed a new commander to its overseas assassination unit and renamed it to Unit 600 after its personnel and structure were exposed, two sources close to the IRGC-QF told Iran International.

Oscar-winning Farhadi says next film will be in Persian, without mandatory hijab. Oscar-winning Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi says his next film will be in Persian and set in Tehran but shot abroad to avoid Iran's mandatory hijab rules and government permit requirements.

Trump says Iran decision coming, suggests Tehran behind Houthi attacks. US President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would make a decision on Iran “very soon,” as fresh attacks hit commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated.

Iran threatens to reconsider UK ties over RAF Fairford allegations. Iran on Tuesday summoned Britain’s ambassador and threatened to reconsider diplomatic relations after London blamed the IRGC for a suspected plot targeting a US-used airbase and Britain’s intelligence chief warned of growing Iranian threats to military sites.

Iran escalates Hormuz tanker attacks in gamble ahead of US midterms. Iran's surge in attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz may be an attempt to exploit US restraint ahead of the midterm elections and undermine a recovery in Persian Gulf oil shipments, experts told Iran International.

Iran executes mountaineer after rights groups warn of imminent hanging. Iranian authorities executed Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a 38-year-old mountaineer from Kerman, the judiciary’s Mizan News reported on Wednesday.

Nowhere else to go? The puzzle behind Iran’s stock rally. Iran’s stock market is raising eyebrows with a sustained rally even as the country’s economy struggles with dwindling foreign-currency inflows, energy shortages and uncertainty over the war.

Iranian wheat farmers face planting cash crunch as payments lag, rial slides. Iranian wheat farmers told Iran International that delayed government payments for their previous harvest are leaving them short of cash for autumn planting, while inflation and the falling rial erode the value of money they are still owed.

Women’s Basij commander, police officer killed in southeast Iran. A women’s Basij commander and a police officer were killed in separate attacks on Wednesday in Iran’s southeastern Sistan-Baluchestan province, adding to a series of deadly shootings, bombings and armed clashes in the region.

Zarif under fire for dismissing nuclear deterrence before war. A resurfaced video of former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif saying Iran lacked enough enriched uranium to produce a nuclear weapon has ignited a fierce debate after successive wars with Israel and the United States.

Iran police killed brothers celebrating Khamenei’s death, source says. Iranian police fired 36 rounds at a car during a seven-minute chase near Tehran, killing two brothers aged 15 and 19 after its occupants honked their horn while celebrating the death of then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei, a source close to the family told Iran International.

Iranians report months-long waits for unemployment benefits. Iranians receiving unemployment benefits say payments have been delayed by up to two months, leaving some struggling to pay for food and service debts, according to messages sent to Iran International.

Tehran signals escalation in conflict IRGC likens to a ‘world war’. A senior Revolutionary Guards official has compared Iran’s conflict with the United States to a world war that could reshape the global order, reflecting a mindset in Tehran that appears increasingly resistant to backing down despite the risk of renewed US attacks.

Man in Iran International attack plot told police he was paid £2,000 to film. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists in Britain told police he had received £2,000 for filming, according to interview transcripts read at Woolwich Crown Court on Wednesday.

How Iran shielded forces over 2022 protest killings. Iran has built impunity for the killing of protesters into its laws and judicial system, Amnesty International said in an investigation detailing how security forces accused of deadly violence can help determine whether their own actions were lawful.

Ignore prices and economy is fine, Iran ex-minister says. A former Iranian labor minister has drawn ridicule after saying the country has no economic problems other than high prices and inflation, remarks that came as official data showed year-on-year inflation approaching 90%.

Shiraz and the wine industry Iran lost after 1979. Nearly five decades after the 1979 Revolution brought an end to Iran's legal wine industry, the country retains vast vineyards and a centuries-old winemaking heritage but remains absent from a global wine export market worth $37.8 billion in 2025.

Iran’s strikes on Persian Gulf water and power were deliberate - Reuters. Iran and its allies hit water plants, airports, refineries and a nuclear power station across the Persian Gulf with a precision that rules out the official story of falling debris, a Reuters investigation has found, showing the civilian damage was the aim, not a side effect.

‘We cannot bring America to its knees,’ former Tehran mayor says. Iran cannot bring the United States to its knees despite inflicting damage on American forces, a former Tehran mayor said in a state television interview, arguing that Iran's military capabilities cannot match Washington's and calling for an end to the war through negotiations.

Tehran hospital locks its main building and treats patients in the courtyard. A Social Security hospital in Tehran has locked its main building and moved treatment into a cramped clinic in its courtyard, a member of the insurer’s healthcare oversight committee said, two months after officials listed it among the capital’s unsafe hospitals.

German court jails two men over spying for Iran's Guards. A German court convicted two men of spying on prominent Jewish figures and preparing attacks against them on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force, sentencing both to prison on Thursday.

Armed suspect arrested over alleged plot to kill ex-minister, reformists say. An armed man was arrested over an alleged plot to assassinate a former Iranian minister after a gathering attended by Mohammad Khatami, the former president associated with efforts to reform the Islamic Republic from within, Iran’s Reform Front said.

Statement on a cyberattack targeting an Iran International correspondent. On 10 October 2026, an unauthorized third party gained access to the work account of one of our correspondents. The correspondent was approached by someone posing as a representative of an established think tank and invited to join an online meeting.

Tehran hardline mayor rolls out economic relief: is he eyeing the presidency?. Tehran’s hardline mayor Alireza Zakani has drawn accusations of using municipal resources to prepare for another presidential bid after announcing a freeze on basic food prices and payments to new parents.

US alert puts Iran’s overseas religious finance networks under scrutiny. The US Treasury’s latest warning over Iran’s alleged abuse of religious charities puts renewed attention on religious and charitable organizations outside Iran that have separately faced criminal, regulatory or government scrutiny over financial or institutional links to Tehran.

Suspect in journalist attack plot says UK-based IRGC officer threatened to kill him. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists told a London court on Thursday that a man he identified as a Revolutionary Guards officer living in Britain threatened to kill him and his mother unless he obeyed.

Iran touts economic resilience while households struggle to afford basics. Iran’s central bank governor has dismissed claims of economic collapse, while domestic media reports describe wages failing to cover basic living costs and families struggling to afford medicines, housing and car repairs.

Iran speaker says government overstepped on anti-terror finance rules. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has ruled that part of the government’s anti-terror financing regulations violates Iranian law, saying decisions on who is designated as terrorist must remain with the Supreme National Security Council.

Iran shipped jet fuel to Myanmar despite US blockade - Reuters. Iran managed to export jet fuel to Myanmar and send several shipments of liquefied petroleum gas out of the region despite a US naval blockade that has largely halted its crude exports, Reuters reported on Friday.

Norwegian teen gets 20-year sentence in UK murder plot linked to Iran. A Norwegian teenager recruited by a Swedish crime group linked by prosecutors to the Iranian government was sentenced to 20 years’ detention in Britain on Friday.

Iran’s rulers face a reckoning with their own people, former US envoy says. Decades of American sanctions strengthened Iran’s Revolutionary Guards by hollowing out the middle class, former US diplomat Joey Hood told Iran International, and once the fighting ends, Tehran will face a reckoning with its own people.

Iran hangs Iraqi man on Saudi spying charge he denied. Iran has executed a 28-year-old Iraqi man convicted of spying for Saudi Arabia, a charge he denied, according to the Oslo-based group Iran Human Rights.

Iranian court sentences woman to 50 lashes for kissing a man in a cafe. A court in the Iranian city of Qom has sentenced a woman to 50 lashes for kissing and hugging a man in a cafe, after her husband filed a complaint and submitted video of the meeting, according to the rights group HRANA. She denies the charge.

Iran raided, summoned and jailed Baha’is in Yazd 34 times in seven months. Iranian security and judicial authorities have taken action against Baha’is in the central city of Yazd at least 34 times in less than seven months, raiding homes, summoning dozens for interrogation and jailing members of the faith, the rights group HRANA reported on Friday.

After the killings, Iran turned on the families of the dead. A bullet is fired once. For the families of those killed in Iran’s Woman, Life, Freedom uprising, the punishment that followed lasted for years: bodies held hostage, false confessions forced on parents, funerals fired upon and killers set free, Amnesty International has found.

Iran cultivated Houthis for years before opening new war front, Yemeni insider says. Iran spent years building influence in Yemen through Hezbollah recruiters and Revolutionary Guards officers, a former Yemeni pro-democracy activist told Iran International, and is now using the Houthis to carry the war to Saudi Arabia and its Western allies.

Iran giving Houthis targeting intelligence for Saudi attacks - WSJ. Iranian support has helped Yemen’s Houthis carry out their most potent and sophisticated attacks yet on Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on intelligence from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s anti-Houthi alliance.

Burkina Faso : Ibrahim Traoré a-t-il confisqué l’héritage de Thomas Sankara ?. Le mémorial consacré à Thomas Sankara, érigé à Ouagadougou, change progressivement de vocation. Pensé par ses fidèles, il est aujourd’hui réinvesti par la junte dirigée par Ibrahim Traoré, qui se rêve en réincarnation du mythe révolutionnaire.

Formule 1 : le pari financier de Kagame peut-il être gagnant ?. En obtenant le retour de la F1 sur le continent, le Rwanda s’offre une vitrine internationale inédite. Et réalise un coup sportif d’envergure dont la facture financière reste un mystère.

Face à l’Éthiopie, que vaut l’armée de l’Érythrée ?. Alors que les tensions entre Asmara et Addis-Abeba ravivent le spectre d’un conflit régional, l’armée érythréenne est sous le feu des projecteurs. Quelles sont ses capacités militaires et son aptitude à tenir sur la durée ? Décryptage.

Éthiopie, Guinée, Bénin… Quels pays d’Afrique affichent la plus forte croissance économique ?. Dans son rapport sur les perspectives économiques régionales, le FMI table sur une croissance du PIB de 4,5 % en 2026 et en 2027 pour l’Afrique subsaharienne, malgré la guerre au Moyen-Orient. Une moyenne qui masque de grands écarts.

Gabon : 10 choses à savoir sur Brigitte Onkanowa, la fidèle ministre de la Défense d’Oligui Nguema. Elle est sans doute la plus discrète des membres du gouvernement gabonais, au sein duquel elle a été reconduite le 11 octobre. Générale de brigade, ex-membre du CTRI, Brigitte Onkanowa ne cesse d’affirmer sa grande loyauté au chef de l’État.

Aérien : avec la reprise de TAP, Lufthansa peut-il bousculer Air France-KLM en Afrique ?. Avec une offre de 1,2 milliard d’euros, Lufthansa intègre le capital de TAP Air Portugal. Une prise de participation qui lui ouvre grand les portes du marché lusophone en Afrique et renforce sa présence face à Air France-KLM.

En Algérie, la chute de Saïd Sayoud, ministre de l’Intérieur et coqueluche des médias. Ses propos polémiques sur le pouvoir d’achat ont scellé son sort mais le ministre, rétrogradé le 13 octobre, paie aussi sa mauvaise gestion des incendies de l’été. Une chute brutale pour un homme qui semblait promis aux plus hautes responsabilités.

Rançons, zakat, territoire : pourquoi la guerre entre le Jnim et l’État islamique s’intensifie au Sahel. Le 10 octobre, de sanglants combats ont opposé le Jnim à l’État islamique au Burkina Faso. Un nouvel épisode dans la rivalité entre les deux groupes jihadistes, sur fond de volonté d’extension et de contrôle des financements, qui menace désormais de déborder au-delà du Sahel.

Carburant de la police : au Cameroun, ce que l’on sait du scandale qui menace Martin Mbarga Nguélé. Le Tribunal criminel spécial enquête sur un présumé détournement de dizaines de milliards de F CFA de carburant par la DGSN. Alors qu’une quarantaine de policiers sont sous les verrous, l’enquête pourrait remonter jusqu’au sommet.

Cameroun anglophone : dix ans après la marche des avocats, un système judiciaire toujours en crise. Dix ans après les manifestations d’avocats anglophones, les revendications initiales ont été largement éclipsées par la lutte indépendantiste et les violences. Si Yaoundé a pris des mesures pour répondre aux griefs, leur mise en œuvre reste incomplète.

Au Maroc, l’opposition comme horizon politique pour le PJD. Laminé en 2021, le parti islamiste a retrouvé une partie de son électorat en 2026, ce qui devrait lui permettre de peser dans les débats tout en restant loin de la coalition au pouvoir. Encore lui faudra-t-il sortir d’une posture limitée à la contestation.

Cacao : pourquoi l’alliance entre la Côte d’Ivoire et le Ghana vacille. L’association nouée en 2018 entre Abidjan et Accra pour peser sur le marché mondial du cacao montre des signes d’essoufflement. Ce tandem vacille alors que les deux pays sont sous pression pour renforcer la traçabilité de leurs fèves.

Au Sénégal, pourquoi Pastef se heurte à répétition à la censure du Conseil constitutionnel. Depuis les législatives de 2024, pas moins de dix textes de loi émanant du parti d’Ousmane Sonko ont été censurés par les « sages ». Décryptage d’un bras de fer institutionnel qui vient encore de rebondir.

En Centrafrique, qui sont les activistes arrêtés après la journée ville morte ?. Cinq responsables de la société civile centrafricaine ont été arrêtés le 15 octobre à Bangui, alors qu’ils s’apprêtaient à s’exprimer sur les suites du mouvement contre la vie chère. L’opposition dénonce une atteinte à l’État de droit.

Cameroun : Samuel Mvondo Ayolo dément de nouvelles rumeurs sur la mort de Paul Biya. Une rumeur annonçant la mort du président Biya a circulé sur les réseaux sociaux. Contacté par Jeune Afrique, Samuel Mvondo Ayolo, le directeur du cabinet civil de la présidence, dément.

Souleymane Diarrassouba : « Avec son nouveau Plan national de développement, la Côte d’Ivoire change d’échelle ». Industrialisation, TGV, recul de la pauvreté : le PND 2026-2030 de la Côte d’Ivoire voit grand. Et le ministre chargé de sa concrétisation défend un programme de 175 milliards d’euros, dont le succès repose largement sur les investisseurs privés.

RDC : ce que l’on sait des perquisitions visant l’entourage de Félix Tshisekedi en Belgique. Plusieurs perquisitions ont été menées en Belgique mercredi 14 octobre, en lien avec une plainte déposée en 2025 contre neuf personnes proches du président congolais. Cette procédure fragilise la relation congolo-belge.

Comment la BDEAC a réussi son pari des marchés internationaux malgré ses fragilités. En mobilisant 222 millions de dollars sur les marchés internationaux de capitaux, la banque régionale entend élargir ses ressources et soutenir le financement des économies de la Cemac. Mais le coût de cette opération et les fragilités financières de l’institution soulignent l’ampleur du chantier qui reste à accomplir.

BGFI : Henri-Claude Oyima réussit son pari de l’introduction en Bourse en deux temps. L’introduction en Bourse de BGFI Holding Corporation franchit un cap avec une deuxième phase largement sursouscrite. Après l’ouverture timide au grand public, les investisseurs professionnels ont accueilli l’opération avec plus d’enthousiasme.

Au Kenya, l’annulation du deal Vodafone-Safaricom menace de peser sur les finances du pays. Le Kenya fait face à une grave crise budgétaire et réglementaire après l’annulation de la vente d’une participation de 15 % de Safaricom à Vodacom. L’État risque de devoir rembourser 1,9 milliard de dollars.

Cameroun : le renseignement d’État, entre guerre des clans et business privé. Officiellement destinés à protéger l’État, les services de renseignement camerounais, affaiblis par la guerre des clans autour de Paul Biya et par la précarité de leurs agents, se mettent régulièrement au service d’intérêts privés. Décryptage en vidéo.

RDC : Joseph Kabila, rebelle après tout. L’ancien président a pris la tête d’une nouvelle rébellion le 12 octobre. Il s’est donné pour mission de renverser Félix Tshisekedi mais court le risque, en faisant le choix des armes, de s’isoler un peu plus.

En Côte d’Ivoire, le PPA-CI et le PDCI face au rouleau compresseur de la justice. Alors que le pouvoir avait promis de « recréer la confiance » avec l’opposition, les convocations devant la justice antiterroriste se multiplient dans l’entourage de Laurent Gbagbo et de Tidjane Thiam, interrogeant la possibilité d’une décrispation politique.

Au Maroc, piliers reconduits et nouveaux entrants : le gouvernement El Mansouri enfin dévoilé. Les principaux arbitrages du nouveau gouvernement nommé ce 16 octobre dessinent une équation familière au sommet de l’État, avec des piliers reconduits, des surprises et une majorité désormais articulée autour de quatre partis.

Au Mali, les dessous de la bataille pour le contrôle de la Maison de la presse. Alors que son second mandat touche à sa fin, Bandiougou Danté se prépare à se représenter à la présidence de la Maison de la presse. Un début de fronde s’organise contre ce proche d’Assimi Goïta, promoteur d’un « traitement patriotique de l’information ».

Cameroun anglophone – Felix Agbor Balla : « Le gouvernement doit comprendre que dialoguer n’est pas une faiblesse ». Dix ans après le déclenchement du conflit dans les régions du Nord-Ouest et du Sud-Ouest (Noso), l’avocat et activiste des droits de l’homme Felix Agbor Balla continue de militer pour « l’autodétermination » des peuples de l’ancien Southern Cameroon, tout en défendant un retour au fédéralisme.

Le Grand Prix d’Afrique au Rwanda, le retour de Joseph Kabila en RDC, le président tchadien à Paris… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur le retour de Joseph Kabila en RDC, dresse le portrait du nouveau président de la Chambre des représentants au Maroc, fait le point sur les relations entre le Tchad et la France, s’interroge sur l’opération F1 du président rwandais et décrypte la montée au capital d’Eramet de Paris.

Lounès Magramane, un diplomate choisi pour succéder à Boualem Boualem au cabinet de la présidence algérienne. Sa nomination a surpris, d’autant que lui-même se voyait plutôt ambassadeur à Paris. C’est pourtant bien Lounès Magramane qui a été choisi pour travailler au plus près du président Tebboune, devenant ainsi un nouvel acteur clé du pouvoir algérien.

Secrétariat général de l’ONU : la menace d’un veto plane sur la candidature de Macky Sall. Lors du sixième tour de scrutin au sein du Conseil de sécurité, tous les candidats, dont l’ex-président sénégalais, se sont retrouvés sous la menace d’un possible veto de la part de plusieurs des cinq membres permanents.

Course à l’hydrogène vert au Maghreb : le Maroc garde-t-il une longueur d’avance ?. Entre les partenariats industriels, les promesses de développement et les milliards d’euros en jeu, la ruée vers le « carburant du futur » s’est-elle vraiment traduite par des projets concrets au Maghreb ? État des lieux en infographies.

Au Nigeria, le milliardaire Aliko Dangote veut faire de l’entrée en Bourse de sa raffinerie de Lagos une opération populaire. Le magnat nigérian des affaires a promis que l’entrée sur la place financière de Lagos de sa raffinerie serait « l’introduction en Bourse du peuple ». Il ambitionne de rassembler 10 millions de souscripteurs.

La formule 1 retourne en Afrique pour la première fois depuis 1993, avec dix ans de Grand Prix au Rwanda « au début des années 2030 ». La formule 1 a officialisé, mardi, sa venue au Rwanda à compter du début de la prochaine décennie. La discipline n’était pas venue sur le continent africain depuis 1993 et le Grand Prix de Kyalami, en Afrique du Sud.

A Paris, Emmanuel Macron et Mahamat Idriss Déby actent le renouveau de leur coopération militaire. Après la brouille provoquée par l’éviction de l’armée française du Tchad, les deux chefs d’Etat se sont rapprochés au cours de l’année écoulée. L’armée française reprend même discrètement pied dans son bastion historique.

Ceuta est « indissociable » de l’Espagne, déclare Felipe VI, en visite historique dans l’enclave. Le roi d’Espagne a affirmé la souveraineté « indiscutable » de l’Espagne sur Ceuta lors d’une visite historique mardi dans l’enclave du nord de l’Afrique, revendiquée par le Maroc.

En RDC, l’ancien président Joseph Kabila prend la tête des rebelles de l’Est. Le nouveau Front pour la refondation de la nation, dirigé par l’ex-chef de l’Etat, dénonce la « tyrannie » de l’actuel président congolais, Félix Tshisekedi.
Niger : les images d’une éruption de pétrole qui provoque l’inquiétude. Selon le ministère du pétrole, il s’agit d’un « incident environnemental d’une gravité exceptionnelle ».

Au Liberia, la création de plus en plus incertaine d’un tribunal pour juger les crimes de guerre. Plus de deux décennies après la fin d’une période de guerres civiles qui a fait 250 000 morts, aucune personne impliquée dans les conflits n’a été jugée au Liberia.

Pour la « gen Z » de Madagascar, un an après le putsch militaire, les lendemains qui déchantent. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (1/4). Lancé en septembre 2025, le mouvement de protestation de la jeunesse malgache, qui a conduit au renversement du président Andry Rajoelina, se heurte aux promesses d’une « refondation » du pouvoir par la junte restée lettre morte.

Le Maroc désapprouve en silence la visite du roi d’Espagne, Felipe VI, à Ceuta et à Melilla. Mohammed VI n’a pas publiquement condamné le déplacement du monarque espagnol dans les enclaves d’Afrique du Nord, mais les signes du mécontentement royal sont là.

A l’île Maurice, un couvre-feu décrété après plusieurs jours de manifestations et de violences, déclenchées par un tir policier. Un policier a grièvement blessé par balle une femme, vendredi, à Camp-Levieux, au sud de Port-Louis. Selon la police, 84 personnes ont été interpellées mardi. Les faits recensés comprennent des pillages, des incendies, des actes de violence et des infractions au couvre-feu.

Navanethem Pillay, Prix Nobel de la paix : sur Gaza, « on nous a accusés d’antisémitisme et de partialité. Mais je sais ce qui est constitutif du crime de génocide ». La juriste sud-africaine a présidé la commission d’enquête du Conseil des droits de l’homme des Nations unies, qui a estimé qu’un génocide se déroulait à Gaza. Dans un entretien au « Monde », elle revient sur son travail, récompensé le 9 octobre par le prix Nobel de la paix.

« Les Damnés de la donnée » : les travailleurs du Sud, invisibilisés et pourtant indispensables au développement de l’IA. Au fil d’une enquête menée auprès d’annotateurs de données à Madagascar, le sociologue Clément Le Ludec met en lumière la centralité du travail de cette main-d’œuvre précarisée et invisibilisée, indispensable au bon fonctionnement des systèmes d’intelligence artificielle.

Ceuta : des ONG accusent l’armée espagnole de « cruauté » à l’égard des migrants et dénoncent le non-respect de leurs droits fondamentaux. Au moment où le roi Felipe VI visitait la ville nord-africaine, mardi, huit ONG ont annoncé la saisine du défenseur du peuple espagnol pour dénoncer l’opacité entourant les retours prétendument volontaires vers le Maroc.

A Madagascar, l’ascension de l’ambitieux colonel Michaël Randrianirina. « Madagascar, un an après le coup d’Etat » (2/4). Depuis son arrivée au pouvoir, le « colonel Michaël » tente de rassurer ses partenaires et multiplie les promesses aux Malgaches, dans l’optique du scrutin présidentiel attendu d’ici à novembre 2027. Des observateurs indépendants alertent toutefois sur une opposition et une justice muselées.

Huit ans après la sortie de « Rafiki », la Cour suprême kényane se prononce sur l’interdiction du film pour « promotion du lesbianisme ». Le long-métrage, qui raconte l’histoire d’amour de deux jeunes femmes à Nairobi, n’avait été autorisé en 2018 que pendant une seule semaine sur décision de justice et avait battu des records au box-office.

Why Israel's claims cannot be accepted at face value Submitted by Faisal Hanif on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 14:00 Any statement from Netanyahu, who has a long and troubling history of twisting the media to serve his agenda, deserves rigorous scrutiny People walk through the entrance to the BBC’s offices in London on 11 November 2025 (AFP) Off Every journalism student learns the same lesson: if your mother says she loves you, check it out. A claim is not a fact until it has been tested, and the more power and self-interest behind it, the more rigorously it should be tested. A BBC Verify investigation has put that principle to a stark test. It identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military said it was investigating allegations that its forces had killed or injured people in Gaza , Lebanon , the occupied West Bank and Israel, but for which no public outcome could be found. Of the 300 cases examined, only 28 had outcomes published on the Israeli army's website. The BBC says it repeatedly approached the military about the cases but received information on only two, both still under review. The findings do not establish that every allegation is true or that every investigation should lead to prosecution. They raise a basic question: what value does "Israel says" have if the public is never told the eventual outcome? Yet in Britain , applying that rule to Israel risks arousing the ire of those whose entire purpose is predicated on promoting or defending the Zionist state narrative. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); MP Ayoub Khan , who has been derided as a “Gaza independent” by the British media for his advocacy against Israel’s genocide in Gaza , was recently denounced by a slew of media and politicians for questioning the speed of Israel’s inquiry into the Flydubai incident that resulted in an emergency landing late last month. Yet Khan’s refusal to simply accept Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s word deserves to be taken seriously, mainly because the ire was not reserved for him alone. The BBC was attacked for adhering to proper editorial standards by putting the word “hero”, used by Netanyahu, in quotation marks in its coverage of the Indian pilot who was stabbed on the Israel-bound flight. Sam Kiley, an experienced foreign editor for The Independent newspaper, was condemned for asking who stood to gain from the incident, daring to suggest that it served Netanyahu as he seeks re-election. Netanyahu had warned of potential attacks ahead of the 27 October vote. After the Flydubai incident, both he and Defence Minister Israel Katz said it proved them right . Asking who benefits from an event, and from how it is framed, is one of the oldest questions in political analysis. The charge against these critics is that doubt itself reveals prejudice. In reality, it is the other way around: credulity is the failure. Pushing a narrative This is not paranoia. It is the historical record. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In 1954, Israeli military intelligence recruited Egyptian Jews to bomb British- and American-owned sites in Egypt , intending to blame the attacks on the Muslim Brotherhood and communists. Israel long denied involvement and only honoured the surviving agents in 2005. Netanyahu's 'eighth front': Israel's billion-dollar war on the truth is failing Read More » After the October 2023 Hamas attack, a spokesperson for Netanyahu said babies had been found decapitated . The claim reached British front pages , and former US President Joe Biden said he saw photos of the beheadings. The White House later had to walk back his claim, which has since been debunked . The pattern is always the same: a confident assertion that rapidly spreads, becoming part of the folklore that seeks to paint Israel as a perpetual victim, before later being shown to be false. “Netanyahu says” is a record of what a politician wants the public to believe. “An Israeli official told us” is the same claim with all accountability stripped out. Neither proves anything. That something was said can be reported, but whether it is true must be shown. Relaying it without that additional work is transcription, not journalism. Remarkably, British news outlets have repeatedly given Israel’s prime minister a megaphone to deride Britain, however absurd his claims. After the UK recognised the state of Palestine , Netanyahu moved to rile an already Islamophobic nation with a jibe about the “ Islamic Republic of Britain ” - a premise that collapses on the facts: Britain is a constitutional monarchy in which Muslims make up around 6 percent of the population. After Britain imposed a settlement trade ban , Netanyahu told the Daily Mail that it had become a “rogue state” under Prime Minister Andy Burnham and accused the Labour government of “appeasing an Islamist-leftist alliance”. He has also reiterated the assertion that Israel helped Britain to thwart an Iranian-backed attack on RAF Fairford, another incident with serious question marks attached. Where the reporting starts All of this raises another question: why does an individual facing an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity command so much space in British media? Why is the quote the headline and the evidence an afterthought? Perhaps Israel’s targeting of major British journalists - including Piers Morgan, Mehdi Hasan and Owen Jones , alongside American commentator Hasan Piker - offers one explanation. All have been, in various ways, critics of Israel’s killing of Palestinian civilians and journalists. Given its well-documented killings of journalists, Israel does not appear to tolerate dissent. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, Israel has killed more than 200 journalists and media workers since October 2023. The committee notes that Israel has repeatedly accused journalists of militant involvement “without producing credible evidence”. It is reasonable for anyone to ask whether Israel is the ally its supporters describe. Journalists cannot help the public to answer that question if they simply relay its statements verbatim The cost of deference is self-censorship, and the evidence of it is stark. The Centre for Media Monitoring found the BBC gave a rationale for Israeli military actions in 75 percent of articles on attacks or suffering in Gaza, compared with 17 percent for Russian actions in Ukraine . It challenged Israel’s justifications in 41 percent of cases, compared with 55 percent for Russia . The centre also found that the BBC reported the deaths of just 6 percent of 176 Palestinian journalists killed by the Israeli army, compared with 62 percent of journalists in Ukraine. With independent journalists barred from Gaza, the world relies on Palestinian reporters and statements from Israeli officials to understand what is happening. If qualifying an Israeli claim brings complaints and political attacks, the response is often silence. It is reasonable for anyone to ask whether Israel is the ally its supporters describe. Journalists cannot help the public answer that question if they simply relay its statements verbatim. Their job is to scrutinise and challenge. “Israel says” is where the reporting starts, not where it ends. While brave voices in the trade continue to speak out after three years of genocide in Gaza, “Israel says” remains the routinely used phrase. This is exactly when questions should sharpen. When trusted media outlets decline to ask the obvious questions, rumours fill the gap. Every question a mainstream newsroom fails to investigate is a question handed to someone who will answer it badly. try { if (window.ResizeObserver && iframe.contentDocument && iframe.contentDocument.body) { new ResizeObserver(updateHeight).observe(iframe.contentDocument.body); } } catch (e) {} } })(); The government on Friday reduced the price of petrol by Rs3.93 per litre, but left that of high-speed diesel (HSD) unchanged at Rs396.96. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs386.30 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices are applicable from Oct 17 (Saturday) to Oct 19 (Monday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm and fuel allocations for official vehicles has been cut by 50 per cent for three months. On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also announced a “ relief scheme ” for users of motorcycles, autos and vehicles of up to 800cc to “alleviate the burden” of rising global oil prices. Previously, on July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Political party head upset over not being appointed KP governor, claims Naqvi. LAHORE: Without taking any names, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Friday claimed that the “head of a party” was “extremely upset” about not being appointed the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “The head of a party is extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship,” Naqvi alleged while speaking to journalists in Lahore. He was seemingly referring to Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, who has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in KP. This politician, Naqvi said, had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”. “These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged. He said such politicians had little justification for criticising others now, particularly after having benefitted from the same system they currently denounced. “Political differences are part of politics. But instead of using inappropriate language and making allegations, political leaders should speak on the basis of arguments and facts,” the minister said. Naqvi’s remarks come days after the Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move has drawn criticism from the opposition, including Fazl, as well as Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan. In the days preceding the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI which was in power in KP — had remained high since jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release. Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results while Fazl was cast as the man who could defuse heightening tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides had held separate meetings with Fazl, reportedly for his intervention to help break the deadlock in the negotiations. And after the federal government imposed governor’s rule in KP, Fazl accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts for mediation. On Thursday, Fazl again censured the Centre, accusing it of depriving the provinces of their rights. Addressing a rally in Multan, he further recalled that his party had expressed reservations over the merger of tribal areas into KP after the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018. “We were not against the merger, but we said that it was an issue of the political future of the people of tribal areas,” he said, alleging that the people of those areas were not consulted on the merger. Raising doubts over the Centre’s reasoning behind imposing governor’s rule that there was a lack of cooperation on counterterrorism, he said the security situation in Balochistan was worse than it was in KP. He alleged governor’s rule was not imposed in Balochistan because the province’s chief minister “praises you”. “In KP, the PTI is in power. […] Where opposition is in power, you topple it. And the resources of former tribal areas, which had become part of the province, you have taken control of them by imposing emergency,” he remarked. During his interaction with journalists on Friday, Naqvi also spoke about the former tribal areas. He was critical of concerns regarding the allocation of resources to former tribal areas. “When the districts … were not getting their rightful share for years, why were these people silent?” he questioned. The minister commented that political leaders had failed to speak out for the rights of the people of the former tribal areas at the time, and stressed that the rights and resources of the people of those areas should be treated as an issue above political interests. Naqvi further said KP was facing serious security challenges , and called on political leaders to play a constructive role in restoring peace and combating terrorism. “Instead of fanning the flames and creating unrest, political leaders should play their role in restoring law and order and eliminating terrorism,” he said, maintaining that the province needed peace, stability and collective efforts rather than political confrontation. Separately, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz railed against Fazl in a post on X. She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitate terrorism — an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism. She added it was unfortunate that he was supporting the party instead of “holding those accountable who were responsible for the ruin of KP because of their incompetence, ineptitude and corruption”. She also criticised Fazl for his remarks about Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, seemingly referring to his comments during the Multan address about the centralisation of power. She concluded her statement by saying that no one but the PTI was “responsible for the end of its government in KP”.

SC questions ‘lofty expectations’ in criminal cases. ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court has taken exception to a prevalent practice in criminal trials which, it said, defied normal human capability and natural perception, and observed that eyewitness accounts should reflect genuine human observation rather than physically impossible details concerning firearm incidents. “To expect mathematical precision regarding the number of firearm shots or the exact location of injuries from eyewitnesses exposed to a horrific event is both unnatural and impractical,” observed Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim in a judgement he authored. Justice Ibrahim was a member of a three-judge SC bench headed by Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar, which took up criminal appeals filed by Muhammad Azhar and the state challenging a Sept 13, 2021, Lahore High Court, Bahawalpur, ruling. The SC, however, rejected the criminal appeal in the 2017 murder case, upholding Muhammad Azhar’s conviction for killing Sakhian Bibi. Expecting mathematical precision from eyewitnesses exposed to traumatic events is ‘unnatural and impractical’, Justice Ibrahim holds “In criminal jurisprudence, human behaviour should not be subjected to a fixed formula, nor should every witness be expected to react to, observe or retain events in an identical manner,” the judgement said. The incident occurred on Jan 11, 2017, when the appellant allegedly entered the victim’s home armed with a .30-bore pistol, seeking the complainant’s uncle in connection with ongoing civil litigation. When the victim said her uncle was not present, the petitioner opened fire, discharging five shots that struck her chest, abdomen and right arm. The additional sessions judge, Minch­inabad, convicted the petitioner and sentenced him to death, with Rs200,000 in compensation payable to the legal heirs. The LHC, Bahawalpur, later commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, prompting both the petitioner’s appeal and the state’s petition for enhancement of the sentence. “We frequently observe prosecution witnesses deposing with microscopic precision, as if watching events in slow motion, describing the exact trajectory and anatomical landing site of each individual bullet discharged from a firearm,” the judgement observed. It is humanly impossible for an eyewitness exposed to the sudden terror and high stress of a deadly attack to track a high-velocity bullet in mid-air and confirm precisely where each shot strikes the victim’s body, it noted. The judge emphasised that every individual reacts differently to a sudden traumatic situation: while one person may observe details, another may freeze or lose awareness of the occurrence. In a sudden traumatic event, when multiple gunshots ring out within a few seconds and a mother is murdered in cold blood before her son’s eyes, a minor divergence regarding the exact number of firearm shots or the precise entry point of each bullet is evidence of natural and reasonable human limitations, he observed. It is common knowledge that most individuals are not frequently exposed to dangerous, life-threatening situations, and the sudden brandishing of a weapon induces an atmosphere of shock and fear, according to the judgement. In such stressful encounters, human cognitive and perceptual capacities are severely impaired, the judgement said. To substantiate this point, it cited renowned cognitive psychologist Elizabeth Loftus, who had stated that a witness confronted by an assailant brandishing a firearm involuntarily fixes their attention almost exclusively on the weapon itself. This cognitive phenomenon, known as “attentional tunnelling”, limits the observer’s capacity to process or recall surrounding details, the judgement said. Trial courts should bear these limitations in mind when scrutinising eyewitness accounts claiming microscopic accuracy despite the stressful circumstances, Justice Ibrahim observed. The judgement expected lower courts to assess witnesses in the light of the circumstances of each case, observing that, under the golden principles of criminal jurisprudence, no piece of evidence should be considered in isolation; rather, all evidence should be evaluated cumulatively alongside other available evidence. Terrorism has no link with Baloch values, says Bugti. QUETTA: Condemning a recent terrorist attack in Dasht Goran, Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti said on Friday that the government had always maintained that such acts have nothing to do with Baloch values, rather were purely terrorism. He was responding to points raised by lawmakers on various issues in the Balochistan Assembly. Earlier, MPA Mir Jahanzeb Mengal, speaking on a point of order, said that “Fitna al-Hindustan” had attacked the house of Mir Qambar Khan Mengal in Dasht Goran at 6am. He said the firing continued until 4pm, leaving Ahmed Nawaz Mengal dead and another person injured. “This is my house, and my mother and sisters are there. This is not Balochiyat. Condemns Dasht Goran attack; directs district administrations to inspect school and college buildings in Balochistan CM Bugti said the people of the province were increasingly realising that the Baloch were being pushed into a futile conflict. “What kind of tradition allows the killing of passengers and unarmed people?” he asked. Rabies death toll rises to 40 in Sindh after elderly man dies. KARACHI: A septuagenarian man died of rabies at a local hospital, raising this year’s tally from the deadly infectious disease in Sindh to 40, officials said on Friday. They said that the victim, a resident of Baldia Town, was bitten by a dog over three weeks back but he did not seek preventive treatment. He passed away at the Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre (JPMC) on Thursday. The JPMC has recorded over 11,000 dog bite cases and 10 deaths from rabies this year, including the latest one. Recently, a 38-year-old man hailing from Diplo, Tharparkar, and a 12-year-old boy hailing from Hyderabad died of rabies. Experts say a large number of rabies cases go unreported as patients use home remedies or turn to faith healers for “treatment”. They emphasised the need for public awareness, humane control of the dog population and the availability of appropriate treatment in hospitals. While dog bites account for the majority of rabies cases, bites from potentially rabid wild animals can also transmit the virus. After exposure, early wound cleansing, timely rabies vaccination and the administration of rabies immunoglobulin, if needed, can effectively prevent the disease, which is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms appear. Pakistan rules out unconditional talks with Afghanistan. • Demands verifiable mechanism to end terrorist attacks from Afghan soil • FO says no formal Russian mediation initiative currently under discussion • Warns India that any future aggression will be met with a stronger response ISLAMABAD: The Foreign Office on Friday said that talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional, while rejecting suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour and saying it would welcome sincere efforts by friendly countries to help resolve the dispute. “Pakistan is not shying away from discussions or dialogue, including with representatives of Afghanistan. Pakistan would welcome any sincere efforts by friendly countries that could help address our legitimate security concerns and promoting regional peace and stability,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly media briefing. The statement came as Russia recently renewed its readiness to mediate between the two countries, although Islamabad denied the existence of any such initiative. “At present, I am not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion,” Mr Khan said, adding that Pakistan remained open to engagement that produced tangible results. Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement. Moscow’s special envoy for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, had earlier this month made this suggestion after the latest round of the Moscow Format consultations on Oct 5 ended without a joint communiqué because of differences between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban delegations over references to terrorist networks operating from Afghanistan. Mr Khan said the absence of an agreed statement at the Moscow Format meeting reflected the Afghan delegation’s unwillingness to accept language on terrorist networks that had been agreed in the previous year’s document. “The fact that no joint communiqué was issued after the Moscow Format is self-evident that Afghanistan did not accept the formulation which had been acceptable until last year particularly about presence of terrorist network in Afghanistan. This shows that there is reluctance on the part of Afghanistan that terrorism is originating from its soil,” he said. The failure to get a joint communique highlighted the central obstacle to normalising relations, which is Pakistan’s demand for action against the Tehreek-i-Taliban Paki­stan (TTP) and other terrorist groups it says are using Afghan territory to launch attacks across the border. The Taliban authorities have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while rejecting Islamabad’s allegations that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan. The dispute has frustrated international efforts to reduce tensions. Qatar and Turkiye last October helped broker a ceasefire, but subsequent round of talks failed to reach a lasting settlement. Saudi Arabia separately hosted discussions, while China held talks between the two sides in Urumqi in April. None of these efforts could resolve the disagreement over terrorist groups and the measures needed to prevent cross border attacks. Pakistan’s position, Mr Khan said, was that dialogue would need to be backed by an arrangement that could verify whether terrorist activity against the country had stopped. “The talks will not be unconditional. Pakistan has been raising the issue of terrorism emanating from Afghanistan at different forums. Unfortunately, the Taliban regime has been taking one step forward and one step backward,” Mr Khan emphasised. “Pakistan has only one demand that there should be a verifiable mechanism to ensure complete cessation of terrorist activities emanating from Afghan soil against Pakistan,” he said. ‘Stronger response’ Mr Khan reminded India of the response it faced during last year’s military confrontation and warned that any future aggression would be met with an even stronger response. FO reaction came after Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh a day earlier threatened a bigger strike in the event of any future terrorist attacks. Singh, while speaking at National Defence Conclave 2026 in Delhi, recalled Operation Sindoor and said that it marked a decisive response to terrorism. He also referred to earlier Indian military operations. “We reject and condemn the Indian Defence Minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risks its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” Mr Khan said. “We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a fitting reply to Indian aggression,” the FO spokesperson said. Mr Khan urged New Delhi to draw lessons from the previous confrontation and avoid further escalation. “India should draw an appropriate lesson from the last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.
