Imran being forced into Benazir, Nawaz-style deal, claims Achakzai. • Demands authorities disclose whereabouts of Sohail Afridi • Mengal says those claiming to be framers of Constitution are ‘trampling it’ • TTAP alliance challenges governor’s rule, emergency before Peshawar High Court PESHAWAR: PTI fou­nder Imran Khan is being forced into an agreement, similar to those given to former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto, Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai claimed on Friday. The opposition leader was referring to the arrangements whereby the two former PMs went into self-imposed exile following their respective ousters. Mr Sharif, who was ousted and imprisoned following a military coup by then-army chief Pervez Musharraf, left the country in 2000 following a deal negotiated by Saudi and Lebanese leaders. Benazir, meanwhile, voluntarily went into self-exile after her party lost the 1997 general elections following her dismissal by then-president Farooq Leg­hari. At the time, her husband Asif Zardari was imprisoned over corruption charges, and was finally released in 2004. “The same is happening today with the PML-N and PPP in government,” Mr Achakzai said at a news conference at the Peshawar High Court (PHC). He was accompanied by Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) leaders Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas. He said they were in contact with all opposition parties and would soon convene a multi-party conference. Resigning from the assemblies was also an option, he said, adding that they had submitted their demands in response to the offer of negotiations. “Nowhere in the world is a prisoner denied meetings,” he said, calling for the withdrawal of the “wrong amen­dment”, empow­erment of parliament and the formation of an independent commission to ensure transparent elections. He said no problem could be resolved until parliament was empowered. Expressing concern over the whereabouts of the KP chief minister and other lawmakers, he demanded that the authorities disclose the chief minister’s whereabouts, calling it their constitutional right to know. “We stand with the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The people of this province have the first right over its minerals. Regardless of political affiliation, everyone must unite for the homeland,” he said, adding that they would be safer if the country survived. Mr Mengal said those claiming to be the framers of the Constitution were trampling on it. He questioned the imposition of governor’s rule in KP on the grounds of terrorism, asking whether military operations had improved or worsened conditions in Balochistan. He said KP’s elected chief minister had been removed, while the provincial assembly speaker and a minister were missing. Those who had won the general elections on Form 47 had become members of the National Assembly, he alleged, adding that the system could not continue this way. Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, said lawlessness had reached its peak. “You cannot run a country, yet you have occupied a province,” he told reporters, adding that a cabinet member had himself acknowledged that the system had collapsed. TTAP challenges governor’s rule Meanwhile on Friday, TTAP leaders challenged the proclamation of emergency and imposition of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa before the PHC, seeking to have the measures declared unconstitutional and illegal. The constitutional petition was jointly filed by TTAP Chairman Mehmood Khan Achakzai, Vice Chairman Senator Raja Nasir Abbas, Balochistan National Party-Mengal chief Sardar Akhtar Mengal and Sindh Taraqi Pasand Party leader Syed Zainul Abideen through Advocates Muazzam Butt and Baseem Ahmad Siddiqui. The court was requested to declare the Oct 11 proclamation of emergency, issued under Articles 232(1) and 234 of the Constitution, unconstitutional and without lawful authority, arguing that the required constitutional conditions had not been met or that the measures exceeded the powers conferred by the Constitution. They challenged the purported transfer of the KP Assembly’s legislative powers to parliament and the displacement of the elected chief minister and provincial cabinet. They also sought the annulment of executive orders and notifications that depended on the validity of the proclamation. The petitioners also challenged the establishment of the purported KP Advisory Council and Area Development Secretariat, arguing that these bodies could not exercise powers beyond those conferred by the Constitution or replace established provincial institutions. They questioned any purported suspension of constitutional provisions, including Article 175(3), unless expressly authorised by the Constitution. The petitioners sought annulment of the Oct 11 notification concerning the deployment of armed forces in the province to the extent where it violated Article 245, failed to meet constitutional requirements or exceeded the scope of the provision. They also sought directions to ensure that elected representatives and constitutionally established institutions in KP were not unlawfully prevented from performing their functions and that no elected representative was detained or restrained except in accordance with the Constitution. Pending a final decision, they sought interim relief to suspend or restrain the impugned measures to prevent the displacement of elected institutions, transfer of legislative authority, creation of parallel executive structures or other irreparable harm, subject to the court’s assessment of constitutional requirements and public safety. Millions may be forced to move as climate change hits South Asia: UN. NEW DELHI: Climate change is threatening livelihoods and forcing people from their homes across South Asia, but technology and government action could help limit the damage, the UN migration chief said on Friday. Rising seas, flooding and drought threaten homes and farmland, Amy Pope, director general of the International Organisation for Migration (IOM), said during a visit to New Delhi. In the Himalayas, she pointed to Nepal’s Aug 26 disaster, when a mountain and glacier collapse triggered deadly flooding, where IOM sent humanitarian aid to help. In a worst-case scenario, up to 40.5 million people in South Asia may be forced to move by 2050, according to IOM. Rising seas, flooding, drought threaten homes and farmland, warns IOM chief “When they can’t produce food, when they can’t feed their livestock, it increases the likelihood of displacement,” said Pope. “The first adaptation is often for people to move.” Pope said climate change was also accelerating urbanisation in India. “As people seek shelter from heat, they’re going into urban centres,” she said. Migration as a tool The risks are particularly acute in South Asia, where a vast population and limited resources leave many communities vulnerable. “There’s a lack of urgency globally about the risks that vulnerable communities are facing,” Amy Pope said, warning that funding to help residents prepare for climate change remained inadequate. “The cost of a humanitarian disaster is in the billions. The cost of investing in some of the resilience measures can be far less,” she said. Better data and artificial intelligence could help governments identify communities at risk before disaster strikes, Pope added. “With the advancements in AI forecasting, you can now better anticipate those communities that are at high risk of displacement,” the IOM chief said. By combining weather forecasts with information about local livelihoods, authorities can identify which communities most need help. “If you know a community is at risk, we don’t need to wait until they’re displaced to respond,” she said. Measures could include improving farming methods, training people for other jobs and, where necessary, relocating communities repeatedly hit by floods or drought. Finding the money for such programmes is a major obstacle, Pope said, with governments often struggling to navigate the systems available to fund climate adaptation. India’s investments in early-warning systems, disaster response and technology offer grounds for optimism, she said. But no government can meet the scale of the challenge alone. International migration can also help people earn a living while filling labour shortages abroad. However, Pope warned that growing demand for workers must be matched by safe, legal routes to employment. Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

‘Pakistan among 10 states bearing brunt of hunger crisis’. ISLAMABAD: Pakistan is among the 10 countries bearing the brunt of the global hunger crisis, with climate-related disasters, economic hardship, displacement and shrinking humanitarian funding pushing vulnerable communities deeper into food insecurity, according to a new report released by international humanitarian organisation Action Against Hunger. The report, Ten Largest Global Food Crises, released on Friday in connection with World Food Day, warns that an estimated 10.6 million people in Pakistan will require humanitarian assistance in 2026, despite ongoing recovery efforts and improvements in some macroeconomic indicators. Globally, approximately 177 million people live in the 10 countries where hunger is most concentrated, while acute hunger has doubled over the past decade, affecting 266 million people across 47 countries, says the report. The countries facing the largest food crises are Nigeria, Congo, Sudan, Yemen, Afghan­istan, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Pakistan, South Sudan and Syria. Report sees 10.6m Pakistanis needing humanitarian assistance in 2026 In Pakistan, persistent poverty, high food inflation, rising living costs, limited employment opportunities and declining household incomes continue to erode families’ purchasing power. Unfavourable agricultural prices and broader economic instability have further undermined livelihoods, leaving millions struggling to afford adequate food. As humanitarian needs outstrip available resources, vulnerable households are increasingly resorting to damaging coping strategies, including cutting food consumption, selling productive assets and withdrawing children from school to cope with financial pressures. The report cautions that these measures may provide temporary relief but can deepen poverty, undermine children’s education and nutrition, and weaken families’ ability to recover from future shocks. Limited access to healthcare, nutrition services, clean water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and social protection is compounding the crisis, particularly in rural and disaster-affected areas. Persistent poverty and acute malnutrition remain major drivers of humanitarian needs, while cuts to support services and livelihood programmes are further eroding community resilience. Pakistan’s exposure to climate-related disasters remains a major source of food insecurity. Recurrent floods, droughts, heatwaves, glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and increasingly erratic monsoon rainfall have damaged infrastructure, reduced agricultural production and weakened livestock-dependent livelihoods. Crop losses and prolonged dry spells have also increased households’ reliance on markets for food at a time when many families have limited purchasing power. Several districts are experiencing prolonged drought conditions, adding to concerns about agricultural output and rural incomes. The report warns that seasonal hardships can intensify these pressures. The lean season from December 2025 to March 2026, characterised in some areas by extended winter conditions and heavy snowfall, was identified as a period likely to worsen food insecurity by restricting access to markets and essential resources. Insecurity and regional tensions are adding another layer of pressure to Pakistan’s already fragile food security situation. According to the report, localised insecurity in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan continues to disrupt livelihoods, restrict access to markets and hamper humanitarian operations. Trump waives new Russia sanctions as Ukraine ties slump. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia’s energy revenues, marking a new low in Washington’s ties with war-torn Ukraine. The move came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged EU leaders to keep financing Kyiv’s fight with nearly $80 billion more next year, insisting he was standing up for his country as Trump’s support slumped. The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — had allowed Trump the authority to impose duties up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. The legislation, which Trump signed into law last month, targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. Trump’s reversal on the Russia sanctions comes after he struck a deal with Putin to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel into global markets. The US president’s war in Iran has sparked crippling oil shortages and price spikes, creating major headwinds for his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections next month. Asked if he was being made a scapegoat for Trump’s domestic woes ahead of the vote, Zelensky just smiled . “This is my answer,” he told journalists in Brussels, after an extended pause. In another sign of strained relations between the United States and Ukraine, Trump branded Kyiv’s actions a “disgrace” after Zelensky ordered his forces to resume strikes on Russian refineries. “I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelensky said after talks with EU leaders. The breakdown between Trump and Zelensky has fuelled fears that the US leader is siding with Moscow. Those concerns have been heightened by disruptions to a critical US-provided satellite system that has hampered Ukraine’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments. Ukraine uses technology from Elon Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, but the tech billionaire — a virulent Zelensky critic — said his company was not behind the disruption, while a US official denied any intervention by Trump. ‘Increase pressure’ European leaders put on a show of unity with Zelensky as he grappled with Trump. “This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions,” European Council chief Antonio Costa said. “Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that “the situation in Ukraine is currently truly dire, with numerous Russian attacks and a tense relationship between Ukraine and the US.” “It is crucial that we, as Europe, demonstrate our unconditional support for them today – and explore what additional steps we can take,” he said. Zelensky asked the bloc — Ukraine’s biggest international backer — to provide more Patriot missiles to shoot down Russian missiles and come up with an extra 70 billion euros ($79 billion) in support next year to help Kyiv keep fighting. Ukraine has been struggling to shoot down Russian missiles and has been left scrambling to boost defences ahead of winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20C and Moscow’s attacks threaten electricity, heating and water systems. Russian strikes on the southern cities of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia killed a 64-year-old man and at least 17 people, including an 11-year-old girl, Ukrainian authorities said Saturday. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that Zelensky’s 70-billion euro plea “has to be covered” and urged partner countries to “step in” and help. French President Emmanuel Macron said Kyiv’s backers will analyse the demand, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the European Union will discuss it before the end of the year. The EU is currently paying out instalments of a 90-billion-euro loan for Kyiv that was set to help cover funding to the end of 2027. But Ukrainian authorities have warned they will still face a major budget black hole as Russian strikes have battered the country’s economy. The talks on new funding have reignited calls for the EU to tap around 200 billion euros in frozen Russian central bank assets to fund Ukraine. “The frozen assets are there. That’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine,” said Latvian premier Andris Kulbergs. But there seems little momentum on that front as Belgium, where most of the funds are held, remains opposed.

Over 340 children killed in Gaza since ceasefire, says Unicef. UNITED NATIONS: More than 340 children have been reportedly killed and hundreds more injured in Gaza since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was announced, the UN Children’s Fund (Unicef) said on Friday, warning that children continue to face grave risks despite the truce. “For families mourning the loss of their children , those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire,” Unicef spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva. The Unicef noted that five boys and two girls had been reported killed in Gaza over the preceding two weeks, while at least 33 children were seriously injured in air strikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the territory. Two other boys died from injuries sustained earlier, Pires said. Around 800,000 children remain displaced, most living in tents or damaged buildings, while an estimated 60,000 have lost one or both parents during the war or since the ceasefire, according to the Unicef. Nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover from the effects of the conflict. The agency called on the parties to the conflict to uphold the ceasefire, comply with UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and meet their obligations under international humanitarian law. “Above all, we need to listen to the voices of children in Gaza,” the Unicef said, stressing that recovery meant more than survival. Children needed to return to school, spend time with friends and family, have dignified shelter, play safely and receive healthcare, the agency said. “Gaza’s children have suffered far too much, for far too long,” it added. The agency stressed the need to maintain an uninterrupted flow of humanitarian and commercial supplies into Gaza, following reports that private traders had halted cooperation with Israeli authorities over the entry of commercial trucks carrying food. Pires recalled that supplies had been unable to enter Gaza before the ceasefire, when famine was declared by UN-backed food security experts. “We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he said. Despite the continuing hardship, Unicef has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including through more than 200 learning centres it supports. The agency has also provided digital cash assistance to more than 380,000 people and safe water to 1.2 million people.

Anthropic proposes law regulating AI to US lawmakers. Anthropic, the creator of the AI assistant Claude, confirmed on Friday it is circulating a draft bill among US lawmakers aimed at regulating artificial intelligence to address the lack of federal legislation on the risks posed by the new technology. According to the draft, first reported by Politico on Friday, Washington could block a model’s release or use if there is an imminent risk of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, or causing more than $1 billion in damages, but only with a judge’s approval. A company spokesperson told AFP that the proposal “grants the federal government the ability to block or deter dangerous deployments of the most powerful models.” “It requires frontier developers to test the most powerful models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program,” the spokesperson said. AI policy in the US under President Donald Trump has relied primarily on voluntary industry pledges and executive orders intended to sustain an AI boom that tech leaders say is driving the country’s economy. Congress, politically divided and heavily lobbied by Big Tech, has yet to pass a federal AI law, and is out of session until after next month’s midterm elections. Security became a hot topic after recent revelations of security incidents caused by AI agents — autonomous software that operates without constant human supervision — that escaped the control of their developers. Anthropic, which was banned from the Pentagon by the Trump administration in February, was forced by Washington in June to suspend its most advanced models for nearly three weeks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry last month to slow down development, fearing that a group of AI agents could take control of “the entire internet” within six to 12 months. Trump has dismissed the numerous calls to slow down the technology as “negative forces.” The proposed legislation would also override certain state laws, such as those in force in California. Anthropic wrote in June that “absent a strong federal law, states should retain full authority to legislate.” Charlie Bullock of the Institute for Law & AI think tank praised the proposal as “pretty reasonable,” and “more than other frontier labs have done.” But he said on X he considers it “weaker” than the FRONTIER Act, a competing bill introduced in the House of Representatives this summer.

Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations. Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak , a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates. Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organisation said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year. So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94 per cent of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said. Mohammad Nasir Ali, 40, strokes the forehead of his seven-year-old son, Adil Ahmed, who has been admitted to the overcrowded measles isolation ward of Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital for treatment, in Sylhet, Bangladesh, September 12, 2026. —Reuters Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95pc, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped. A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents. “This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University. Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said. Bilkis and other parents take care of their children receiving treatment at the overcrowded measles isolation ward of Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital after developing symptoms of measles, in Sylhet, Bangladesh, September 12, 2026. —Reuters “The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said. Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article. ‘They came only after i Buried my son’ In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived. His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said. Urmi, 19, mourns as her 11-month-old son, Mohammad, deteriorates while receiving treatment in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) of a hospital in Narayanganj, Bangladesh, May 11, 2026. —Reuters Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition. In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine. “No health worker came to tell us,” her father said. Amin Mia, 26, and Sajina Begum, 27, adore their four-year-old daughter Fatima, after losing their 34-month-old son, Arman Hossain, to suspected measles during a recent deadly outbreak, in Sunamganj, Bangladesh, September 15, 2026. —Reuters In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90pc, while second-dose coverage was 86pc, several percentage points below the 95pc needed for herd immunity. The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025. It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100pc of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

Pakistan has enough energy supplies to last through November, planning for winter spike: Aurangzeb. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Saturday told AFP that Pakistan had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the US-Israeli war on Iran , but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were “worrying” for the country’s longer-term economic outlook. In an interview on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF)-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Aurangzeb said the country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike. “The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan,” he said. “We’ve had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries.” He added that unless the government saw “an absolute dire need”, it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments. Since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran’s retaliatory action has targeted Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies. With Yemen’s civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure , including energy facilities and airports, in recent days. Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy. “What is now [the] worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit,” he said. “I, to be very honest, I don’t know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer.” ‘Pushback’ Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the IMF, the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default. It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund — at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts — since gaining independence in 1947. With global debt stocks running high, the IMF has called at this year’s annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis. “Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while,” Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile. The country’s tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts. Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained “room for improvement” on increasing income tax collection as well. He said the government’s reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests. “Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback,” he said. The minister is leading Pakistan’s delegation and is holding high-level engagements with international financial institutions, finance ministers, policymakers and investors. Yesterday, he met World Bank Group President Ajay Banga at a dinner hosted by the Thai prime minister on the sidelines of the annual meetings, state-run Pakistan TV reported. “The occasion provided an opportunity for informal interaction alongside the high-level engagements at the annual meetings”, it said. Pakistan remains engaged with the IMF under a $7 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and a $1.4bn Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). The two reached a staff-level agreement after a fourth review under the EFF and a third review under the RSF earlier this month, which qualified Pakistan to draw about $1.2bn from the Fund’s resources.

Any miscalculation by adversaries will invite response beyond their ‘imagination, calculation’, warns CNSC. Commander National Strategic Command (CNSC) General Aamer Raza warned the country’s adversaries on Saturday that “any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or the calculation of the initiator”. “To those who harbour hostile designs across our borders, our stance remains resolute and unambiguous. There is no space for conflict or war in a nuclearised environment and any miscalculation will be met with a response far beyond the imagination or calculation of the initiator,” warned the commander of Pakistan’s strategic command. Addressing the passing-out parade of cadets of the 154th Long Course at the Pakistan Military Academy (PMA), Kakul, he reiterated that the country’s armed forces stood ready to “defend every inch of the motherland” at all costs. The warning by the strategic command commander comes after provocative remarks by Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh. He had warned Pakistan on Thursday that any “fresh terrorist activity from across the border would invite a strike even bigger than the last time”, according to Indian news agency ANI . Gen Raza said that in the “post-truth era”, the country’s adversaries sought to drive a wedge between the people of Pakistan and its armed forces through “calculated disinformation and narrative warfare”. He elaborated that following the failure of Operation Sindoor , the adversaries sought to “fracture Pakistan’s social cohesion and state infrastructure” through an escalation of proxy terrorism and sub-conventional warfare. Gen Raza further said that hostile elements continue to attempt to exploit the country’s internal vulnerabilities to “cultivate proxy instruments against our national unity”. “You must understand unequivocally that this conflict is waged directly against the security of our people and the freedom secured by the supreme sacrifices of our predecessors.” The strategic command commander added that the people of Pakistan must remain acutely mindful that safeguarding the country’s unity, sovereign integrity and territorial inviolability is “an absolute imperative, which we shall uphold at all costs and under every circumstance”. Addressing the newly-graduated cadets, he added that they must remain steadfast in their duty and unwavering in their resolve and “immune to malicious propaganda and narrative warfare”. Pakistan’s role in regional peace Gen Raza said the recent shifts in global geopolitics, particularly amid the escalating conflict in the Middle East , had “once again underscored Pakistan’s pivotal strategic importance on the international stage”. “Our decisive role in restoring regional stability, exemplified by the landmark Islamabad Accord, demonstrates our enduring commitment to peace and diplomacy,” he said, adding that the Makkah Accord was “a sequel to the same vision of durable peace”. Expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people, he said: “Our hearts remain heavily burdened by the ongoing tragedy in Palestine, where innocent men, women and children continue to endure unspeakable hardship and systematic oppression.” He said the Pakistani nation stood “resolute and unwavering in its diplomatic, moral and political support” for the Palestinians. “The persistent violence, targeting of non-combatants and destruction of civilian infrastructure are profound violations of international law and a grave stain on the collective conscience of humanity,” Gen Raza added. “Today, the world witnesses increasing volatility, where grey-zone warfare and hybrid threats attempt to destabilise sovereign states,” he added. FO condemns Singh’s ‘provocative remarks’ A day earlier, the Foreign Office (FO) condemned Singh’s “provocative remarks” threatening aggression against Pakistan, saying such statements highlighting the neighbouring country’s “hegemonistic mindset”. “Pakistan rejects and condemns the Indian defence minister’s provocative remarks entailing a threat of Indian aggression against Pakistan. Such reckless statements reflect India’s hegemonistic mindset and the risk its belligerent posture poses to regional peace and stability in South Asia,” FO spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said. “We wish to remind India of the consequences of its military aggression in May last year, when Pakistan demonstrated both its capability and resolve to defend its sovereignty and territorial integrity and gave a befitting response and reply to Indian aggression,” he said, referring to the brief military conflict between the two countries. He said that there should be “no ambiguity” that Pakistan remained fully prepared to safeguard its “sovereignty and territorial integrity” against any “ill-advised aggression”. Haider said Pakistan’s “restraint and commitment to peace” should not be mistaken for weakness, warning that any aggression would be met with a “forceful response”. “India should draw an appropriate lesson from last year’s experience and abandon its belligerent posture and dangerous rhetoric and act with responsibility for lasting peace in the region,” he said.

5.9-magnitude earthquake jolts Balochistan's Khuzdar. A magnitude 5.9 earthquake jolted Balochistan’s Khuzdar district on Saturday, according to the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD). The quake occurred at 10:07am at a depth of 25 kilometres, the PMD said in a post on X. The PMD said the earthquake’s epicentre was located 48 kilometres northwest of Khuzdar, at latitude 28.02 degrees north and longitude 66.20 degrees east. The department released the seismic data through its Islamabad office. In August, an earthquake of magnitude 4.8 jolted parts of Balochistan, including Zhob and Chaman. According to the seismological centre, the earthquake was recorded at a depth of 15 kilometres, with its epicentre located 122km northeast of Zhob. The tremors caused fear and panic among residents, with many people coming out of their homes and reciting verses from the Holy Quran. No loss of life or property damage had been reported from the earthquake. In July, a moderate earthquake of magnitude 4 struck Quetta, Ziarat, Harnai, and surrounding areas, forcing people to come out of their homes and take refuge in open places. However, no casualty or damage to property was reported from the areas hit by the earthquake. Pakistan falls on three major tectonic plates — the Arabian, Euro-Asian and Indian — which create five seismic zones under the country. The intersection of multiple fault lines means that tectonic movements remain a frequent occurrence in the region.

North Korea says tested AI-assisted torpedo system. North Korea has tested a “new-type” precision-guided torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence for target detection and guidance, state media reported Saturday, as the nuclear-armed country steps up weapons testing. The announcement came days after Pyongyang said it had test-fired two types of cruise missiles from a submarine after weeks of friction with Seoul over a landmine explosion along their border. Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile and weapons technology with support from Russia received in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine. The underwater test-fire of the “super-speed” Zam-2.0 torpedo system took place on Thursday “to confirm the successful technical updating” of the weapon, the Korean Central News Agency said. “AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the new-type super-speed precisely guided torpedo,” KCNA said. The test proved “the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion device”, it said, adding it had completed “more than 180 rounds of different tests over the past five years”. Earlier this month, North Korea announced the AI-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile. Pyongyang said at the time there was “no way to avoid” the hypersonic missile, which was “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude”. Torpedoes are designed to strike enemy targets underwater at high speed, but the stated introduction of AI could also allow North Korea to carry out evasive manoeuvres and make autonomous decisions to confuse an adversary, analysts say. “South Korea and the United States deploy decoy targets to divert torpedoes, but AI could potentially help distinguish real targets from decoys,” Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University, told AFP. “From torpedoes to submarine-launched weapons, Pyongyang is pouring resources into demonstrating that US strategic assets can be rendered ineffective.” In September, Pyongyang’s leader Kim Jong Un emphasised the need to raise “the level of artificial intelligence” in the country’s weapons systems. ‘Arms race’ Saturday’s announcement came as the two Koreas appear to be intensifying an arms race over hypersonic missiles. Hypersonic missiles travel at more than five times the speed of sound and can manoeuvre mid-flight, making them significantly harder to track and intercept. Days after North Korea announced it had tested its AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile, Seoul test-fired its own weapon – a hypersonic glide vehicle it called a “key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield”. North Korea this week cast doubt on Seoul’s test, saying it may have “failed to achieve hypersonic flight”, a claim South Korea rejected a day later. The latest weapons tests come amid growing speculation over a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim, as world leaders prepare to gather for November’s APEC summit in China. After several overtures met with silence from Pyongyang, Trump said again this week he “may” meet North Korean leader Kim during his Asia tour next month. Ahead of a possible North Korea-US summit, Pyongyang appears to be “playing down South Korea’s hypersonic missile programme to portray itself as ahead of Seoul — Washington’s ally — in the arms race”, Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP. But North Korea may need more time to advance its torpedo system, particularly in reducing the noise it generates underwater, he said. “At high speeds underwater, a torpedo generates significant noise, making it easier to detect,” Yang said. “Reducing that noise is a major technical challenge requiring advanced technology — and North Korea does not yet appear to have reached that level”.

India's 'cockroach' movement founder arrested after detention, media reports say. Police arrested Indian “cockroach” movement founder Abhijeet Dipke, according to several media reports on Saturday, after he was ​detained on Friday ahead of a Delhi rally that drew hundreds of people ‌waving the national flag and demanding the resignation of India’s election chief. Dipke was arrested to prevent a breach of the peace and will be called before a Special Executive Magistrate on Saturday, broadcasters NDTV and ​ India Today said. Delhi police did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. The ​youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), opposition groups and student organisations have held near-daily protests ⁠this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over a revision of voter lists that ​they say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). More than 130 million voters were deleted ​during the revision. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. Student activist Neha ​Bora, a prominent face of the protests, who was also detained on Friday as she ​tried to reach central Delhi with dozens of supporters, was released on Saturday. “Please, spare the people of India. ‌Impeach ⁠Gyanesh Kumar and halt SIR (special intensive revision), so that the ordinary citizens of this country can breathe a sigh of relief, feel at ease, and have their voting rights ensured,” Bora told ANI news agency after she was released. Dipke was detained on Friday as he stepped out of ​a house in central ​Delhi, with police hauling ⁠him into a police car and driving away after a brief argument. Dipke had called Friday’s protest in support of two CJP leaders detained ​and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at ​a protest ⁠site in violation of a ban. Earlier on Friday, police had met Dipke and warned him against going ahead with the protest. The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced ⁠by ​Modi and the BJP in the prime minister’s 12 ​years in power. A weeks-long sit-in by supporters of the movement earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation over ​exam paper leaks.

After the emergency. THE much-anticipated, and somewhat dreaded, emergency in KP was finally proclaimed by the president on Oct 11. The federal cabinet’s recommendation, the summary of the prime minister’s advice to the president, and the proclamation — all three momentous developments — occurred on the same day. The subsequent actions like t aking the chief minister — non-functional but still the elected chief minister of the province — into preventive custody by his subordinate police from within the chief minister’s official residence along with many other senior elected officials; transfer and posting of senior and mid-level Civil Service officials; formation of an advisory council to help the governor in his newly acquired functions; the advisory council’s first meeting and the convening of the meeting of the long-neglected provincial apex committee took place within 48 hours of the proclamation, indicating that the federal government had done its homework in anticipation of the proclamation. Besides debating whether the emergency would be imposed or not, the media had also been speculating about the specific article in Part X ‘Emergency Provisions’ of the Constitution that would be finally invoked. Articles 232 and 234 were the ‘favourites’ on TV talk shows and, in the end, the federal government did not disappoint either group betting on the choice of articles, as the proclamation invoked both Article 232 and 234. It seems that the government was not taking any chances. While Article 232 was apparently favoured because it does not set a limit on the period of emergency, it contains a ‘flaw’ in the federal government’s view, as it does not bar the provincial assembly from functioning during the period of emergency under Article 232. The federal government simultaneously invoked Article 234 apparently to render the provincial assembly non-functional during the emergency and to vest all legislative powers in parliament. Invoking both articles simultaneously appears to be unprecedented, although an emergency has been proclaimed about seven times in Pakistan since the adoption of the 1973 Constitution. This manifests the hard line with which the federal government wants to implement the proclamation of emergency. In most media reports, Article 232 has been frequently referred to as the instrument to proclaim emergency, in contrast to Article 234 that, according to these reports, has been used to proclaim governor’s rule. A plain reading of the Constitution, however, does not bear out this distinction. Both articles concern the proclamation of an emergency, and both give the federal government the option to either exercise executive powers directly in the province or designate the provincial governor to do so on its behalf. Article 234 is invoked either on a report from the provincial governor to the president, or after the two Houses of parliament separately pass a resolution asking the president to proclaim an emergency under Article 234. The president may or may not act based on the governor’s report. Still, if the two Houses pass a resolution to this effect, the president must invoke Article 234. Both articles lay down different requirements for parliamentary approval of the proclamation. Article 232 requires that the proclamation be laid before the two Houses for approval by each within 10 days of the proclamation if the latter has been made by the president on his own (which is the case for the emergency proclaimed on Oct 11), and not based on a resolution passed by the provincial assembly. The federal government easily fulfilled this requirement on Oct 14, despite the fiery speeches and the opposition’s subsequent boycott of the proceedings. Article 232 also provides that the proclamation issued under the article be laid before a joint sitting of the two Houses within 30 days. This formality was also fulfilled . The government might survive constitutional challenges, but can face political risks. Article 234 simply requires that the proclamation issued under the article be laid before a joint sitting of parliament. The proclamation will cease to be valid at the end of two months unless the joint sitting extends the validity by another two months. The joint sitting is authorised to grant up to two extensions of two months each, meaning the proclamation of emergency under this article can continue for a maximum of six months. Given the clear majority of the ruling coalition and the PPP, continuing the proclamation of emergency under this article for six months doesn’t seem to pose a challenge for the federal government. The provincial assembly will become functional after six months, but, as seen in the past, federal governments manage to engineer such a change within the assembly during this period that it doesn’t pose a major challenge to the centre. This is more likely because the provincial government will remain non-functional indefinitely under Article 232. While the federal government may be able to surmount constitutional challenges, it might still face serious political difficulties. Although contrary to the warnings of the non-functional chief minister of KP and other PTI leaders, no serious agitation has been witnessed in the country or even in KP so far, it should cause some discomfort to the federal government that none of the political parties other than those in the ruling coalition has supported the proclamation. Articles 232 and 234 do not restrain the high court’s powers, but a serious judicial challenge appears unlikely. However, the majority of proclamations of emergency challenged in the courts previously could not be sustained. Last but probably not least, the federal government and the security establishment have put their prestige at stake by taking on total responsibility to combat and defeat terrorism in the province. After the proclamation of emergency, there is no longer a provincial government to blame for the rising arc of terrorism. The writer is the president of Pakistan-based think tank Pildat. president@pildat.org X: @ABMPildat Published in Dawn, October 17th, 2026

Armed men abduct 20 under-training police personnel in Mastung: officials. QUETTA: Unidentified armed men kidnapped 20 police recruits undergoing training at the Kalat Police Training Centre while they were travelling in a passenger van along the Quetta-Karachi Highway in Mastung district, officials said. A senior Balochistan government official confirmed the abduction to Dawn on condition of anonymity, saying the recruits were heading home for the weekend when armed men intercepted their van. “Yes, 20 police personnel who were going home for the weekend were taken away by armed men while they were travelling in a passenger van on the Quetta-Karachi Highway in Mastung,” the official said. He said a group of armed men riding motorcycles and carrying automatic weapons intercepted the van and took the recruits away along with the vehicle to an undisclosed location. The armed men, however, released the driver and three other passengers travelling in the van. Police officials in Mastung also confirmed the abduction, saying the recruits belonged to the Levies Force, which has since been merged with the police. The abducted personnel belonged to the Rakhshan division, government officials said. Security forces have launched a search operation in the nearby mountains to trace the abducted recruits. However, no information about their whereabouts has emerged so far. No group has claimed responsibility for the abduction. A day earlier, Rakhshan Division Commissioner Asad Ullah Kakar was abducted in Balochistan’s Kharan district. In a separate incident, Kharan Deputy Commissioner Munir Ahmed Soomro was released safely on Oct 3 after nearly two weeks in captivity following negotiations between local tribal elders and the armed men who had abducted him from the Noshki-Kharan highway the previous month. On July 21, three excise officials were kidnapped after an attack on a checkpost in Balochistan’s Chagai district.

Minister rebukes JUI-F chief for seeking ‘share’ in KP governance after imposition of governor’s rule, emergency. State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry on Saturday rebuked Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman for reportedly seeking his “share” in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s governance following the imposition of governor’s rule and an emergency in the province. Addressing the media in Jaranwala, Chaudhry emphasised that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was not a political move aimed at strengthening the PML-N’s presence in the province by dismissing the PTI-led government. “This was an administrative setup,” he said, adding that it had been formed with a “one-point agenda: combating terrorism”. “I am upset. We did not expect Maulana sahab […] to consider this as spoils of war and seek his share in the absence of a PTI government in the province,” Chaudhry said. “This is not spoils of war,” he reiterated, adding that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule in KP was an “immensely responsible” decision taken after every other option had been considered. He said the federal government had no intention of establishing a political setup in KP. “I am unable to understand why Maulana sahab says that he was forced to accept defeat [in elections],” he said, arguing that Fazl’s party had been defeated by the PTI in KP and the Pashtunkhwa Milli Awami Party in Balochistan. Chaudhry said the JUI-F was worthy of respect only if it stood by Pakistan’s interests. The state minister also rejected the impression that the imposition of an emergency and governor’s rule was aimed at taking control of KP’s natural resources. He also criticised Fazl for bringing up the 1971 separation of East Pakistan — now Bangladesh — from Pakistan in his recent statements. “You bring up 1971 after losing the 2024 elections,” Chaudhry said. “This KP setup is not about distributing shares, forming coalitions and governments, or engaging in politics,” he stressed, clarifying that only one member of the KP Advisory Council has a political background, as she represents the families of martyrs. Chaudhry again offered to implement the National Action Plan and combat terrorism jointly with all stakeholders. “Politics is possible only where there is peace,” he said. At the outset of his address, Chaudhry reiterated that there must be “a relationship or a mutual interest arrangement between the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and the PTI”. “Since 2015, no PTI leader, gathering or member has been targeted by terrorists,” Chaudhry said. “On the other hand, over the past 11 years, no political or religious party, security force, public office, funeral or wedding has been spared terrorist attacks.” He said the federal government had exhausted all avenues to bring together stakeholders and urge them to condemn terrorism by naming those involved, whether the TTP, the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), or groups funded by India or Afghanistan. The state minister claimed that in 2013, when the government decided to hold talks with the TTP and representatives were proposed by both sides, the TTP had nominated PTI founder Imran Khan to its committee. He also alleged that the PTI founder had allowed the TTP to open offices in Peshawar. During his address, Chaudhry also criticised the PTI, showing a press release issued by the TTP, that condemned the dismissal of the party’s government. Speaking at a press conference in Sialkot, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said that the sacrifices made by the security forces, officers, and the public in the fight against terrorism were “matchless”. Criticising the JUI-F chief, Asif said that he constantly targeted the country’s security forces. The defence minister referred to Fazl’s accusations that the emergency and governor’s rule was imposed to capture KP’s mineral resources, saying that he had shared a full list of people who had the mining contracts in KP. Asif maintained that the whole PTI and opposition leadership was engaged by the government before the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule. “But it was fruitless,” he said. “The situation will improve in KP […] parliament can roll back the decision of imposing the emergency only if the improvement of the situation in the province is guaranteed,” the defence minister said. He said that some individuals in KP were expecting to get a share in the administrative changes in the province. “We will ensure free and fair elections. Whenever the time comes, everybody can take part in it,” he said. ‘Extremely upset’ A day earlier, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had also said that a “head of a party” was “extremely upset” about not being appointed the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. “The head of a party is extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship,” Naqvi alleged while speaking to journalists in Lahore. He was seemingly referring to Fazl who has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in KP. This politician, Naqvi said, had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”. “These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged. He said such politicians had little justification for criticising others now, particularly after having benefitted from the same system they currently denounced. Naqvi’s remarks came days after the Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. The move has drawn criticism from the opposition, including Fazl, as well as Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Raja Nasir Abbas of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan. In the days preceding the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition — including the PTI which was in power in KP — had remained high since jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release. Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule had failed to yield any results while Fazl was cast as the man who could defuse heightening tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides had held separate meetings with Fazl, reportedly for his intervention to help break the deadlock in the negotiations. And after the federal government imposed governor’s rule in KP, Fazl accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts for mediation. On Thursday, Fazl again censured the Centre, accusing it of depriving the provinces of their rights. Addressing a rally in Multan, he further recalled that his party had expressed reservations over the merger of tribal areas into KP after the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018. “We were not against the merger, but we said that it was an issue of the political future of the people of tribal areas,” he said, alleging that the people of those areas were not consulted on the merger. Raising doubts over the Centre’s reasoning behind imposing governor’s rule that there was a lack of cooperation on counterterrorism, he said the security situation in Balochistan was worse than it was in KP. He alleged governor’s rule was not imposed in Balochistan because the province’s chief minister “praises you”. Naqvi further said KP was facing serious security challenges , and called on political leaders to play a constructive role in restoring peace and combating terrorism. “Instead of fanning the flames and creating unrest, political leaders should play their role in restoring law and order and eliminating terrorism,” he said, maintaining that the province needed peace, stability and collective efforts rather than political confrontation. Separately, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz railed against Fazl in a post on X. She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitate terrorism — an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism. She added it was unfortunate that he was supporting the party instead of “holding those accountable who were responsible for the ruin of KP because of their incompetence, ineptitude and corruption”. She also criticised Fazl for his remarks about Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, seemingly referring to his comments during the Multan address about the centralisation of power. She concluded her statement by saying that no one but the PTI was “responsible for the end of its government in KP”.

Five Energy Market Factors That Could Tip the Scales in the Middle East War pfranz Thu, 10/01/2026 - 19:11 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List A garbage truck drives past gas prices above $6 a gallon and diesel prices above $8 a gallon as they are displayed outside of a Shell gas station in Carson, California on September 22, 2026. Patrick T. Fallon / AFP Commentary / United States 01 October 2026 20+ minutes Five Energy Market Factors That Could Tip the Scales in the Middle East War Oil, gas and fuel prices are central to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, with Washington striving to lower them and Tehran to keep them high. With both sides determined to prevail, five market-shaping developments in particular could affect whether fighting ramps up or de-escalates. Share BlueSky E-mail Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Salva Stampa Related Tags Global Order and Peacemaking United States Iran Israel/Palestine As Iran and the United States trade blows in the Gulf, they are both trying to sway at least one shared audience: global energy markets. The public and private companies that produce, refine, move and consume oil and gas around the world are listening rapt to what the belligerents say and watching every move they make in an attempt to understand where the war is headed. These commodities have many prices: for instance, what a barrel of crude oil is fetching today; how much customers are paying for derivative products like diesel or jet fuel in major markets like East Asia, the European Union or the U.S.; and what future delivery of such items is projected to cost. Together, these actual and estimated prices serve as a rough indicator of what the market thinks about the conflict’s likely trajectory. In turn, the price fluctuations are monitored in both Tehran and Washington, which factor them into strategy. U.S. President Donald Trump is plainly keeping one eye on the markets at all times. In June, when he signed a now defunct memorandum of understanding meant to end the war, he noted a market motivation, saying, “We run out of [oil] reserves at about four weeks”. On 13 August, with November’s midterm elections getting closer, Vice President JD Vance cited low fuel prices as Washington’s main war aim, saying “That’s goal number one – keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country”. Preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons – Washington’s ostensible motive for launching its airstrikes in February – was apparently, at least for a time, goal number two. Iran, for its part, is trying to maintain the clout it obtained by asserting control of the Strait of Hormuz, for which it is willing to pay a big price. The Iranian economy is being hammered by intensifying sanctions and a resumed U.S. naval blockade that has halted exports from Iran’s southern coast. Washington has repeatedly hailed the impending death of Iran’s oil industry, due to lack of export and storage capacity. While these predictions were overblown, Iran is still reeling economically. As both the U.S. and Iran pin their hopes on being able to manage prices, the energy markets have proven unpredictable. Despite disruptions, the markets have displayed unexpected resilience, helping dilute the conflict’s economic consequences. Apocalyptic prophecies that oil would reach $200 a barrel have so far been incorrect. Instead, the price of the global benchmark, Brent crude, has risen from below $75 before the war to peaks that have not yet topped $130. These prices are high, but adjusted for inflation, they pale in comparison to previous spikes. Part of the explanation owes to buffers that have kept the markets from careening out of control. It helps that the world had an oil surplus when the war began, the U.S. had a few hundred million more barrels in its federal stores, Russia had more functional refineries and export terminals, China was building up rather than depleting its reserves and the Red Sea was largely open to tanker traffic. Since the war began, higher prices have pushed demand lower and raised production in some countries while new workarounds – in part orchestrated by the U.S. and Gulf states like the United Arab Emirates – and growing risk tolerance are sending a significant amount of oil through Hormuz despite Iran’s attacks. [T]he question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. Still, the question remains whether the U.S. or Iran will outlast the other in what has become an endurance test. The feared tipping point at which a shortfall in oil supply causes a rapid price increase until demand falls has seemingly been forestalled by greater crude flow through Hormuz. But surging diesel and other fuel prices may now matter more than crude oil alone. U.S. retail diesel prices are soaring to record highs, generating support for a 90-day U.S. diesel export ban and even a measure of dissent from the war among members of Trump’s Republican Party (in many other parts of the world, rising fuel prices are already stoking significant public anger). Iran is cognisant of the correlation between fuel prices and the Republicans’ political fortunes; with the November midterm elections approaching and major Republican losses a significant possibility , Iran may think that such a result would produce new constraints on Trump’s war-making, in the form of more vigorous oversight from a Congress controlled by opposition Democrats. For this reason, many Iran watchers believe Tehran, along with its allies, will seek to prevent the U.S. from stabilising prices, even if it involves a mutually hurting re-escalation of the conflict. Indeed, in September, the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels advanced in Yemen, positioning themselves to more effectively threaten shipping in the Red Sea, a major energy corridor. But while Iran looks for ways to keep oil and gas bottled up in the Middle East, Washington and its partners continue to work on means of getting these items out, with the outflow of crude through the Strait of Hormuz reportedly hitting its pre-war baseline by the end of September, though refined products like fuel lagged far behind. Efforts are under way to keep raising this Hormuz outflow, and land routes add a few million more barrels. The U.S. conundrum now is that crude needs to reach refineries, and the resulting products to hit global markets, for the world to get out of its growing fuel crisis. As the U.S. increasingly looks to others to help manage the fallout of its war with Iran, it is also pursuing a number of costly mitigation measures, whose sustainability is questionable. This Crisis Group analysis examines the relationship between global energy markets and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. It looks at the cushions that have helped absorb war-related shocks to oil markets so far and the extent to which they are under pressure. It identifies five particular factors that could contribute to re-escalation or de-escalation of the conflict.
