AFP / Anthony Wallace Report 359 / Asia-Pacific 09 October 2026 20+ minutes Toward a Thaw in the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict Hostilities between Cambodia and Thailand ceased in late 2025, after two rounds of combat along the frontier. But the truce is under growing strain. To avoid more war, the two countries should restore normal diplomatic ties and resume work on demarcating their shared border. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Related Tags Thailand Cambodia What’s new? Fighting between Cambodia and Thailand over a border dispute killed at least 150 people and displaced almost a million more in 2025. Now, the ceasefire between the two countries is fraying, while diplomacy has stalled. Why does it matter? The 2025 combat was the costliest yet between the two countries and the worst confrontation ever between two members of the Association of South East Asian Nations. War could break out again if Bangkok and Phnom Penh do not improve relations. What should be done? Leaders in Bangkok and Phnom Penh should work to normalise diplomatic ties, reconvene the Joint Boundary Commission in order to resume the surveys that will let the sides demarcate the land border, when circumstances allow, and cooperate on a program of demining affected areas. Executive Summary After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along their 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides and mutual allegations of violations. Tensions between the two countries resurfaced early in 2025, erupting into combat that dwarfed earlier clashes in scale. When the shooting stopped on 27 December, Thailand had the upper hand, holding most of the contested areas as well as slivers of Cambodian territory. In May, Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 bilateral agreement on how to resolve overlapping maritime claims, leading Phnom Penh to initiate compulsory conciliation – a non-binding international legal proceeding – under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. In turn, Thailand suspended participation in bilateral mechanisms on land border demarcation, leaving negotiations in limbo. To avoid more war, the two countries should put nationalist fervour to the side and overcome their mistrust, starting with restoring normal diplomatic ties and resuming efforts to jointly demarcate the land border. Following an exchange of fire in May 2025 that killed a Cambodian soldier, fighting broke out along the border in late July. With Malaysian mediation, backed up by U.S. President Donald Trump’s vow to suspend trade talks with both countries so long as hostilities continued, the two sides agreed to a ceasefire after five days of combat. Tensions simmered over the following months, however, with regular confrontations between troops and a series of landmine explosions that wounded sixteen Thai soldiers. The ceasefire collapsed in November, and a second round of hostilities ensued, displacing almost a million people on both sides before halting with another truce, brokered this time with China’s help near year’s end. The conflict is linked to domestic politics in both countries. Border tensions were pivotal in the disqualification from office of Thailand’s Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra in 2025. Her successor Anutin Charnvirakul, leader of the Bhumjaithai (Thai Pride) Party, took office that September, dissolved parliament in December and won in a general election the next February, in part by maintaining a hard line on Cambodia amid a wave of Thai nationalism. The episode evoked memories of the 2008 conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, when royalist opponents of Paetongtarn’s father, the controversial former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, fanned nationalist discontent over the border to undermine the Thaksin-aligned government of the day. Nationalist zeal has also appeared to bolster the government of Prime Minister Hun Manet in Cambodia, though further fighting could shake the unity of the ruling Cambodian People’s Party and the regime built by his father, and current senate president, Hun Sen. While the ceasefire has held thus far, the conflict continues through diplomatic channels, with Cambodia decrying Thai occupation of its territory. While the ceasefire has held thus far, the conflict continues through diplomatic channels, with Cambodia decrying Thai occupation of its territory. Thailand insists it is observing the ceasefire agreement, which provides for troops to remain in positions they held when it came into effect, and accuses Cambodia of attempting to internationalise the dispute. Compulsory conciliation on the overlapping maritime claims will take at least a year to conclude. In the meantime, Bangkok has declined to resume the technical work of a Joint Boundary Commission to survey and demarcate the land border between the countries, while cooperation on demining the frontier has been suspended since the 2025 fighting. Both sides are angry, with each portraying the other as the obstacle to resolving the conflict. Amid the mutual recriminations, it would be easy for a minor border incident to blow up into something bigger, including a third bout of major fighting. Ideally, a third party would mediate between Cambodia and Thailand to head off the possibility of escalation. But several factors impede movement toward dialogue. First, strident nationalism on both sides makes compromise appear hazardous. In Bangkok, the government seems content with the status quo and is following the military’s lead on border security. In Phnom Penh, senior leaders recognise the risks another round of fighting could pose to the government’s legitimacy, but they cannot appear to be bending on sovereignty or territorial integrity. Confrontation continues, for now, to bring political rewards to decision-makers on both sides, especially the Thai military, which has been able to polish a tarnished image. Secondly, while the conflict has been economically damaging to both countries, it has not been sufficiently costly to precipitate a thaw in the interest of resuming cross-border commerce. Both Thai and Cambodian leaders perceive the political costs of conciliatory moves as greater than the prospective benefits. Thirdly, international powers have limited leverage to push the two sides toward a deal. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, the rotating chair of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2025, took the lead in brokering the July ceasefire – with decisive help from Trump’s trade talks threat. But since that truce unravelled, the bloc has been unable to expedite resolution of the dispute. Current ASEAN chair the Philippines has used its good offices to bring the Cambodian and Thai prime ministers together, but it is in no position to spur dialogue. Preoccupied with the Middle East, the U.S. shows no interest in mediating. China would be able to convene talks, but it is unlikely to jeopardise its relations with either country by attempting to impose an agreement. Under these circumstances, immediate prospects for concerted efforts to resolve the border issue are poor. But until the dispute is resolved, the possibility of another war, with all the associated death, displacement and other human suffering, will remain. Both sides should dial down official rhetoric that casts the other as an enemy and seek areas of common interest, starting by normalising diplomatic relations and reposting ambassadors in the other’s capital. Though the Joint Boundary Commission has neither the mandate nor a mechanism to resolve the political impasse, its work of surveying and demarcating the border is a prerequisite for settling the dispute and should be restarted as soon as possible. Demining is a priority for both countries that should offer another politically acceptable platform for cooperation. Crucially, both border demarcation and demining are already stipulated in the ceasefire agreement. The alternative to honouring these truce terms that the two neighbours have agreed upon could be more bloodshed, which is highly unlikely to put this long-running border dispute to rest. Bangkok/Phnom Penh/Brussels, 9 October 2026 I. Introduction The border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand is hardly new, but the fighting that erupted between the two South East Asian neighbours in July and December 2025 was deadlier and more widespread than earlier clashes, killing at least 150 people and displacing roughly one million. 1 For background, see Crisis Group Asia Report N°215, Waging Peace: ASEAN and the Thai-Cambodian Border Conflict , 6 December 2011; and Matthew Wheeler, “ Border Dispute with Cambodia Sparks Political Disarray in Thailand ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 July 2025. See also “Situation Report 20 – Displacement Crisis as a Result of the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict”, World Vision International in Cambodia, 2 January 2026; and “Thai deadly border clashes displace over half a million in Cambodia”, France 24, 21 December 2025. By 27 December, when the parties reached the latest ceasefire, Thai troops had taken high ground in many locations along the 800km border, occupying contested areas as well as patches of Cambodian territory. 2 Given that portions of the border are undemarcated and disputed, its exact length is not known. Cambodia’s estimate is 817km; Thailand’s is 798km. Since then, the ceasefire has been tested regularly. Bangkok and Phnom Penh have made little progress toward delimiting the border or resuming normal diplomatic relations. The risk of a third round of war is real. In the wake of the 2025 fighting, bilateral relations are at a low ebb. Each side accuses the other of having started the conflict, while indulging in provocative rhetoric and actions that undermine prospects for resolution. Cambodia alleges that Thailand aims to annex parts of its territory seized in the December 2025 fighting. Thailand maintains that it is observing the ceasefire deal, which stipulates that troops remain in positions they held when the agreement entered into force. The territorial dispute extends out to sea as well. In May, Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 memorandum of understanding on overlapping maritime claims, leading Phnom Penh to initiate compulsory conciliation, a non-binding dispute resolution mechanism under the UN Convention of the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). This report examines the roots of the conflict, its domestic political drivers and the current diplomatic impasse. It is based on research conducted since February in Bangkok and Phnom Penh, including interviews with officials of both governments, some of whom have retired but have direct knowledge of developments, as well as diplomats, analysts and journalists covering the conflict. Women made up about a fifth of the interlocutors. Research was also carried out in Siem Reap and Anlong Veng in Cambodia, as well as in the Thai border provinces of Buriram, Sa Kaeo, Si Sa Ket and Surin. The report uses both Khmer and Thai place names on first reference. It uses the Khmer name for the 11th century Preah Vihear temple, known in Thai as Khao Phra Viharn, in view of the 1962 International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling that the temple is situated in Cambodian territory. 3 “Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)”, International Court of Justice (ICJ), 15 June 1962. After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along the 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides. Source: Openstreetmaps; CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative / CRISIS GROUP II. The Weight of History The contemporary border conflict is a legacy of both colonialism and nationalist historical narratives, which elites in both Cambodia and Thailand have repeatedly exploited for domestic political advantage. A. Preah Vihear and Thailand’s “Lost Territories” In the 18th and 19th centuries, Siam and Vietnam vied for control of Cambodia, while Khmer kings sought room for manoeuvre by playing the larger powers against each other. 4 The Khmer Empire, renowned for building Angkor Wat, dominated mainland South East Asia from roughly the 9th to the 15th century. Siam gained suzerainty over what is now western Cambodia in 1794, but it did not actively colonise the area. 5 David Chandler, A History of Cambodia (Boulder, Colo., 2008), pp. 142-143; 183-184. France then established a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863, stopping the kingdom’s neighbours from swallowing it whole. In 1893, French gunboats dropped anchor in waters near the royal palace in Bangkok to press Siam to cede territories east of the Mekong River, as well as the eastern provinces of Chantaburi and Trat, to France. This event, known as the Pak Nam Crisis, marks the origin of a still-ubiquitous Thai historical narrative of “lost territories” sacrificed by King Chulalongkorn to preserve his domain from the encroachment of Western colonialism. 6 Thongchai Winichakul, Siam Mapped: A History of the Geo-Body 0f a Nation (Honolulu, Hawaii, 1994), pp. 111, 150-153; Shane Strate, The Lost Territories: Thailand’s History of National Humiliation (Honolulu, Hawaii, 2015). Franco-Siamese treaties of 1904 and 1907 established that the border between Siam and French Indochina would follow the watershed of the Dangrek Mountains. In 1908, Siam received a series of maps, drafted by a French expedition, depicting a border line. 7 The expedition that drafted the map was supposed to be a joint Franco-Siamese endeavour, but Siam did not send surveyors to participate. These maps, known as Annex I of the 1907 treaty, deviate from the treaty’s text; the border line departs from the watershed to place the ancient temple complex of Preah Vihear – a vestige of the Khmer empire – within French Indochina. Siamese officials did not detect the discrepancy until they made their own survey in 1934, but they raised no objection until much later. 8 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., pp. 161-162. The 1:200,000-scale Annex I border maps remain the only legally recognised ones. In Thailand, Preah Vihear became a national cause under Field Marshal Phibun Songkhram, a strongman who governed the country from 1938 to 1944 and again from 1948 to 1957. In 1939, the Department of Education included the temple complex on maps of Thailand’s historical sites. During World War II, Thailand reclaimed Cambodia’s western provinces, encompassing the Preah Vihear complex. The Thai government promoted the temple as a symbol of territories earlier surrendered to colonial powers to retain Siam’s independence. 9 Ibid., pp. 162-163. As a condition for admission to the UN, Thailand then ceded the Cambodian provinces to France under the 1946 Washington Treaty, but it asserted Thai sovereignty over Preah Vihear after Cambodia gained independence in 1953. 10 Sok Udom Deth, A History of Cambodia-Thailand Diplomatic Relations, 1950-2020 (Glienicke, 2020), p. 26. In Thailand, press coverage of the [1958] negotiations stirred up nationalist sentiments, helping turn Preah Vihear [temple] into a popular issue. After years of wrangling, formal bilateral talks about the disputed temple began in 1958. In Thailand, press coverage of the negotiations stirred up nationalist sentiments, helping turn Preah Vihear into a popular issue. Similarly, Cambodia’s King Norodom Sihanouk promoted the historical monument as a national cause, portraying Thailand as a perennial threat to the nation’s sovereignty. 11 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., pp. 165-166. Cambodia withdrew from negotiations in October 1959 and appealed to the ICJ to settle the dispute. In 1962, the court ruled that Preah Vihear was situated in Cambodian territory, reasoning that Siam’s failure to object to the Annex I map in the decades after it was issued signified acceptance. 12 “Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand)”, op. cit. In Thailand, the verdict inflamed popular opinion, helping entrench the idea of “lost territories” and national humiliation at the hands of Cambodia and colonial powers. 13 Strate, The Lost Territories , op. cit., p. 170. Satellite imagery of the Preah Vihear temple. Source: Google Earth / CRISIS GROUP B. Managing a Disputed Border The Khmer Rouge victory in Cambodia in 1975 opened a new chapter along the border. After Vietnam’s 1978 invasion of Cambodia, almost a million refugees fled to Thailand. Refugee camps became strongholds of armed groups, including the Khmer Rouge, resisting Vietnam’s occupation with Thai, Chinese and U.S. assistance. 14 Nicole Jenne, “The Thai-Cambodian Border Dispute: An Agency-centred Perspective on the Management of Interstate Conflict”, Contemporary Southeast Asia , vol. 29, n0. 2 (2017), p. 329. In the late 1980s, Thailand reoriented its regional diplomacy, seeking a change from “from battlefield to marketplace”. 15 Chatchai Choonhavan, Thai prime minister from 1988 to 1991, advanced this policy. Meanwhile, the 1991 Paris Peace Accords and the UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia brought relative peace and the prospect of economic development. In accordance with these changes, the two countries took steps to establish a new relationship, leading them to sign a bilateral agreement on border management in 1995. 16 “Agreement between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia on the Establishment of Border Committees”, Phnom Penh, 26 September 1995. This pact set up the General Border Committee (GBC), chaired by the countries’ defence ministers, and three Regional Border Committees (RBC), chaired by regional military commanders charged to “consider and agree on appropriate measures to promote cooperation in the maintenance of peace, order and stability in the border area”. 17 Ibid. The agreement empowered the RBCs to “solve specific problems that may arise” and promote cooperation and communication links “to enable immediate contact at all times”. 18 Ibid. The relevant commands are: Thailand’s 2nd Army Region and Cambodia’s 4th Military Region; Thailand’s 1st Army Region and Cambodia’s 5th Military Region; Thailand’s Chanthaburi-Trat Border Defence Command and Cambodia’s 3rd Military Region. The [Joint Boundary Commission] has ... succeeded in delimiting some 600km of the [Thailand-Cambodia] border, with roughly 200km outstanding. Five years later, Cambodia and Thailand signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a Joint Boundary Commission (JBC) to govern border surveys and demarcation. 19 “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia on the Survey and Demarcation of Land Boundary”, 14 June 2000. This document – known as MOU 43 for the Buddhist year 2543 in which it was signed – provides for a five-step process, including identifying the 73 boundary markers installed between 1909 and 1919, jointly surveying the boundary and demarcating the border. In 2003, the two sides then agreed on Terms of Reference dividing the border into seven sectors. 20 “Terms of Reference and Master Plan for the Joint Survey and Demarcation of Land Boundary between the Kingdom of Thailand and the Kingdom of Cambodia”, p. 14. The JBC has since succeeded in delimiting some 600km of the border, with roughly 200km outstanding. 21 “Thai-Cambodian border row: Does 1:50,000 or 1:200,000 mapping give the edge?”, The Nation , 16 June 2025. In 2001, Bangkok and Phnom Penh signed a separate memorandum of understanding on overlapping maritime claims. Known as MOU 44, it provided for boundary delineation and joint development of hydrocarbons in a portion of the 26,000 sq km disputed area, which may contain as much as eleven trillion cubic feet of natural gas and between 300 and 500 million barrels of crude oil, with a combined value of some $300 billion. 22 “Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the Kingdom of Thailand and the Government of the Kingdom of Cambodia regarding their Overlapping Maritime Claims to the Continental Shelf”, 18 June 2001; Supalak Ganjanakhundee, “Beyond scrapping the MOU: Navigating maritime disputes under UNCLOS”, Prachatai English , 1 June 2026. Appended to the document is a map depicting the two sides’ continental shelf claims and the resulting areas of overlap. This map has spurred criticism in Thailand as the Cambodian claim line appears to cross the island of Koh Kut, which the 1907 treaty had clearly identified as Siamese territory. C. Politics and Conflict The historical dispute over territory does not in itself explain why conflict erupted in 2025. Contemporary tension between the two countries is intimately linked to Thailand’s turbulent domestic politics, which for two decades has revolved around a contest for power between the tycoon-turned-politician Thaksin Shinawatra and his conservative opponents. 23 See Crisis Group Asia Reports N°274, Thailand’s Lengthening Roadmap to Elections , 10 December 2015; N°263, A Coup Ordained? Thailand’s Prospects for Stability , 3 December 2014; and N°192, Bridging Thailand’s Deep Divide , 5 July 2010; as well as Crisis Group Asia Briefings N°121, Thailand: The Calm before Another Storm? , 11 April 2011; N°82, Thailand: Calming the Political Turmoil , 22 September 2008; and N°80, Thailand: Political Turmoil and the Southern Insurgency , 28 August 2008. Thaksin also had close ties with Cambodia’s Hun Sen, who served as prime minister from 1985 to 2023, currently presides over the senate and still controls the ruling Cambodian People’s Party. That relationship crumbled in dramatic fashion in June 2025, with direct repercussions for bilateral relations. 1. Thailand Thaksin became prime minister in 2001. His Thai Rak Thai Party won support by delivering on popular policies but earned the enmity of conservatives and the military over alleged conflicts of interest and challenges to the prerogatives of the royal palace. Led by conservative royalists, the People’s Alliance for Democracy (PAD) took to the streets to call for Thaksin’s resignation in 2005. The military ousted him in a September 2006 coup, sending him into exile, but his proxy parties continued to win elections. The Thaksin/conservative divide was the fulcrum of Thai politics for more than a decade. In May 2008, under a Thaksin-aligned government, Thailand signed a joint communiqué with Cambodia supporting inscription of Preah Vihear temple as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The PAD promptly began using this issue as a cudgel against Thaksin, playing on the memory of the 1962 ICJ decision and the theme of lost territory, and portraying Thaksin’s purported business dealings in Cambodia as a threat to Thai sovereignty. 24 Crisis Group Report, Waging Peace , op. cit., pp. 4-5. Ever after, despite a lack of hard evidence of any conflict of interest, Thaksin’s opponents would accuse the Shinawatra family of “selling out” the national interest to Hun Sen. 25 Puangthong Pawakapan, State and Uncivil Society in Thailand at the Temple of Preah Vihear (Singapore, 2013), pp. 37, 62-64. With Preah Vihear [temple] ... a live political issue in Thailand, tensions increased on the border [with Cambodia]. With Preah Vihear again a live political issue in Thailand, tensions increased on the border. The two sides exchanged fire on six occasions between October 2008 and May 2011, claiming at least 34 lives. 26 Martin Wagener, “Lessons from Preah Vihear: Thailand, Cambodia and the Nature of Low-Intensity Border Conflicts”, Journal of Current Southeast Asian Affairs , vol. 30, no. 3 (2011), pp. 32-33. In April 2011, Cambodia requested that the ICJ interpret the 1962 verdict, particularly Thailand’s obligation to withdraw troops from the Preah Vihear temple or “its vicinity on Cambodian territory”. In July, the court issued a provisional ruling, including establishment of a demilitarised zone around Preah Vihear. In 2013, the ICJ affirmed Cambodia’s sovereignty over the promontory on which Preah Vihear is situated but referred delineation of the border in adjacent disputed territory to bilateral negotiations. “Request for interpretation of the Judgment of 15 June 1962 in the Case concerning the Temple of Preah Vihear (Cambodia v. Thailand) Request for the indication of provisional measures”, Summary of the Judgment, ICJ, 11 November 2013. In 2009, in a provocation to his political opponents, Thaksin accepted an appointment as an adviser to Hun Sen, who also offered refuge to his supporters fleeing a 2010 Thai army crackdown. Thaksin’s sister Yingluck, prime minister from 2011 to 2014, then took refuge in Cambodia after the Constitutional Court disqualified her from office, just before the military staged a coup. With the Thai military firmly in power and both Thaksin and Yingluck in exile, the pro/anti-Thaksin antagonism no longer defined Thai politics. But in 2023, the Thaksin-aligned Pheu Thai Party struck a bargain with its erstwhile conservative foes, joining forces to keep the progressive People’s Party from power after its massive general election victory. The deal allowed Thaksin proxy Srettha Thavisin to become prime minister and Thaksin himself to return home from fifteen years in exile. Hun Sen was Thaksin’s first visitor from abroad. 2. Cambodia Cambodia is ostensibly in transition from rule by Hun Sen to government by Hun Manet, who replaced his father as prime minister in 2023. During his 38 years as prime minister, Hun Sen consolidated power through a mix of co-optation and repression, while casting himself as Cambodia’s saviour. Beginning in 2017, a crackdown on dissent saw the main opposition party outlawed, scores of politicians jailed and driven into exile, and independent media suppressed. 27 Lee Morgenbesser, “Cambodia’s Transition to Hegemonic Authoritarianism”, Journal of Democracy , vol. 30, no. 1 (2019); Neil Loughlin, “Beyond Personalism: Elite Politics and Political Families in Cambodia”, Contemporary Southeast Asia , vol. 43, no. 2 (2021); “Cambodia: Hun Sen Extinguishes Media Freedom”, Human Rights Watch, 13 February 2023. Hun Sen remains extremely powerful, both as senate president and as the leading figure in the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP). Hun Manet’s rise to the prime minister’s office is part of a generational succession designed to secure the Hun family’s pre-eminence by safeguarding the interests of other senior CPP figures; the sons of some of Hun Sen’s long-serving ministers took over their fathers’ posts at the same time. 28 Tea Banh, defence minister since 1993, handed down his position to his son Tea Seiha and Sar Kheng, interior minister since 1992, turned over his post to his son Sar Sokha. Hun Manet’s younger brothers also ascended to high-ranking positions. Will Brehm, “How did Hun Sen engineer a seamless succession in Cambodia?”, East Asia Forum , 9 September 2023. Unassuming and technocratic, Hun Manet appears focused on governance and economic reforms, but he governs in his father’s shadow, and it remains to be seen if he can keep Hun Sen’s coalition intact. 29 Crisis Group interview, former official, Phnom Penh, May 2026. See also Chheang Vannarith, “Hun Manet’s Worldview”, Southeast Asian Affairs 2025 (Singapore, 2025). While domestic political opposition is weak, Hun Sen appears worried about popular discontent. 30 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and analysts, Phnom Penh, February 2026. The Hun family’s grip on power is not necessarily secure, as CPP factions weigh a post-Hun Sen future. 31 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, former official, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. On 1 June, Hun Sen warned, “Only the ‘angels’ [CPP members] and their children have the right to govern this country”. 32 “Hun Sen warns extremists against ouster attempts”, Khmer Times , 3 June 2026. While Khmer nationalism has generally been the province of the CPP’s political opponents, confrontation with Thailand has offered Hun Sen an opportunity to burnish his own nationalist credentials and bolster his family’s political legitimacy during the period of generational succession. 33 Crisis Group interviews, analysts, Phnom Penh, February 2026. III. The Path to Conflict A convergence of heightened Thai nationalism, linked to conservatives’ antipathy for Thaksin, and escalatory actions by Cambodia, led to two rounds of fighting in 2025. A. The Resurgence of Thai Nationalism The unlikely bargain between Thaksin and conservative parties struck in 2023 to keep the progressive People’s Party from power set the stage for a revival of Thai nationalism anchored in anti-Cambodia sentiment. In February 2024, Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin agreed to open talks with Hun Manet on joint development of hydrocarbons in the maritime overlapping claims area, providing Thaksin’s opponents with a pretext to reopen the 2008 “lost territories” playbook. 34 “Thailand, Cambodia to discuss joint petroleum exploitation”, Bangkok Post , 7 February 2024. The refrain only grew stronger after Thaksin gave a speech that included a pledge to “unlock” the Gulf of Thailand’s oil and gas resources in August. 35 William J. Jones, “Thai nationalism rears its ugly head again”, East Asia Forum , 17 January 2025. Thaksin’s daughter Paetongtarn Shinawatra became prime minister in August 2024 and continued these nascent efforts, stirring the disquiet of conservatives and old PAD networks about MOU 44. 36 Thailand’s Constitutional Court removed Srettha Thavisin from office on 14 August 2024 for violating ethical standards in a cabinet appointment. Critics of the agreement argued that it jeopardised Thai sovereignty over the island of Koh Kut, conferred structural advantages upon Cambodia and reflected conflicts of interest on the Shinawatra clan’s part. 37 Tita Sanglee, “Doubt and Dissent: Thai Nationalist Views on the Thailand-Cambodia Maritime Dispute”, ISEAS Perspective , no. 9, 2025, p. 3. As a prominent Thaksin critic asked: “[F]or whose benefit is the Thai government rushing to negotiate within the old framework, given that [MOU 44] contradicts the 1973 Royal Decree [codifying Thailand’s continental shelf claim] and risks territorial loss, as in the Preah Vihear case?” 38 “‘Mom Korn’ points out that MOU 44 contradicts the royal decree of King Rama IX, risks losing territory and urges its immediate cancellation”, Thai Post , 25 October 2024 [Thai]. In June 2024, Paiboon Nititawan, deputy leader of the military-backed Phalang Pracharat Party (PPRP), petitioned the Constitutional Court to determine whether MOU 44 was illegal because parliament had not approved it. 39 “PPRP seeks ruling on MoU with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 14 June 2024. The court dismissed the petition in September of that year, on the grounds that Paiboon lacked the standing to bring such a case. 40 “Court verdict empowers Thai government to push energy deal with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 17 September 2024. The PPRP then held a press conference a month later alleging that joint development under MOU 44 could jeopardise Thailand’s sovereignty over Koh Kut, putting the government on the defensive. 41 “Thai territory bordering Cambodia is safe, says government”, Bangkok Post , 31 October 2024. Amid demands from the party and conservative activists to scrap MOU 44, Thailand’s defence minister visited the island to assert Thailand’s sovereignty. 42 “Thailand cannot scrap MOU 44 without Cambodia’s okay: Anutin”, The Nation , 4 November 2024; “Thai deputy PM makes case for Cambodia deal”, Bangkok Post , 9 November 2024. B. Border Tensions With maritime tensions simmering, friction increased along the land border. On 13 February 2025, a group of Cambodians visited the disputed Ta Muan Thom/Tamone Thom temple, reportedly escorted by Cambodian soldiers, and sang a patriotic song. Thai soldiers objected to the implicit assertion of sovereignty, which contradicted the “gentlemen’s agreement” governing the area since 2011, and asked the group to leave. 43 The arrangement permitted villagers from both nations to visit the temple but prohibited political or nationalist demonstrations. William J. Jones, “Cambodia undermines ASEAN centrality in 2025 border conflict”, Geopolitical Monitor , 29 January 2026. Video of the incident went viral. 44 “Thai-Cambodian tensions over anthem at temple”, Bangkok Post , 17 February 2025. Two weeks later, on 1 March, a pavilion in the Cambodia-Laos-Thailand tri-border area, built to commemorate neighbourly relations among the three countries, burned down. 45 “Thailand and Cambodia to discuss pavilion fire”, Bangkok Post , 6 March 2025. While the Thai military officially called it an accident, rumours circulated that Cambodian troops had set off the blaze. 46 Crisis Group interview, retired senior Thai military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. See also “Thailand and Cambodia to discuss pavilion fire”, op. cit. The situation escalated on 28 May, when Thai and Cambodian troops exchanged fire in a disputed area between Chong Bok in Thailand’s Ubon Ratchathani province and Cambodia’s Preah Vihear province, killing a Cambodian soldier; both sides claimed the other shot first. 47 “One killed after Thai and Cambodian soldiers briefly clash in a disputed border area”, Associated Press, 28 May 2025. A week earlier, Thailand had alleged that Cambodian troops had been digging trenches and building fortifications in disputed territory in the area but had agreed to withdraw after talks between local commanders. “Thai, Cambodian troops hold talks over border patrol dispute”, The Nation , 18 May 2025. Prime Minister Paetongtarn spoke to Hun Manet the same day. “We don’t want this to escalate”, she told the media. 48 “Paetongtarn discusses with Hun Manet after Thai-Cambodian border clash”, The Nation , 29 May 2025. The countries’ army chiefs met two days later and agreed to pull back their troops. 49 “Army chiefs try to resolve Thai-Cambodian border dispute”, Bangkok Post , 30 May 2025. A welter of developments ensued in June. On 4 June, more than a week after the clash with Cambodian troops, Paetongtarn’s government released a statement affirming “unwavering commitment to safeguarding sovereignty and territorial integrity”. 50 “Statement by Thai Government on Thailand-Cambodia Border Situation”, Thai Government Public Relations Department, 4 June 2025; “Thailand, Cambodia mobilise troops, evacuate villages”, The Nation , 5 June 2025. Two days later, Thailand’s National Security Council delegated full authority to military commanders to administer all border crossings; within a day, the army halved the opening hours at Ban Khlong Luek-Poipet, the main checkpoint along the frontier. 51 “Thailand enforces border controls to safeguard communities amidst rising tensions”, The Nation , 7 June 2025; “Early border closure in Sa Kaeo strands thousands”, Bangkok Post , 7 June 2025. In mid-June, Hun Sen called on Cambodian workers in Thailand – more than 1.5 million people – to come home, while Hun Manet ordered border provinces to prepare for a wave of returnees. 52 “Hun Sen calls upon Cambodian workers to return home from Thailand, before Thai authorities expel them”, Khmer Times , 14 June 2025; “Cambodia braces for mass deportation, mobilises to welcome workers home”, Cambodianess , 14 June 2025. In 2024, Thailand recorded some 459,863 documented Cambodian workers. Estimates of the total, including undocumented persons, range between one and two million. “Cambodia CTIP and Thailand CTIP”, Winrock International, September 2024, p. 4. Satellite imagery of three Khmer Empire-era temples: Ta Moan Thom/Ta Muen Thom (top), Ta Moan Toch/Ta Muen Toch (left) Ta Krabey/Ta Khwai (right), along the Cambodia-Thailand border. Source: Google Earth / CRISIS GROUP As tensions rose, the two sides convened a meeting of the Joint Boundary Commission – the first since 2012. 53 “Press conference on the 6th meeting of the Thailand-Cambodia Joint Boundary Commission”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 15 June 2025. The JBC affirmed agreement on the position of 45 of 73 boundary markers and revised the 2003 Terms of Reference to incorporate light detection and ranging technology in aerial photographic maps. 54 Light detection and ranging is a remote sensing method that determines distance by emitting laser pulses at a target and measuring how long the reflected light takes to return to a receiver. Airborne light detection and ranging units can accurately measure and map ground elevation across large areas. Galen Scott, “Lidar: Lasers, Airplanes and Drones!”, The Earth Scientist , vol. 40, no. 3 (2023), pp. 3-4. Experts said it was a breakthrough, because these instruments can quickly produce accurate 3D terrain maps. 55 William J. Jones and Narut Chareonsri, “The Sovereignty Straitjacket: Cambodia-Thailand Relations, Withdrawal from Memorandum of Understanding 2001 and Regional Security”, Kyoto Review of Southeast Asia , no. 42 (March 2026). Nevertheless, the two sides issued contradictory statements, with Cambodia asserting that the JBC had agreed to use the 1:200,000 scale map annexed to the 1907 treaty, while Thailand’s foreign ministry denied that any such discussion had transpired. 56 “Cambodia categorically refuses to recognize the map drawn unilaterally by Thailand as a basis for border issues”, Khmer Times , 15 June 2025; “Tension lingers following Thailand-Cambodia JBC talks”, Prachatai English , 17 June 2025. On 15 June, Cambodia formally petitioned the ICJ to determine the sovereignty over four disputed sites, three of which encompass Khmer Empire-era temple ruins that nationalists on both sides have imbued with cultural and political significance. 57 The sites are Ta Moan Thom, Ta Moan Tauch, Ta Krabei temple and Mom Bei/Chong Bok. “Cambodia turns to World Court over Thailand border disputes”, Reuters, 15 June 2025. Two weeks earlier, Hun Manet raised the possibility of Cambodia and Thailand seeking a joint ICJ referral, but Bangkok rejected it, having withdrawn recognition of the court’s compulsory jurisdiction in 1960. “Hun Manet calls for urgent border talks with Thailand, proposes ICJ resolution for disputed areas”, Khmer Times , 2 June 2025; “Thailand urges positive engagement after Cambodia threatens to take dispute to World Court”, Reuters, 5 June 2025. The move antagonised Bangkok, which has long maintained that the dispute should be settled bilaterally. 58 “Thailand’s position in response to Cambodia’s submission on 15 June 2025 of a letter to the International Court of Justice related to the Emerald Triangle (Mom Bei), Ta Moan Thom, Ta Moan Tauch and Ta Krabei temples”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 16 June 2025. C. The Fateful Telephone Call On 15 June, Prime Minister Paetongtarn had a telephone conversation with Hun Sen, a nine-minute recorded excerpt of which was made public three days later. 59 Hun Sen acknowledged that he had recorded the call and shared it with some 80 party officials, suggesting that one of them leaked the audio. He later released the full seventeen minutes on his Facebook page. “Hun Sen admits to recording phone call with Thai PM and sharing with 80 officials”, The Nation , 18 June 2025; “Cambodian-Thai tensions escalate on diplomatic and economic fronts”, Khmer Times , 23 June 2025. It revealed that, in her efforts to de-escalate, she was deferential to Hun Sen, addressing him as “uncle” and seeking his understanding regarding the precarious political situation the border dispute had created for her government. Most damagingly, she described the 2nd Army Area commander, Lieutenant General Boonsin Padklang, who was in charge of the areas where clashes had occurred, as belonging to “the opposite side”, a reference to the Thaksin/conservative divide. For his part, Hun Sen asked her to prevail on the Thai military to reopen the border. 60 Nattan Casey Plewissara, “The leaked call shaking Thai politics: Translated”, The Asia Cable (blog), 22 June 2025. The leaked audio roiled Thai politics, confirming the open secret of dissension between government and military, already exacerbated by popular perceptions that the Pheu Thai-led government had been slow in dealing with Cambodia. In contrast, the military, and especially Boonsin, gained public support for adopting an uncompromising stance. 61 “A general at ease: Lt Gen Boonsin’s quiet weekends amid Thai-Cambodian tensions”, Bangkok Post , 14 June 2025. As an analyst put it, the government’s response “accidentally [made] Thai nationalism cool again”. 62 Ken Lohatepanont, “Thai government fails to meet the nationalist moment”, The Coffee Parliament (blog), 8 June 2025. For Thaksin’s critics, the telephone call also appeared to confirm longstanding suspicions that the Shinawatra clan was ready to collude with Hun Sen and “sell out” the country for personal gain. 63 Susannah Patton, “A border skirmish and leaked phone call sees the Thailand-Cambodia dispute surge back to life”, The Interpreter , 20 June 2025; “Thai protesters vent their exasperation with the prime minister”, The New York Times , 28 June 2025. In their view, the call also showed Paetongtarn – Thailand’s youngest-ever prime minister – to be out of her depth in a crisis and thus ripe for unseating. 64 Crisis Group interviews, officials and journalists, Bangkok, April and June 2026. The political consequences unfolded rapidly. The day the recording was exposed, Deputy Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul pulled his Bhumjaithai Party out of the coalition government and called on Paetongtarn to take responsibility for harming the nation’s honour. 65 “Bhumjaithai party announces withdrawal from government coalition”, The Nation , 18 June 2025. The Constitutional Court suspended her from office on 1 July while it considered a petition submitted by 36 senators that she had breached constitutional ethical standards. 66 Deputy Prime Minister Phumtham Wechaiyachai became acting prime minister. “July legal battles fuel momentum for political reset”, Bangkok Post , 25 June 2025; “Constitutional Court suspends Paetongtarn as PM because of Hun Sen’s clip”, The Nation , 1 July 2025. The Pheu Thai Party-led government ... adopted a firmer stance toward Cambodia, highlighting its role as a hub of transnational crime. The leaked audio also had bilateral repercussions, strengthening the Thai military’s hand. 67 Paul Chambers, “The 2025 Thai-Cambodian Conflict from Thailand’s Perspective”, Asia Policy , vol. 21, no. 2 (April 2026), pp. 18-19. On 23 June, the army spokesman announced the closure of all border checkpoints. 68 “Military seals border with Cambodia”, Bangkok Post , 24 June 2025. The Pheu Thai Party-led government also adopted a firmer stance toward Cambodia, highlighting its role as a hub of transnational crime, particularly industrial-scale fraud in scam compounds. 69 “Thai PM seeks international crackdown on Cambodia-based scams”, Bangkok Post , 23 June 2025. On his own social media accounts, meanwhile, Hun Sen kept up a steady stream of invective directed at Thaksin. He spoke of betrayal by the Shinawatras, recalling his hospitality to Thaksin, Thaksin’s sister Yingluck and their supporters; he also predicted that Thailand would have a new prime minister within three months. 70 “Hun Sen: ‘I predict that Thailand will have a new prime minister within the next three months, and I already know who it will be’”, Khmer Times , 25 June 2025. Why Hun Sen severed his longstanding relationship with Thaksin in this way remains a matter of speculation, but analysts in Phnom Penh attribute it to unhappiness that Thaksin had not delivered on joint development of maritime hydrocarbon deposits. 71 Crisis Group interviews, analysts and academics, Phnom Penh, February 2026. See also Gregory V. Raymond, “Patronage Networks, Personal Relationships and the Return of the Thai-Cambodia Border Conflict: A Nontraditional Account”, Asia Policy , vol. 21, no. 2 (April 2026). Others point to Paetongtarn’s plans to legalise gambling in Thailand, which would undercut Cambodia’s casinos, or the intensifying Thai campaign against scam centres across the border, which by one rough estimate generate one quarter to two fifths of Cambodia’s GDP. 72 Crisis Group interviews, analyst, Phnom Penh, February 2026; former government official, Phnom Penh, February 2026. The GDP share estimate appears in Jacob Sims and Bopha Phorn, “The Scam Economy in Cambodia”, Southeast Asian Affairs , 2026, p. 78. Many in Cambodia also believe it was an emotional decision, as Hun Sen was irritated by Paetongtarn calling Hun Manet “unprofessional” for issuing statements on social media. 73 Crisis Group interviews, former official, academic, Phnom Penh, February 2026; Western diplomat, Phnom Penh, May 2026. Thailand’s Constitutional Court removed Paetongtarn from office on 29 August, as it had done with all five Thaksin-aligned prime ministers since the 2006 coup. 74 On 9 September 2025, the Supreme Court sentenced Thaksin to serve the prison term he had avoided upon returning from exile in 2023. He was released the following 11 May. Anutin was elected prime minister a week later, promising fresh elections within four months. 75 Anutin dissolved parliament on 12 December 2025, and the general election took place on 8 February. IV. Fighting and Ceasefires The balance of power between Cambodia and Thailand is lopsided. Thailand dwarfs its neighbour in population (roughly 70 million to 17 million), gross domestic product ($577 billion to $51.2 billion in 2025), military spending ($5.7 billion to $1.3 billion in 2024) and armed forces (360,850 active personnel to 124,300). 76 World Bank data; “The Military Balance 2025”, International Institute for Strategic Studies, pp. 238; 302-303. These asymmetries weighed heavily on the battlefield, especially during the protracted December fighting in which Thailand gained the upper hand. A. Round One Tensions rose sharply after landmines wounded eight Thai soldiers on 16 and 23 July 2025 on the border area of Nam Yeun district, Ubon Ratchathani province. 77 “Landmine dispute escalates tensions between Thailand and Cambodia”, Reuters, 22 July 2025; “New mine blast inflames border tensions”, Bangkok Post , 23 July 2025. Thailand said the mines were newly laid; Cambodia said they were remnants of earlier conflicts. 78 Cambodia is among the countries most affected by landmines and other explosive remnants of war, with an estimated contaminated area of 1,856 sq km as of January 2024. See the Cambodian Mine Action Centre website. Thailand then expelled Cambodia’s ambassador and withdrew its own. The Preah Vihear temple has long been at the centre of the border dispute between Cambodia and Thailand. Renewed fighting along the border in 2025 killed at least 150 people and displaced almost a million more. Sources: UN OCHA Humanitarian Data Exchange, Subnational Administrative Boundaries (Cambodia, Thailand); OpenStreetMap; Google Earth satellite verification / CRISIS GROUP On 24 July, fighting broke out between ground troops near Ta Muen Thom and Ta Krabei temples, between Thailand’s Surin and Cambodia’s Oddar Meanchey provinces, with each side accusing the other of firing the first shot. 79 “Thailand launches airstrikes on Cambodia as border clash escalates”, Washington Post , 24 July 2025. The combat escalated quickly to unprecedented levels. Cambodian BM-21 rockets hit civilian areas in Thailand’s Kantharalak district, killing seven people, including two children, at a petrol station some 20km from the border. 80 “Strikes on civilians a ‘war crime’”, Bangkok Post , 25 July 2025. Thailand launched airstrikes on military targets in Preah Vihear, the first use of airpower across the Thai-Cambodian border since the early 1970s. 81 “Thailand and Cambodia exchange fire in new border clashes that kill at least 1 civilian”, Associated Press, 24 July 2025. Altogether, in five days, the exchanges killed at least 48 people and displaced some 300,000 civilians. 82 “Thailand-Cambodia border calm as military commanders hold talks”, Reuters, 29 July 2025; “Thai police fire tear gas at Cambodian protesters at a disputed border village”, Reuters, 18 September 2025. On 24 July, Malaysian Prime Minister and acting ASEAN chairman Anwar Ibrahim appealed for a ceasefire. 83 “Thailand, Cambodia must ‘stand down’ over border clash: Malaysian PM”, Thai PBS World, 24 July 2025. China also pushed for negotiations. Phnom Penh was ready for dialogue, but Bangkok was reluctant until the U.S. also weighed in. President Donald Trump stated that if the two countries did not negotiate, he would suspend trade talks with both. As Thailand was eager to use these talks to secure lower tariffs on exports to the U.S., Trump’s threat was sufficient to bring it to the table with Cambodia. 84 “Exclusive: Trump’s call broke deadlock in Thailand-Cambodia border crisis”, Reuters, 31 July 2025. On 28 July, acting Prime Minister Phumtham Wechaiyachai met Hun Manet in Putrajaya and agreed to a ceasefire, as well as a meeting of regional military commanders the next day and a meeting of the General Border Committee in early August. 85 “Joint Press Release on the Special Meeting Hosted by Malaysia to Address the Current Situation between Cambodia and Thailand”, Malaysian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 28 July 2025. The prime ministers also agreed to Anwar’s proposal for ASEAN observers to monitor the ceasefire. 86 Crisis Group interview, retired senior military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. See also “ASEAN chair deploys observer team to monitor Thai-Cambodian ceasefire”, The Nation , 28 July 2025. B. Interregnum The ceasefire was fragile from the start, with allegations of violations soon emerging from both capitals. 1. Developments on the border The situation was particularly fraught at Ban Nong Chan and Ban Nong Ya Kaeo in Khok Sung district, Sa Kaeo province abutting Cambodia's Chouk Chey and Prey Chan villages, where thousands of Cambodians had settled as refugees in the 1980s, on land Thailand claims. The Thai military, reportedly impatient with the government’s failure to evict these people, pressed it to act. 87 “Thai military increases pressure on govt, Cambodia to relocate encroachers”, The Nation , 2 September 2025. Thai riot police scuffled with Cambodians at Ban Nong Ya Kaeo on 17 September, injuring 23 with tear gas and rubber bullets; Thai officers also reportedly sustained injuries. 88 “Thailand gives Cambodia 30 days to withdraw after border clashes”, Khaosod English , 17 September 2025; “Thai police fire tear gas at Cambodian protesters at a disputed border village”, Reuters, 18 September 2025. In early October, Thailand began stacking up shipping containers to build walls, cordoning off parts of Ban Nong Chan to prevent Cambodians from entering. 89 “Cargo containers arrive in Ban Nong Chan to reinforce border wall”, Thai PBS World, 10 October 2025. The situation was particularly fraught at Ban Nong Chan and Ban Nong Ya Kaeo, Sa Kaeo province, abutting Cambodia’s Chouk Chey and Prey Chan villages, where thousands of Cambodians had settled as refugees in the 1980s. Sources: UN OCHA Humanitarian Data Exchange, Subnational Administrative Boundaries (Cambodia, Thailand); OpenStreetMap; Google Earth satellite verification / CRISIS GROUP Amid these confrontations, bilateral border mechanisms kept functioning. On 27 August, a Regional Border Committee meeting affirmed the ceasefire and pledged cooperation on demining and crime suppression. 90 “Second Army outlines 11-point RBC, Cambodia defers demining and scams to GBC”, The Nation , 27 August 2025. On 10 September, at a special General Border Committee meeting convened in Koh Kong, Cambodia, the parties agreed to remove heavy weapons from the border, develop terms of reference for ASEAN Observer Teams on each side of the border and cooperate on demining. They also said they would refer the matter of Chouk Chey/Nong Chan to the next JBC meeting as a priority for joint survey and demarcation, “peacefully manag[ing] the situation on the ground” in the meantime. 91 “Joint Press Statement of the Special General Border Committee Meeting, Koh Kong, Cambodia”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 10 September 2025. Despite the positive tone, tensions lingered, as Thai conservative activists whipped up nationalist sentiment. On 10 October, with the Thai military’s permission, social media celebrity Kanthat Pongpaiboonwet began broadcasting piercing, “ghostly” noises through loudspeakers at Ban Nong Chan and Ban Nong Ya Kaeo to intimidate Cambodians. 92 “Thai army defends psych-ops along Cambodian border”, Bangkok Post , 12 October 2025. Earlier, in late August, Kanthat had brought fourteen sewage trucks to Ban Nong Chan. He had intended to spray protesting Cambodians with sewage, but authorities prevented him from doing so. “Thai social media star stages sewage stunt at tense border”, Bangkok Post , 28 August 2025. The Thai military put a stop to the stunt after a week, but prominent figures who spoke out against it had to seek police protection after receiving death threats. 93 “Army orders halt to ‘sound war’ against Cambodians in Sa Kaeo province”, Thai PBS World, 19 October 2025; “Action urged after border comment death threats”, Bangkok Post , 21 October 2025. 2. International peace efforts Meanwhile, in an 8 October letter, President Trump urged Thailand’s new prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, to reach a peace deal with Cambodia. 94 “Thailand snubs Trump’s mediation, tells Cambodia to remove border troops”, Bloomberg, 9 October 2025. Trump agreed to attend the forthcoming ASEAN summit on the condition that he could preside over a peace accord signing ceremony. 95 “Trump seeks peace ceremony spotlight at ASEAN summit”, Politico , 6 October 2025. Anutin responded that Trump should press Cambodia to meet four conditions: withdrawing heavy weapons, removing landmines, eliminating scam centres and relocating Cambodian settlements on Thai territory. 96 “Anutin to notify Trump, urging Cambodia to comply with Thai conditions”, The Nation , 9 October 2025. As the ASEAN summit approached, Thai officials suggested that peace prospects hinged on a JBC meeting and the second Special GBC meeting, both scheduled for 20-23 October. 97 “Anutin chairs security meeting ahead of GBC-JBC talks”, The Nation , 20 October 2025. These achieved a measure of success: the JBC assented to expediting the joint survey in the Chouk Chey-Nong Chan and Prey Chan-Nong Ya Kaeo area, while the GBC delegations produced an in-principle agreement to withdraw heavy weapons, clear mines and cooperate against scam centres. 98 “Border talks agree to repair markers, review land holdings”, Bangkok Post , 23 October 2025. On 26 October, Trump presided over the signing of a joint declaration by Prime Ministers Anutin and Hun Manet, endorsed by Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur. Despite the fanfare, the joint declaration amounted to a recommitment to the terms of the 28 July ceasefire: withdrawing heavy weapons, coordinating demining and border demarcation, and desisting from dissemination of false information and “harmful rhetoric”. 99 Thailand also committed to promptly release eighteen Cambodian prisoners of war. “Joint Declaration by the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Cambodia and the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Thailand on the outcomes of their meeting in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia”, White House, 26 October 2025. Speaking at the summit, Anutin sought to reassure the Thai public, saying the agreement would not put Thailand at a disadvantage. He specified that the 1:200,000 map was not discussed and that light detection and ranging technology had rendered the Annex I map obsolete. 100 “PM claims joint declaration with Cambodia won’t disadvantage Thailand”, Thai PBS World, 26 October 2025. C. Round Two Just two weeks after the Kuala Lumpur accord, the ceasefire began to unravel. On 10 November, Prime Minister Anutin said Thailand would stop observing the joint statement after a landmine wounded four Thai soldiers in Kantharalak district. 101 “Anutin halts Thai-Cambodian peace declaration after Thai troops hit landmine again”, The Nation , 10 November 2025. The four incidents that wounded sixteen Thai soldiers in 2025 all involved recently laid PMN-2 antipersonnel mines, of which Cambodia has stocks. All the incidents occurred on customary patrol routes in contested territory previously known to be safe and often used by both armies. According to an independent analysis, “these incidents [have] the appearance of a targeted military activity”. “Investigation into New Use of Antipersonnel Landmines on the Thai-Cambodia Border”, Landmine Monitor, 1 March 2026, p. 20. On file with Crisis Group. The U.S. briefly tried to intercede, saying it would suspend talks about a reciprocal trade framework agreement – which would have meant higher tariffs – if Bangkok did not reverse course. 102 “US halts trade talks with Thailand over peace pact compliance”, Bangkok Post , 15 November 2025. But Thai officials learned that no such penalty was forthcoming. Within a month, troops exchanged fire in the same district, and fighting soon spread. 103 “Thai-Cambodia border clash injures two Thai troops, triggers evacuation”, Khaosod English , 7 December 2025; “Briefing to the Diplomatic Corps and International Organizations on Developments on the Thailand-Cambodia Border Situation”, Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 8 December 2025. Thai officials made clear that this round of combat would differ from the first. “The aim of the Thai army is to disable Cambodia’s military capability for a long time, for the sake of our children’s safety”, army chief of staff Chaiyapruek Duangprapat explained. 104 “PM Anutin says no more negotiations with Cambodia”, Thai PBS World, 8 December 2025. On 9 December, Anutin said Thailand was determined to push ahead, notwithstanding calls for dialogue: “We can’t stop now. We’ve already given our commitment to the armed forces that they can fully carry out the planned operations”. 105 “Border battle expands as Thailand and Cambodia clash for second day”, Reuters, 9 December 2025. At its height, the fighting had displaced over 600,000 people in Cambodia and some 400,000 in Thailand. Combat continued for twenty days, including rocket and artillery exchanges and Thai airstrikes that hit targets deep inside Cambodia. 106 “Cambodia counts the cost of its border war with Thailand”, BBC, 19 December 2025. At its height, the fighting had displaced over 600,000 people in Cambodia and some 400,000 in Thailand. 107 Roughly 84.5 per cent of the displaced in Cambodia were women and children. “Situation Report 20 – Displacement Crisis as a Result of the Cambodia-Thailand Border Conflict”, op. cit. At least 101 people were killed, including 26 Thai soldiers. Cambodia did not release military casualty figures, but media estimates put the toll at roughly 130 killed. 108 “Cambodian deaths exceed 110 in December border conflict with Thailand”, Nikkei Asia , 13 January 2026. Reported Thai military estimates of the number of Cambodian troops killed range from 200 to 500. “Army places district out of bounds”, Bangkok Post , 16 December 2025; “Thailand carries out more airstrikes on Cambodia as deadly border conflict flares”, Associated Press, 18 December 2025. Again, Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar played an important role in ending the hostilities. 109 “Anwar calls Thai, Cambodian leaders to discuss border clashes”, Thai PBS World, 10 December 2025. As ASEAN chairman, he convened a special foreign ministers’ meeting that called for an immediate ceasefire, withdrawal of troops under the watch of interim ASEAN Observer Teams and bilateral dialogue. 110 “ASEAN Chair’s Statement Special ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on the Current Situation between Cambodia and Thailand”, 22 December 2025. Washington urged talks, but Thailand was less inclined to respond to U.S. pressure than it had been in July, as the Trump administration had not imposed the higher tariffs it threatened after Bangkok stopped observing the ceasefire in November. 111 “On Fighting on the Cambodia-Thailand Border”, press statement, U.S. State Department, 9 December 2025; “Thailand says US trade talks to proceed despite Cambodia dispute”, Reuters, 15 November 2025. China, meanwhile, played a more prominent mediating role in December. 112 Immediately after the first ceasefire agreement, China’s vice minister for foreign affairs, Sun Weidong, hosted Cambodian and Thai officials for an “informal consultation” in Shanghai. “China vows to continue Thailand-Cambodia peace efforts after ‘informal’ post-truce talks”, South China Morning Post , 30 July 2025. Foreign Minister Wang Yi called his Cambodian and Thai counterparts directly, and Deng Xijun, Beijing’s special envoy for Asian affairs, visited both countries. 113 “Special Envoy for Asian Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Makes Another Shuttle-Diplomacy Trip for Peace between Cambodia and Thailand”, Chinese Foreign Ministry, 25 December 2025. Cambodia and Thailand eventually agreed to a ceasefire at a special GBC meeting on 27 December. Key provisions include commitments to resume “at the earliest” efforts to survey and demarcate the border using the JBC’s existing mechanisms, as well as to refrain from building up forces along the border. 114 The two parties also agreed to cooperate against scam centres. “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special General Border Committee between the Kingdom of Thailand and the Kingdom of Cambodia at Ban Pak Kard (Chanthaburi Province of Thailand)-Prum (Pailin Province of Cambodia) International Point of Entry”, 27 December 2025. The day after the agreement was signed, Wang Yi hosted Foreign Ministers Sihasak Phuangketkeow and Prak Sokhonn in Yuxi, Yunnan province. 115 “Foreign Ministers of China, Cambodia, and Thailand Hold Trilateral Meeting”, Chinese Foreign Ministry, 29 December 2025. According to a Thai official, China played a constructive role outside the media glare: “They are fair, not trying to impose a solution”. 116 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Thai Foreign Ministry, Bangkok, April 2026. V. Not Turning the Page Following the December ceasefire, relations have remained tense with little movement toward restoring normal diplomatic relations or delimiting the land border. Instead, the two governments have remained locked in a contest for international public opinion amid regular border provocations and fears of a third round of war. A. A New Status Quo When the dust settled from the December fighting, the Thai military had most of the high ground. Thailand now holds not only territory in contested areas, but also land that is indisputably Cambodian, beyond Bangkok’s proposed border line. Bangkok justifies its action by arguing that the ceasefire froze the conflict where it stood on 27 December, citing point 2 of the joint statement, which says, “Both sides agree to maintain current troop deployments without further movement”. 117 “Joint Statement of the 3rd Special GBC”, op. cit. Following the same logic, Thai troops have built walls of stacked shipping containers and barbed wire in disputed areas, notably those from which they forcibly repatriated Cambodian refugees who had settled there in the 1980s. 118 The areas in question are Ban Nong Chan/Chouk Chey and Nong Ya Kaeo/Prey Chan, in Thailand’s Khok Sung district, Sa Kaeo province and Cambodia’s O’Chrov district, Banteay Meanchey province. Thailand has also built container walls in Bang Tha Sen, Muang district, Trat province/Thma [Thmor] Da, Pursat province; and Chong An Mah, Ubon Ratchathani/An Seh village, Choam Ksan district, Preah Vihear province. According to Cambodian officials, Thailand expelled 1,200 families from these areas. 119 “A tale of two villages: Cambodians lament Thailand’s border gains”, Agence France-Presse, 7 February 2026. The Thai military, which has also destroyed homes in these locations, describes the barriers as a “reorganisation” needed for security, strictly in accordance with the 27 December joint statement. 120 “Cambodia says Thai troops still occupy civilian areas, testing December truce”, Reuters, 14 January 2026; “Army denies blocking return of displaced”, Bangkok Post , 29 March 2026. C. Nationalism as Policy Constraint Thailand’s policy appears to be conditioned by consideration for the views of ultranationalist Thais, including serving and former military officers, who espouse the narrative of lost territories and oppose even the appearance of conciliation. 142 Crisis Group interviews, analyst; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. “The land border has grown into an emotional issue”, a senior security official said. “The government can’t back down”. 143 Crisis Group interview, senior security official, Bangkok, April 2026. Privately, Thai officials acknowledge that Bangkok finds the status quo acceptable. 145 Crisis Group interviews, senior official, Bangkok, April 2026; retired senior Thai military officer, Bangkok, June 2026. As one put it: “For domestic political reasons, this works well. There’s no strong desire to normalise [relations]”. 146 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, April 2026. VI. Averting a Third Round Demarcating the land border is essential if the two countries are to remove disputed territory as a source of conflict, leading to the loss of hundreds of lives over the past eighteen years. The means of specifying the land border already exist: the JBC has already demarcated three quarters of it. The main impediment is not technical complexity – the revised 2003 Terms of Reference and advantages offered by light detection and ranging should suffice – but rather the mistrust between Bangkok and Phnom Penh. Given events of the past year, there are genuine worries on both sides that a third round of fighting is likely – a former high-ranking Thai officer even called the prospect “inevitable”. 167 Crisis Group interviews, diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. See also “Ex-deputy commander of Second Army Area warns third round of fighting ‘will happen’”, The Nation , 28 January 2026. Ideally, third-party mediation would make the necessary compromises more politically palatable. As Hun Sen noted in June 2025, any Cambodian or Thai leader who retreats from maximalist positions at this point would risk incurring public disapproval. 168 “Selected Comments of Samdech Akka Moha Sena Padei Techo Hun Sen, President of the Senate, on the Cambodia-Thailand Border Issue”, 2 June 2025. A disinterested third party could shield decision-makers from some of the political costs of compromise. The most logical candidate to play such a role remains the ICJ. Even if many in Thailand regard the ICJ’s 1962 ruling on Preah Vihear as unjust, it does not establish a binding precedent for other disputed areas of the land border. If Cambodia and Thailand agreed to have the court rule on all these areas, it could very well lead to an equitable resolution. 169 William Roth, “Tackling Thai-Cambodian border row”, Bangkok Post (editorial), 12 November 2025. Unfortunately, such a path is, for now, politically untenable in Thailand, both because of bitterness over the 1962 ruling and the establishment’s objections to internationalising the conflict. The reality of heightened nationalism is that the Thai government is unlikely to attempt to sell the public on trading even a small amount of territory for peace. 170 Jones and Narut, “The Sovereignty Straitjacket”, op. cit. Prime Minister Anutin was rewarded at the polls for maintaining a hard line on Cambodia. In turn, he is intent on keeping the Thai military’s support. He also does not wish to run afoul of right-wing nationalists who perceive bargaining as a betrayal of sacrifices, military and civilian, in the 2025 fighting. 171 “New government faces MOU 43 dilemma as Cambodia pushes JBC talks”, The Nation , 2 January 2026. Furthermore, conflict with Cambodia has allowed the Thai military to burnish its image, which had been sullied by its overt political role, including coups d’état. 172 Crisis Group interviews, journalist, Bangkok, April 2026. In this charged environment, those advocating compromise risk being labelled traitors. 173 Crisis Group interviews, Western diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. The costs of conflict are not high enough to impel [Thai and Cambodian] leaders toward a resolution. More broadly, political elites in both countries perceive benefits from the conflict, principally from popular support arising from nationalism and as a distraction from domestic economic and political problems. For decision-makers, especially in Thailand, these benefits continue to outweigh the conflict’s costs, whether economic or reputational. In any event, the costs of conflict are not high enough to impel leaders toward a resolution. Cambodia adapted to the border closure better than many anticipated, though it has compounded pre-existing economic pressures as time goes by, contributing to a marked slowdown in growth. 174 Crisis Group interview, government minister, Phnom Penh, February 2026. See also “IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Cambodia”, International Monetary Fund, 28 September 2026. The IMF projects growth to slow to 3 per cent in 2026, from 5.3 per cent in 2025. In any case, disruptions of bilateral trade have been damaging, but not bad enough to trigger a policy change. 175 Closure of the land border caused trade to decline by 40 per cent to $1.3 billion for the first half of 2026, year-on-year, according to Cambodian government data. “Cambodian economy suffers as Thai conflict blights bilateral trade”, Nikkei Asia , 24 July 2026. Some 900,000 Cambodian migrant workers returned from Thailand in 2025; two thirds of them found employment, though generally lower-paid. The UN estimated remittance losses at $277 million in 2025 and $665 million in 2026. “Socio-economic Impact Assessment of Cambodia–Thailand Border”, UN, April 2026, p. 10. Perhaps the most significant obstacle is that, for now, political elites in Bangkok appear to see greater reward in hardline policies than in the risks of reconciliation. Delaying border demarcation [between Thailand and Cambodia] only heightens the risk of renewed fighting. These actions could help build trust with Thailand. Both governments would serve their own interests by toning down statements that have hardened opinion and narrowed the room for compromise. Cambodia, in particular, would benefit from speaking with one voice on the border. Hun Sen’s statements, especially in 2025, attacked Thai leaders personally and raised tensions. Hun Sen often speaks before the prime minister, setting a line from which Hun Manet cannot easily depart. 184 Crisis Group interviews, Phnom Penh, February and May 2026. Leaving border matters to the prime minister, the foreign ministry and the bilateral mechanisms would give Cambodia a more coherent posture and Hun Manet room to seek a new relationship with Bangkok. Restraint is also needed on the Thai side, where senior military officers accused Hun Sen of lying and labelled him the real commander of Cambodian forces during the December fighting. 185 “RTA says Hun Sen lied, ordered provocative acts against Thailand”, The Nation , 10 December 2025. Such charges may play well at home, but they make it harder for Thai officials to treat Hun Manet as the preferred counterpart. 186 Crisis Group interview, senior official, Bangkok, September 2026. International bodies and foreign states lack sufficient leverage to push [the Thai and Cambodian officials] to the negotiating table. International bodies and foreign states lack sufficient leverage to push the sides to the negotiating table or otherwise decisively influence the course of events. U.S. diplomats remain engaged, but Washington is preoccupied with the Middle East war and shows little appetite for leading mediation efforts. 187 “US to provide $45m for Thailand-Cambodia ceasefire”, Nikkei Asia , 9 January 2026. For its part, China is unlikely to risk souring its relationship with either country by attempting to impose an agreement touching on the sensitive issue of sovereignty. Beijing should nevertheless intensify its Track II efforts, which have provided a welcome platform for civil society engagement and could furnish creative ideas for mending people-to-people ties. 188 “Summary Report: The Second China-Cambodia-Thailand Track II Dialogue, 20-21 April 2026, Beijing, China”. On file with Crisis Group. For its part, ASEAN should play a greater role. Ceasefire monitoring could help build confidence between the two sides, but the current configuration of the ASEAN Observation Teams leaves that potential unrealised. The teams, staffed by military attachés and ASEAN representatives based in Bangkok and Phnom Penh, can observe border areas only with the host country’s permission and coordination. 189 “Domestic pressure holds Thailand-Cambodia peace deal hostage”, Thai PBS World, 30 October 2025. Consequently, the teams have become implicated in the rival information strategies, with both Bangkok and Phnom Penh using site visits to cast blame on their adversary. 190 Crisis Group interview, analyst, Bangkok, April 2026. See also “Can ASEAN keep the Thailand-Cambodia peace?”, South China Morning Post , 5 July 2026. Both sides should permit observers greater independence. 191 Crisis Group interviews, diplomat, Phnom Penh, February 2026; senior official, Bangkok, July 2026. VII. Conclusion The fighting in 2025 has given way to an uneasy ceasefire that leaves Cambodia and Thailand no closer to resolving the underlying border dispute. With nationalism running high on both sides, political elites in Bangkok and Phnom Penh perceive greater rewards in hardline posturing than in compromise. To prevent the recurrence of a conflict that has already caused hundreds of deaths and displaced over a million people, Cambodia and Thailand will eventually have to survey and demarcate the land border, requiring compromise on both sides. Current prospects for a rapprochement are poor, however, and foreign states lack the leverage or commitment to impose a settlement. In the near term, the priority should be modest steps: restoring normal diplomatic relations by returning ambassadors, resuming the JBC’s technical demarcation work without preconditions and expanding cooperation on demining. The two sides should also permit ASEAN Observer Teams a more independent monitoring role. None of these measures will resolve the territorial dispute, but they could help rebuild the trust and communication needed to manage tensions and reduce the risk of renewed violence while a comprehensive settlement remains politically out of reach. In this episode of Hold Your Fire! , Richard is joined by Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa director, Alan Boswell, to discuss the fighting in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, the risk of direct war between Ethiopia and Eritrea and what may prevent further escalation. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Horn of Africa Ethiopia/Eritrea This week on Hold Your Fire! , Richard is joined by Alan Boswell, Crisis Group’s Horn of Africa director, to discuss the fighting in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region and the risk of an all-out war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. They examine federal forces’ recapture of Tigray’s capital Mekelle and what has changed since the previous war. They explore Eritrea’s calculations in backing its former enemy, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, and whether Ethiopian advances toward the Eritrean border could bring the two countries into direct conflict. They also discuss Ethiopia’s push for Red Sea access and how it has further fuelled tensions with Eritrea. Turning to the wider region, they assess how Middle Eastern powers’ competing interests could shape their responses to a war between Ethiopia and Eritrea, and the risk of such a conflict becoming entangled with wars in Sudan.
