A psychologist at Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar said that her consultations on campus “have tripled” since March. “Many patients are young men experiencing severe anxiety, hypervigilance, withdrawal from social life, and obsessive behaviors driven by fear of being perceived and attacked as LGBT.” Recommendations To Senegal’s President Order the immediate release of everyone arbitrarily detained since February 2026 under article 319 of the penal code. Refer the amended law to the Constitutional Council for constitutional review of its compatibility with constitutional guarantees of the right to privacy, equality before the law, non-discrimination, and fair trial rights. Publicly commit, ahead of the Youth Olympic Games, to ensure that all participants, visitors, and residents alike, will be protected from discrimination and arbitrary arrests. To the National Assembly Repeal article 319 in its entirety, including the provisions of the amended penal code that criminalize the “promotion” or “glorification” of homosexuality, as well as the financing or support of LGBT individuals and organizations.Initiate a legislative review to remove HIV status as a criminal aggravating factor. To Senegal’s Government Open an investigation of abuses documented against LGBT people and hold those responsible accountable.Instruct judicial authorities to uphold national and international laws to guarantee access to legal representation for all detainees and ensure lawyers can represent clients without intimidation, harassment, or risk of prosecution.Ensure that pretrial detention is an exceptional measure, not a standard procedure, and that anyone in such detention is guaranteed a trial within a reasonable time or release.Prohibit forced HIV testing, ensure informed consent for all medical testing, prevent the use of confidential health information in criminal proceedings, and protect medical confidentiality, including by prohibiting the disclosure of detainees’ health information to the media.Open an independent investigation into the case concerning a gendarmerie commander who pressured a detainee to waive his right to legal representation before leaking the detainee’s HIV status to journalists.Respect and protect the rights to freedom of expression, association, and peaceful assembly, including for individuals and organizations advocating for the rights of LGBT people. To the National Medical Council Reaffirm that forced HIV testing violates medical ethics.

Türkiye: End Internet Censorship. Click to expand Image Tags, with “Access blocked” and the name of blocked accounts belonging to journalists and media outlets, LGBT and women’s rights groups, and other rights defenders, are tied to the gates of Turkey’s Constitutional Court, to protest the Turkish authorities’ blocking of hundreds of social media accounts and websites. Ankara, October 7, 2026. © 2026 Yıldız Yazıcıoğlu (Istanbul, October 12, 2026) – The Turkish authorities over the last month have substantially escalated internet censorship, Human Rights Watch said today, along with ARTICLE 19, the Freedom of Expression Association, and 18 other organizations. Social media platforms should take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to suppressing independent media and violating the right to freedom of expression. The Turkish authorities should stop issuing blocking orders to restrict content and accounts on social media and websites in violation of the right to freedom of expression. The following is the groups’ statement: ARTICLE 19, Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD), Human Rights Watch, and the undersigned human rights and media freedom organisations are deeply concerned by the severe escalation of internet censorship in Türkiye in the past month. We urge social media platforms to take meaningful steps immediately to uphold their human rights responsibilities and avoid contributing to the suppression of independent media and violations of the right to freedom of expression. We call on the Turkish government immediately to cease the use of blocking orders and other restrictive measures that violate the right to freedom of expression, and to ensure that any restrictions on online content fully comply with Türkiye’s obligations under international human rights law. In the month of September 2026 alone, İFÖD documented Turkish authorities and courts ordering the blocking of access to at least 1,270 accounts on the social media platform X, which had a combined following of 35 million. X complied with at least 90 percent of the orders by geo-blocking them (withholding access to them in Türkiye only). In many cases, the accounts were blocked in the context of an ongoing and wide-ranging crackdown on associations and activists defending the rights of LGBTQ+ people. In other cases, the authorities cited unspecified “national security and public order” grounds. Accounts withheld include news outlets such as soL Haber and Mezopotamya Ajansı; rights organisations including Amnesty Türkiye and the Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA); LGBTQ+; and women’s rights organisations such as Kaos GL and the Federation of Women’s Associations, as well as those of numerous journalists and academics. X also withheld the accounts of İFÖD, its co-founder, Yaman Akdeniz, and its Engelliweb account, which monitors and documents internet censorship in Türkiye. This account plays a critical role in enabling civil society, journalists, and the public to monitor and track websites, social media accounts and content subjected to access restrictions. Blocking T24, one of Türkiye’s biggest and oldest remaining independent news outlets, is particularly troubling. On 29 September, access was blocked to the T24 website and X account with 1.9 million followers, with a court order citing 118 news articles published on the site. The order claimed that the content was “aimed at disrupting and weakening the Turkish family structure” and of a nature “that would adversely affect the developmental process of young and underage individuals concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.” The order cited preventing crime and protecting public order as grounds for the measure but provided no explanation about how the cited content posed a threat to either objective or why blocking an entire news website and social media account was necessary and proportionate. The website has been inaccessible in Türkiye since 30 September. T24 changed its X handle in an attempt to prevent the account from being withheld in Türkiye, then changed it again, after another order blocked access to its second handle. Bianet, another online news outlet which focuses on human rights, also changed its X handle to escape censorship after its account with 400,000 followers was blocked. The court order blocking access to T24 was taken in the context of the “my family is safe” criminal investigations – a crackdown on LGBTQ+ people which targets activists, associations and a journalist advocating for their rights. The websites and social media accounts of at least 96 organizations and individuals were blocked on the same grounds. While most of the cases concern X, Meta has also withheld access to the Instagram and Facebook accounts of several media and civil society organisations, including, Kısa Dalga, Kaos GL, and the Civic Space Studies Association as part of the same operation. Türkiye’s long-standing abuse of Article 8/A of its Internet Law Most of the blocking decisions in September and October invoked Article 8/A of Türkiye’s Internet Law. Article 8/A, used as a tool for internet censorship since its introduction in 2015, provides that online content deemed a threat to national security, public order or presenting a risk on other grounds listed in the article can be removed or blocked on orders of the executive in urgent cases, subject to review later by a Criminal Peace Judgeship, the court assigned such cases. Major examples include blocking access to Wikipedia for 2.5 years in 2017, and to Türkiye’s leading user-generated online discussion platform Ekşi Sözlük for a year in 2023. The Constitutional Court eventually restored both, finding that blocking the entire sites had violated freedom of expression. The use of Article 8/A intensified sharply from 2025, with few safeguards or independent oversight and limited redress for those affected. The Constitutional Court has not ruled on any restrictions under Article 8/A since 2023. Concerning developments aimed at expanding censorship There is no indication that this pressure will ease. On the contrary, the government is taking further measures to accelerate and centralise internet censorship. On 31 July, Law No. 7590 transferred the powers previously exercised by the Information and Communication Technologies Authority (ICTA) contained in the Internet Law, to the Cybersecurity Directorate. This includes the authority to block sites on the request of the presidency or relevant ministries based on Article 8/A. This transfer of authority is troubling. The Cybersecurity Directorate is directly attached to the presidency, consolidating executive control over information and serving as the command centre for Türkiye’s censorship regime. Separately, on 24 September, the justice minister announced the establishment of new “Digital Space Security and Countering Disinformation Bureaux,” where specialised public prosecutors will closely monitor “criminal content and activities encouraging crime on digital platforms” including ‘spreading disinformation.” They are tasked in particular with identifying suspects and initiating criminal proceedings to intervene “more swiftly.” Social media platforms should take urgent action to uphold their human rights responsibilities The conduct of social media platforms forms an essential part of internet censorship in Türkiye. In September and early October, account holders reported receiving only a notification from platforms stating that their account had been withheld in Türkiye under Article 8/A, without any reason or explanation why or how the article had been applied. Some were unable to access the underlying blocking orders even after repeatedly requesting them from the platforms. Without access to the orders, users cannot examine the legal basis for the restriction or even identify to which Criminal Judgeship of Peace to submit their objections. Even when users were able to obtain the orders, the orders often failed to identify the specific content allegedly justifying the blocking of the entire account. Neither X nor Meta have provided public explanations about their responses to the September-October censorship waves. Human Rights Watch wrote to the two platforms requesting comment on their compliance with Turkish courts’ recent blocking orders. Neither platform had responded by the time of publication. Under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, companies have a responsibility to respect human rights by avoiding causing or contributing to adverse human rights impacts and by addressing impacts directly linked to their operations, products, or services. This responsibility should also inform social media platforms when they respond to government requests that violate international human rights law, and in particular freedom of expression. We therefore urge X, Meta, and any other platform faced with such orders by the Turkish government to also follow these recommendations: Resist complying with arbitrary 8/A requests Refuse to comply with account blocking requests under Article 8/A of the Internet Law unless Turkish authorities identify the specific content at issue and provide sufficient reasoning and evidence demonstrating that the content gives rise to a clear, serious and imminent danger to the right to life and property, national security and public order, public health or other ground listed in the provision. Where account blocking orders provide sufficient information to enable a meaningful assessment, assess them against international human rights law and resist complying with blocking orders that restrict access to protected expression. This includes but is not limited to legally challenging such orders. Where relevant, limit restrictions in scope and duration, for example by restricting access only to the specific content identified in the order rather than withholding the entire account. Ensure transparency Immediately notify users when their accounts are withheld in Türkiye and provide them with the orders on which the restriction is based. This allows account holders to take necessary steps to challenge the orders. Provide transparency concerning account blocking measures, at least by publicly sharing the number of orders received, the number of orders complied with, and publishing case studies. This information is essential for enabling public scrutiny of government censorship and platforms’ role in it. Engage with Turkish civil society Meaningfully engage with Turkish civil society to understand the human rights implications and broader impact of platforms complying with account blocking measures, including the significance of the accounts targeted and the potential consequences of withholding them in Türkiye. Urgently review appeals to restrictions Review user appeals to account restrictions imposed in Türkiye in September and October 2026 and immediately restore access to accounts if the underlying orders fail to meet the requirements of identifying the specific content at issue, establishing a link between that content and the alleged threat to national security, public order and other grounds listed in Article 8/A, and providing adequate reasoning demonstrating that blocking the entire account is necessary and proportionate. We call on Turkish authorities to take urgent steps to end internet censorship and uphold freedom of expression, including by Immediately halting new restrictions on online content that violate freedom of expression, media freedom, and access to information as protected under international law and Türkiye’s human rights obligations.Restoring access to content which has been restricted in violation of international law and Türkiye’s freedom of expression obligations Signatories: ARTICLE 19 Freedom of Expression Association (İFÖD)Human Rights WatchAmnesty International Association of European Journalists (AEJ)Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN)Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ)Çağdaş Gazeteciler Derneği (ÇGD, Progressive Journalists Association)Foreign Media Association (FMA Turkey)IFEXInternational Press Institute (IPI)Media and Law Studies Association (MLSA)Norwegian Helsinki Committee (NHC)Osservatorio Balcani Caucaso Transeuropa (OBCT)P24 Platform for Independent JournalismPEN AmericaPEN DenmarkPEN InternationalPEN NorwaySouth East Europe Media Organisation (SEEMO)Turkey Litigation Support Project (TLSP)

Philippines: Flood Control Project Disregards Rights. (Manila) – Philippine authorities disregarded the rights of residents who were removed from a small island in Pampanga province for a flood control project and relocated to a site with chronic flooding and few livelihood opportunities, Human Rights Watch said today. In 2022, the Macabebe, Pampanga government relocated 90 families without adequate consultation and information from Pulo Island on the Pampanga River. The relocation site, in the town of Macabebe, is a low-lying area that was formerly a fish pond that floods throughout the year, causing residents to struggle to access services and work. Although the Pulo community wanted to stay together, some family members have since left because of the effects of the flooding on their lives and livelihoods. “Philippine authorities in Pampanga have threatened the safety and livelihoods of Pulo Island residents by relocating them to a low-lying area as part of a flawed flood control project,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should consult the community to find a better solution and ensure that future relocations related to flood control projects respect affected people’s rights.” Play Video Pampanga province in the Philippines’ northern island of Luzon experiences the country’s most severe flooding, which is exacerbated by storms, sea-level rise, and limited dam capacity, and is likely to worsen as climate change accelerates. From 2015 to 2025, floods and sea-level rise displaced 6.6 million people in the Philippines. The Philippine government has adopted a national policy for moving entire communities, called planned relocation or resettlement. However, the authorities responsible for moving the Pulo Island community did not follow national or international standards to protect affected people’s rights. Planned relocations, according to the United Nations Guidance on Protecting People from Disasters and Environmental Change through Planned Relocation, should be a measure of last resort to protect life and health, and based on consultation with affected communities or at their request. One of the community boats used to ferry people during the day’s most flooded time at the Pulo relocation site, July 12, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Some residents built elevated houses anticipating frequent flooding, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Aidaliza Aquino supports her husband, Eduardo Aquino, who uses a walker for mobility, at the Pulo relocation site in Barangay Candelaria, Macabebe, Pampanga, Philippines, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The river tide reached 1.6m during the high point of flooding at the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Human Rights Watch interviewed 35 residents of the Pulo relocation site in Pampanga’s Barangay Candelaria, Macabebe, between July and August 2026, as well as 9 authorities in Pampanga, and climate change experts. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery of Pulo Island and the relocation site, and employed photogrammetry—using a camera to obtain precise measurements—to determine the difference in elevation between the relocation site and the dike. Between 2020 and 2023, the Pampanga municipal government and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) dredged Pulo Island and relocated the island’s residents. Human Rights Watch found that the relocation did not involve adequate consultation, access to information, or the selection of a suitable site. “They removed us [from Pulo Island], and they put us in a place where we feel we were thrown here like trash,” said a 48-year-old mother of two children. Ria Clarin looks out to water surrounding her house, her daily view since moving to the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Ria Clarin’s house is unfinished because floodwater occasionally enters her house despite added elevation at the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Maria Mallari’s home at the Pulo relocation site was built without elevation, allowing flood waters to enter her home every day, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Residents like Evangeline Bansil have a pair of rain boots for daily wear due to flooding at the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The community boat that ferries people across the flooded Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Public works department engineers told Human Rights Watch that the late mayor of Macabebe, Anette Balgan, had requested the dredging—excavating sediment, soil, and other material from the bed of the Pampanga River—and to relocate the community. They said that removing the island would increase the river’s capacity and prevent flooding in the area, making the relocated residents and communities along the river safer. Beginning in 2018, government officials held several meetings with the affected families, some in the local Kapampangan language. None of the residents interviewed by Human Rights Watch felt they were given a choice about the relocation. Community members said they were informed about the relocation site in 2021, and expressed concerns about its suitability during meetings with authorities. The relocation site is below a dike, an elevated ridge built parallel to the river bank to prevent floodwaters reaching nearby residential areas. A road runs along the top of the dike beside the relocation site and serves as the main route to the town. “They did not present any other solutions,” said the 48-year-old mother. “There were no options.” Longtime residents said they felt pressured to move without understanding the reasons, or the compensation and assistance being provided. Residents were required to demolish their own homes to receive compensation. Many feared that if they did not demolish their houses quickly enough, the funding allocated would run out, based on rumors spread in the absence of official information. Some said they felt intimidated by the authorities. “The personnel on site were slightly harassing us too, telling us that we are obligated to leave, that we have no choice, and that they will tell on us to higher authorities,” said a 57-year-old farmer. Evangeline Bansil and Rina Tolentino wade through thigh-deep flood waters, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The level of the river reached 1.6m during high tide at the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch A resident looks out to water, her daily view in the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Maria Luz Suñga stands in front of her home at the flooded Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch A man carries a boy on his back as they wade through floodwater around the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Many of the families are related and wanted to stay together. The UN Guidance provides that planned relocation should “maintain social cohesion and kinship ties.” A massage therapist, 44, said an official became angry when she posed questions about the suitability of the relocation site: “The engineer pointed at me and said they studied engineering and would not risk their licenses over the project [if it weren’t suitable].” Community members said that in response to their concerns, local authorities told them the site would be raised to the same height as the road dike to protect them from flooding. However, the embankment works never reached that elevation, and the site remains below the dike. One engineer who worked on the relocation said that the road dike design does not allow raising the site to the same level. Human Rights Watch visited the relocation site from July 12 to 14, at the beginning of the rainy season, when at high tide the floodwater was knee- to thigh-deep. Human Rights Watch observed children wading through floodwaters, and older people who could not leave their homes while they were flooded. Residents, who described similar flooding year-round, needed to wade through flooded areas to reach the dike road. Click to expand Image The main street at the site where the Pulo Island community has been relocated lies 1.9 meters below the dike road. On the day Human Rights Watch visited, when there was light rain, the street was flooded 20 centimeters deep. Analysis and graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development, which would normally have been involved in the relocation project, told Human Rights Watch that, pending further on-site assessments, the “reported physical characteristics of the site raise concerns regarding its suitability for permanent housing.” The Philippines is obligated under international human rights law to respect, protect, and fulfill everyone’s economic, social, and cultural rights. This includes protecting people from reasonably foreseeable climate change risks, including flooding and other impacts. The relocation of Pulo Island residents was inconsistent with international standards as reflected in the UN Guidance. The Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that had the project been referred to them, they could have helped ensure that rights-based processes were followed. The commission also said it will conduct a fact-finding investigation into the matter. “Communities in the Philippines living in flood-prone areas are already facing the consequences of climate change and shouldn’t have to suffer further from botched government relocations,” Buan said. “Donors supporting the Philippine response to the effects of climate change should press the government to ensure that every aspect of relocation meets international human rights standards.” For more details and accounts about the planned relocation in Pampanga, please see below. Relocation from Pulo Click to expand Image Satellite imagery showing the progressive removal of Pulo Island beginning in 2021 through dredging by the Department of Public Works and Highways. Images © 2026 US NARA, Airbus, Vantor, Google Earth. Analysis and graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch Pulo is a 24-hectare island on the lower Pampanga River in Macabebe, Pampanga province, about 60 kilometers north of Manila, the Philippine capital. Most families had lived there for generations in a roughly three-hectare area in the northwest corner of the island. Families who lived there recalled rich agricultural land with abundant fruit and vegetables, and fish ponds. Few owned the land on which their houses stood, but many were farmer tenants or “share tenants,” for whom the landowner provides the capital and the tenant provides labor, and both share in the harvest. Residents did not pay rent, but they paid the property tax that the local government collected annually on residential lands. Under the Philippine Right-of-Way Act, those without legal claims on the land are still entitled to compensation for their structures. Macabebe is part of the Pampanga Delta, the portion of Pampanga, Bulacan, and Bataan provinces composed of low swampy lands prone to flooding. In the early 1990s, the Japan International Cooperation Agency funded the Pampanga Delta Development Project Phase I (PDDP I/Delta I), under which 1,851 households were to be resettled, but the project was never completed. The Pulo Island residents opposed being relocated by the project and remained. Two engineers from the flood control cluster of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), Tomas Edison Olalia and Alvin Diaz, told Human Rights Watch that the removal of the island was “already long overdue” because it had been proposed under the earlier project. Since 2011, the Philippine government has spent Php 1.93 trillion (US$30 billion) on flood control projects across the country through the department. Almost one third, or Php 545 billion ($8.7 billion), was spent between July 2022 and May 2025, during the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., amid allegations of massive corruption in flood control projects. At least 45 public officials have been charged in the anti-graft court in connection with various flood-control projects, most of them DPWH officials.The officials interviewed have not been implicated, nor did Human Rights Watch investigate corruption in the Pulo Island project. In 2019 and 2020, the department’s flood control cluster awarded two contracts worth Php 157 million ($2.6 million) to remove Pulo Island through its yearly flood mitigation program, according to contracts and budget line items. DPWH officials told Human Rights Watch that the project was initiated by then-Mayor Balgan. In separate letters sent by the former mayor to the agency and the agency to the residents, the community was termed “informal settler families” who needed to be removed from a “danger zone.” Under Philippine law, informal settler families occupy land without consent, or live in places considered “danger areas.” Olalia and Diaz, the engineers involved in the project, said Balgan requested the island’s dredging under a 2017 policy that instructs local government to “immediately commence the removal of illegal structures in all danger areas,” and communicated directly with now retired DPWH project manager Isabelita Manalo. Danger areas included “river banks, shorelines, creeks, waterways, esteros (estuaries) ... which when occupied for residential purposes actually pose danger to the life, safety and property of either the concerned residents, or of the general community.” Other Philippine agencies were not involved in the project, based on interviews with officials and written responses sent to Human Rights Watch by the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development and the Commmission on Human Rights. “This was an isolated case,” said Olalia, referring to the lack of involvement by other government departments. “We just responded to the request of the LGU [local government unit] because it had a valid reason; the island was in a danger zone.” The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development is normally the lead agency for planned relocation, along with the National Housing Authority, which are responsible under the National Resettlement Policy to check the feasibility of the relocation site and can provide financing for new houses. When informal settlers are affected by a resettlement, the Presidential Commission on Urban Poor should monitor the situation, according to the Department of Interior and Local Government’s resettlement guidelines. The Commission on Human Rights also has an oversight role in such cases, as its internal rules require the agency to “ensure strict compliance to the Commission on Human Rights Advisory on the Right to Adequate Housing and Humane Treatment of Informal Settlers.” In addition, the interior department’s resettlement guidelines require oversight by a local inter-agency committee or a local housing board. Human Rights Watch sent right of reply letters outlining the findings on September 21 and received responses from the human settlements department and the Commission on Human Rights. The DPWH, the municipal office in Macabebe, and the Presidential Commission on Urban Poor did not reply. “There was no check and balance,” said Ferdinand Zambrano, the project development officer at the local Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development office. The current mayor, Leonardo Flores, is Mayor Balgan’s brother. Flores’ office referred Human Rights Watch to Jomel Cruz, the disaster risk reduction officer, who was the municipal administrator during that time. Cruz said that there are no documents pertaining to the project among the files turned over by the former administration. The relocation site may be further affected by the planned Pampanga Delta Development Project Phase II (PDDP II or Delta II), which is undergoing feasibility studies, according to plans seen by Human Rights Watch that show Macabebe within the PDDP II project area. Key Human Rights Issues Relating to Planned Relocation Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch International human rights law on planned relocations derives from various human rights treaties that the Philippines has ratified, notably the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. It is also reflected in international standards and guidance, such as the UN Guidance on Planned Relocation and the UN special rapporteur on internally displaced persons Report on Planned Relocation, to help governments plan and carry out relocations of communities at risk in a rights-respecting manner. Consultation Under international human rights law, planned relocation and other government action that directly affects protected economic and social rights—particularly housing, land, relocation, eviction, water, or livelihoods—needs to be preceded by meaningful, informed, and participatory consultation with affected communities as an important procedural safeguard. Such consultation requires timely and accessible information, an opportunity to express views, and genuine consideration of those views. UN guidance and human rights standards establish that national and local governments need to ensure that planned relocation is a measure of last resort, and ensure that affected communities are meaningfully involved in decisions about a potential move. The UN Guidance says there needs to be some “flexibility to accommodate persons who may choose not to participate in the relocation,” and an opportunity for affected residents “to propose alternative options.” All members of the relocated community interviewed by Human Rights Watch said their concerns and questions about relocation were not given due consideration. What happened was not consultation but an “imposition,” said an 81-year-old woman. During meetings held by officials, including in the local language, residents said their opposition was merely noted. “They simply gave out forms for us to sign and promised us a relocation,” said Jenny Datu, 50. DPWH officials acknowledged that their staff did not conduct detailed consultations with residents, saying that their role was limited to technical assistance on the project. Pulo Island’s former residents said they ultimately agreed to move because officials said they could have a relocation site that would allow the community to stay together. In 2021, residents received “Agreement to Demolish and Remove Improvements” forms that were in English, which is not their preferred language. Some residents said they were frustrated that they received no assistance from anyone, such as a lawyer, to discuss the form. “We had no choice,” said Mary Grace Liguid, 38. “People just arrived measuring our houses, our lands. We had no choice but to agree, because you can’t be left there.” Right to Information The right to receive information, set out in article 19(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, is a core component of a human rights-based approach to planned relocation. Information should be provided in a clear and accessible manner, and should include anticipated disaster and climate risks as well as the social, physical, and economic impacts of the relocation. The UN Guidance provides that adequate, advanced, up-to-date, and accessible information on the rationale for relocation, as well as alternatives considered, is essential to minimize the risk of forced evictions. Residents said they were told various reasons for their removal from the island, including that the island was blocking the flow of the river, which is the reason stated in government documents. Community members also said they were told the island was shaped like a cone, being eroded from underneath, and could collapse at any time. “They scared us that our island was running out of soil, and we will be washed away,” said a 46-year-old man. Olalia and Diaz said this information about the island being eroded did not come from their office. The current municipal engineer of Macabebe said the local government would have no capacity to come up with such an assessment. Satellite imagery analysis by Human Rights Watch shows that, in the 36 years preceding their removal, the surface area of the island reduced by 5.2 percent, from 25 hectares in 1984 to 23.7 hectares in 2020. Relocated residents said they could not recall being given the opportunity to discuss any risk assessment with government officials. None could recall any discussion about ways they could stay on the island. A lack of information and community concerns about compensation also caused delays, as documented by DPWH itself. “Unless the people paid for the houses to be demolished, they will not transfer to the designated relocation site,” said a 2021 department order, rescheduling that phase of the dredging, which was only completed between 2022 and 2023. The payment arrangement left residents with no choice but to demolish their homes. Once they signed the demolition forms, they could receive 70 percent of the assessed value by traveling to Metro Manila to cash their compensation check. They were expected to immediately demolish their homes upon receiving the partial payment and would only receive the remaining 30 percent after providing photos and videos of their demolished homes. Most of the residents interviewed said they felt rushed to demolish their homes and cited rumors of allocated funds running out. “We were panicking,” said Esmeralda Tubig, a 46-year-old daycare teacher. “First of all, you’d demolish your house without complete payment, then you have your daily life to think about. We didn’t know where we’d get our livelihood, then suddenly we also did not know where we’d live.” More than a dozen residents said they also felt intimidated by local officials. “It was raining heavily that time, and they wanted us to start demolishing our houses,” said a 61-year-old construction worker. Residents said that they never received other forms of compensation, including for their crops. The UN Guidance states that people should “have the right to equitable compensation for their land and any other relinquished assets related to that land.” One resident burned their own trees to turn them into charcoal to at least earn some money before moving. The Philippine National Resettlement Policy Framework states that relocated people should be given a pathway to secure land tenure in their resettlement site, whether through leasehold or the right to use other property or another contractual arrangement. A 33-year-old man said he remembered discussing with authorities whether they would receive land titles at the relocation site. “Because if we don’t have titles, we’re squatters here,” he said. Suitability and Standard of Living at the New Site The national and local governments are responsible for ensuring an adequate standard of living at relocation sites. The UN Guidance says that in relocating a community, the government must “provide the necessary conditions [for them] to build a sustainable life of dignity in their place of settlement.” The National Resettlement Policy Framework also states that “resettlement sites should not be located in areas with exposure to natural hazards” such as “low-lying and flood-prone areas.” Human Rights Watch, on August 5, visited the relocation site and measured that the main street was flooded to a depth of 20 centimeters. Using a smartphone scan, the researcher then processed the images with photogrammetry to determine that the elevation difference between the top of the floodwater and the road dike was about 1.7 meters. Human Rights Watch found that the main street of the relocation site was built about 1.9 meters below the dike. Residents said that the site floods to the same level frequently throughout the year during high water levels in the Pampanga River, even during the hot dry season, from March to May. They must wade through flooded streets to reach the road dike year round but more often simply stay in their houses. Officials involved in the relocation had promised that the former fishpond would, after embankment works, match the height of the road dike beside it, several people said. The engineers said they made no such promise and had no role in selecting the relocation site, although one of their contractors did some embankment work on the site to reassure the community. The residents said that when they began moving to the site in 2022, work was ongoing to raise the site. “The site was unfinished when we moved,” said Ely Barsana, a 44-year-old massage therapist. “It was half-baked.” The work stopped eventually, with no update from authorities. Representatives from the municipal office in Macabebe said they had limited knowledge of the project. Families decided to start building their houses because their compensation money was better spent on their new home instead of on rent. “How can we wait longer?” said a 58-year-old woman. “We already demolished our house. We were renting. The payment on our house would run out the longer we rent.” Some residents were able to afford to elevate their houses, but many others could not. The authorities did not warn them that their relocation site could flood. Maria Mallari, 50, lives in a bungalow that she says is rarely dry. Her furniture is damaged, and she lifts heavy appliances every day to protect them from water. When the water subsides, the family scrubs the floor clean, only for it to be flooded again the next day. “I’m sick of it, so sick of it,” she said. Residents said they had fewer options for livelihood now. Several of them relied on selling fruit and vegetables they grew on the island to supplement their irregular incomes as laborers, construction workers, tricycle drivers, farmers, and fisherfolk. Some residents have left their families in the relocation site to seek work elsewhere. Although the relocation site is closer to the town center, frequent flooding requires a longer journey to access services like the hospital than when the community lived on Pulo Island. In July, a woman fell ill but could not be immediately transported to the hospital because the water level was too high, making boat transfer risky. She was in critical condition in the hospital for weeks, but has since recovered. Children have to wade through flood to get to and from school every day.

Türkiye: COP31 Host Curbs Environment Defenders. Click to expand Image Local residents of Perşembe Plateau and representatives of environmental organizations stage a protest against gold mining exploration in the area, July 19, 2026. © 2026 Private (Istanbul, October 13, 2026) – The authorities in Türkiye, the host of the upcoming 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), are arbitrarily arresting and prosecuting activists and others involved in environmental protests even as the summit nears, Human Rights Watch said today. “With Türkiye about to host the annual UN climate change summit, its environmental crackdown is a salient reminder of its intolerance of dissent,” said Deniz Bayram, assistant Europe and Central Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Turkish authorities should listen to people’s concerns about the environmental impact of activities such as mining in their areas and address them, instead of arresting and prosecuting protesters.” In August 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 23 people who had been at environmental protests and reviewed relevant media reports, documents, and judicial proceedings. Human Rights Watch also documented the treatment of environmental protesters in two of the areas currently affected. Protests against coal mining in the Akbelen forest in Türkiye’s southwest Muğla province have been taking place since 2023, while gold mining exploration in the Perşembe Plateau and surrounding areas in the eastern Black Sea region has sparked protests throughout 2026. Authorities in both areas have forcibly dispersed nonviolent protesters, including by using tear gas, water cannons, and pepper spray. Police have arrested and fined protesters and intimidated local residents with arbitrary identity checks. In September, Human Rights Watch wrote to the Interior Ministry, the Milas Chief Prosecution Office in Muğla, the Korgan Chief Prosecution Office in Ordu, and the Tirebolu Chief Prosecution Office in Giresun seeking further information and a response to the findings. None have responded at the time of writing. Law enforcement and security forces have arrested community members, lawyers, and journalists at protests. Protesters face a variety of criminal charges and investigations on dubious allegations including illegal gathering, using violence to prevent a public official from carrying out their duty, trespassing, insulting public officials, and spreading false information. The authorities have also temporarily arrested at least two people who expressed support for the protests online. In one instance, on July 29, the authorities arrested protesters in the eastern Black Sea area for up to eight hours without legal due process. Those arrested included two children and an 84-year-old woman. Environmental defenders have also faced criminal charges, administrative fines, and other legal pressure for monitoring environmental harm or seeking to protect their land and environment. In advance of a July NATO summit in Ankara, the authorities ordered the arrest of 225 people, ranging from political activists to nature conservation supporters, on suspicion of “membership in armed organizations.” Courts on June 25 and 26 placed 178 in pretrial detention and 34 under judicial control, without citing compelling evidence of criminal activity. Among those detained were 13 members of a nature conservation organization who were later released, along with 14 others who had been under house arrest. The continuing criminal investigations and arrests of environmental protestors since 2023 have created a significant chilling effect on the rights to expression and assembly, protected under international human rights law and the Turkish constitution. Many have ended in decisions not to prosecute or acquittals, but investigations impose an immense burden on those targeted, as they last for years and require them to appear repeatedly before law enforcement agencies. A 75-year-old woman in Denizli, in western Türkiye, was fined in May 2024 when she refused to allow two mining company staff access to her property in a protest against coal mining. She was accused of beating the staff members, allegations she strenuously denies. The decision is under appeal. Police and gendarmes have prevented journalists and bystanders from filming environmental protests in the affected areas, in some cases using violence, and arrested and opened investigations against journalists covering the protests, media reported. Human Rights Watch has previously raised concerns with Turkish authorities that its efforts to expand coal mining and coal-fired power capacity in Türkiye pose serious risks to public health, environmental protection, and the protection of other human rights. The crackdown on environmental defenders is part of a wider attack on civic space in the country, Human Rights Watch said, including the detention of activists in Istanbul protesting an anti-LGBT crackdown on September 15, 2026. Some of them allege that they were ill-treated during the more than 24 hours they were arrested. Civil society participation is important for holding states to account for their environmental policies, Human Rights Watch said. It is also essential in contexts where decisions made by the central government can have serious local environmental impact. As host of COP31 in November, Türkiye has an obligation to facilitate the participation of civil society in the conference. “The Turkish government has ignored environmental protections and turned on local people who are speaking out against environmental damage to their communities,” Bayram said. “States attending COP31 should speak out against Türkiye’s crackdown on environmental defenders and remind their hosts that civil society participation is critical to achieving COP goals.” For additional details, please see below. Methodology In August 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 23 people who had been at environmental protests: 15 community members, 6 lawyers, and 2 journalists. Human Rights Watch documented investigations and prosecutions related to long-running environmental protests in Akbelen forest in Muğla, western Türkiye, between 2023 and 2026, and protests in the eastern Black Sea region in 2026, as well as investigations linked to those protests. Human Rights Watch also reviewed media reports, indictments, traffic penalties, and other administrative fines issued against protesters; court decisions, court-appointed expert reports relevant to the protests, and forensic medical reports; and photographs from protesters documenting their injuries. Human Rights Watch examined the judicial proceedings against protesters in four cases in İkizköy village, in the Milas district of Türkiye’s southwestern Muğla province, including relevant investigation documents and the decisions on conviction and acquittal, and assessed the laws used to prosecute them. Akbelen: Protests Banned Over Coal Mining in Forest, Olive Groves Click to expand Image Since 2023, local residents have been protesting forest clearance for coal mining, İkizköy, Muğla, Türkiye, August‎ ‎6‎, ‎2023. © 2023 Kazım Kızıl Since 2019, residents of İkizköy have been pursuing court cases to prevent the expansion of an open-pit lignite mine into Akbelen forest, the clearance of the legally protected forest, and the expropriation of nearby olive groves. The forest clearing case is pending while a court halted the expropriation of the olive groves. On July 17, 2021, after the Muğla Forestry Directorate cut down about 30 trees, community members began to monitor Akbelen forest for potential unlawful activity. On August 10, about 250 gendarmes intervened and arrested 11 protesters, including Füsun Ergün, who was forcibly removed after tying herself to an olive tree. Ergün and another environment defender, Gülören Demir, were convicted of resisting public officials and sentenced to 6 months and 20 days in prison, subsequently converted to fines. Click to expand Image During protests, the gendarmerie intervened with riot shields and water cannon against demonstrators, July, 28, 2026, İkizköy, Muğla, Türkiye. © 2026 Kazım Kızıl When the authorities resumed clearing the forest in July 2023, police used tear gas and water cannons against protesting villagers. The media reported that at least 40 people were arrested, including 14 later charged with resisting police officers. A broad coalition of civil society groups from across the country soon joined the protests. By August 2023, the authorities had cut down about three-fifths of the forest, despite the pending court case. Click to expand Image Despite pending court cases challenging the forest clearance and urgent expropriation, large areas of Akbelen Forest have already been cut down, İkizköy, Muğla, Türkiye, July 30, 2023. © 2023 Kazım Kızıl The government has prosecuted six community members for their participation or presence at various protests since 2023. Four were convicted for resisting public officials and are appealing. Two of them, Ahmet Tatar, 63, who faced multiple charges of resisting public officials, and an 85-year-old man accused of insulting the president, were acquitted. At least 55 others have been criminally investigated, 3 lawyers representing community members said. Many of the investigations have remained open for years. İsmail Atal, a lawyer who is himself the subject of two investigations, said that “keeping the investigations [open] for years leaves the threat of prosecution hanging over protesters like a Sword of Damocles, deterring them from taking part in further protests.” The Human Rights Watch review of the cases and interviews with those investigated suggests a pattern of intimidation aimed at discouraging protests. The authorities have arrested Tatar three times, and he said prosecutors had opened ten criminal investigations against him, most for allegedly resisting public officials or preventing them from performing their duties. Eight are ongoing, and two resulted in prosecutions both ending in acquittals. The prosecutor appealed the acquittals, and to date one acquittal has been upheld. “Of course I will continue to join protests,” Tatar said. “It is my moral obligation to humanity. But it is difficult and burdensome to deal with all these investigations.” Prosecutors have, however, failed to effectively investigate allegations against security officers for violations of protesters’ rights in Akbelen. On September 13, 2023, Tatar said, gendarmes broke his camera, struck him with their hands on his back and ankles, forced him face-down to the ground, pressed on his neck and back, cuffed his hands behind his back, and searched his tent. Tatar said he identified the gendarmes by name and filed complaints, supported by medical reports documenting his injuries, but the court dismissed his complaints. İpek Sarica, another lawyer, also filed a criminal complaint about violence she says she experienced during a protest in 2023. After a prosecutor declined to prosecute the case, Sarica appealed, but her complaint has remained unresolved for over three years. In a third case, Nejla Işık, the village head of İkizköy, filed a complaint alleging a violation of her right to privacy after a siginal jammer and a large number of gendarmes were deployed very close to her house. Prosecutors declined to open a case, which Işık’s lawyers challenged. The case is pending before the Constitutional Court. Güven Göknar, 66, from Muğla, said he intervened in a July 2023 protest against deforestation when gendarmes used pepper spray against protesters at close range. He was sentenced to five months in prison for allegedly resisting public officials, after footage showing him raising his hand was misinterpreted as showing him throwing a stone. He said he raised his hand to tell the gendarmes to stop; his appeal is pending. On March 30, 2026, Esra Işık, 26, was arrested during a protest against an expropriation order covering 649 land parcels in İkizköy. She spent 42 days in pretrial detention. On July 6, the Milas Criminal Court convicted her of “resisting officials” and sentenced her to two years and one month in prison, together with a suspended sentence for insulting public officials. Esra Işık’s lawyers have appealed. Another lawyer interviewed said that community members have been fined between 40,000 to 250,000 Turkish lira (about US$825 to $5,160) for acts including putting up tents and banners in connection with the Akbelen protests. People who have been fined and their lawyers said that in some cases fines were finalized without proper notification, with officials falsely recording that recipients had refused to accept notifications being served. As a result, some community members faced seizures of their bank accounts and property, while some were forced to pay. A lawyer said they had succeeded in having some fines cancelled, but not all of them. In 2023, prosecutors investigated 25 environmental activists in Edremit, on the north Aegean coast, for an unauthorized protest in solidarity with environment defenders in Akbelen. The case was later dropped. The authorities have also exerted pressure on lawyers representing the Akbelen community. Atal said that gendarmes arrested him on allegations of obstructing public officials as he traveled to the village on July 29, 2023, held him for several hours, and that he has been kept under investigation. Prosecutors opened a criminal investigation against Arif Ali Cangı, another lawyer, for allegedly inciting hatred and hostility among the public after he posted a social media post criticizing continued mining activity in Akbelen in the aftermath of the 2023 earthquake. The investigation remains open. The experience of journalists covering environmental protests suggests that the authorities open criminal investigations deliberately to interfere with their work. Prosecutors summoned a citizen journalist, Zeynep Kuray, on August 3, 2023, while she was reporting on the Akbelen protests. She then learned that the Milas Prosecution Office had opened an investigation against her for “spreading misleading information,” a criminal offense punishable with a prison term of one to three years, which eventually closed in 2024. Two other journalists arrested at their homes in İzmir in February 2024 said that police had questioned them about their presence at the Akbelen protests. Eastern Black Sea: Crackdown against Gold Mining Protests In Türkiye’s eastern Black Sea region, residents of the Perşembe Plateau have been protesting gold mining exploration since early 2026. The high plateau is in the northern part of Korgan-Aybastı districts, about 110 kilometers from Ordu, the provincial capital. The residents raise livestock for their livelihoods. The area designated for gold exploration is classified as pasture under Turkish law and requires specific permits to be mined. Türkiye’s Environment Ministry issued a permit in 2024. Human Rights Watch interviewed 11 residents who said they had been excluded from consultation and information about the project, which could potentially force them to relocate. They became aware of the project after it began affecting water they needed for livestock and household use, as well as from public statements by environmental groups. The community challenged the Environment Ministry’s permit. A court-assigned expert report dated June 15, 2026, warned that the project could disrupt the area’s hydrogeology, or groundwater flow, and that local water resources were critical to pastoral activities, livestock farming, and the community’s drinking and domestic water needs. Click to expand Image Local residents of Perşembe Plateau, together with the Ordu Environmental Organization, gathered to make a press statement opposing the gold exploration project, July 19, 2026, Korgan, Ordu. © 2026 Private The authorities fined the protesting community members in June and August in Giresun and Ordu provinces for hanging banners and issued traffic penalties for alleged “improper parking,” which residents believe was retaliation for protesting. On July 29, more than 50 residents protested drilling in Perşembe Plateau. Gendarmes arrested about 15 people. Human Rights Watch interviewed four men who were among at least 11 taken to the Tepealan gendarmerie station in Korgan, some handcuffed. They said they were held for about eight hours without being told why or whether they were under investigation, then released. One said gendarmes made some arrestees sign a document stating that they would not attend any further protests. The men said they have received no information since about any investigation or legal basis for their arrest. Leyla Acerce, 40, attended the protest with her husband and four children. She said that gendarmes formed a large circle, their shields pointing outwards, and pushed her into the circle, where she fainted. She was dragged and left sitting in a chair outside in heavy rain for hours. She was later transferred alone to Korgan State Hospital by ambulance. Acerce said she called the police from the hospital to report that she had been beaten by the gendarmes. The police came to the hospital. The hospital gave the police the medical report documenting her injuries but refused her a copy. Her husband, Ali Acerce, 47, said that when he tried to help his wife, three gendarmes handcuffed him, twisted his arm, and forced him into a container, where he was held for about two hours. He was then taken to the Tepealan gendarmerie station, where he was held for six hours and then released. He said that their 22-year-old son, İlyas, was also arrested for about six hours. Police made the family wait for hours when they went to the police station to file a complaint about their treatment by the gendarmes. They are not aware of any action on their complaint. Nuriye Dilek, 48, and another woman in her 50s who requested anonymity out of fear for her family, said four gendarmes dragged them from the protest and forced them into an unmarked white van. “They threw me into the van like a sack,” Dilek said.” I thought they would break our arms as they twisted them.” Human Rights Watch observed bruising on Dilek’s wrists and on the other woman’s chest and arms six days after the protest. Interviewees also said that they saw gendarmes drag two girls, both under 18, by their hair and put them into an unmarked van. Dilek said she saw gendarmes and plain clothes officers pointing out community members who had spoken out about defending the plateau in videos shared on social media. Musa Duman, 60, said that during questioning in a separate investigation, a prosecutor asked him about photos and videos he had shared online from the protests. Click to expand Image Gendarmerie block local residents from Perşembe Plateau from reaching the gold mining drilling site to stage a protest, July 16, 2026. © 2026 Private Residents said that after the protest, they faced a range of apparent retaliatory measures by the gendarmerie, including repeated identity checks in the small community where they had lived for years. If they did not carry identification, gendarmes photographed their faces at close range “as if we were criminals,” one resident said. Residents also reported verbal harassment and that following a solidarity protest on August 1, 17 traffic fines were issued to protesters and visitors for alleged improper parking or tinted windows. Local activists also said gendarmes used a signal jammer during the protest to disrupt communications, and Human Rights Watch reviewed photographs showing gendarmes carrying jamming equipment. Jammers were also used at other protests in Akbelen. An 84-year-old woman who had been arrested said she was now hesitant to appear in protest photos or videos after gendarmes contacted her sons, who live in other cities, and told them not to let their mother attend protests. Dilek also said that authorities had contacted her son. Dilek said that her husband, Halil Dilek, 53, and another man were arrested on suspicion of theft of materials related to mining operations and detained overnight at the Tepealan gendarmerie station. Halil Dilek said that he was distressed because his wife was travelling and that his teenage daughter was alone at home. He said that the prosecutor who questioned him the following day asked about his participation in the protests and photos he had shared on social media, raising concerns of surveillance and pressure over his environmental activism. On August 27, residents of Perşembe Plateau, including Duman and Nuriye Dilek, met with Ordu’s governor to discuss the project and the excessive use of force and violence by the gendarmerie. When Dilek said that gendarmes had beaten and dragged her and that her clothes had been torn open during the altercation, she said the governor asked what she was doing there in the first place. Duman said that on September 9, gendarmes summoned him to give a statement about his Facebook post criticizing the governor’s response. He was told he was suspected of publicly disseminating misleading information. The authorities have sought to suppress environmental protests in other areas of the eastern Black Sea designated for gold mining exploration. On April 5, residents of Görele and Tirebolu in Giresun province, east of Ordu, gathered to protest work at a gold mining project, despite a court order suspending the work. A large number of gendarmes confronted them, said a lawyer, Sevda Karataş, and the company complained the protesters had interfered with its “freedom to work.” Subsequently, Karataş, Ömer Cebeci, a municipal council member, and Nihal Nakıpoğlu, a local environmental association member, were summoned for questioning by the prosecutor. Karataş, who represents two community members from Tirebolu in Giresun, said that a prosecutor investigated her clients for alleged threats, disseminating misleading information, and interfering with the company’s “freedom to work.” The investigation remains open. Mesut Yilmaz, a 33-year-old local resident who actively posts about the protests on social media, said that police questioned him for about six hours about more than 100 pages of his social media posts. On June 2, he was fined, paying the maximum penalty of 115,000 lira (about $2,500) for putting up banners announcing a gold mining protest for May 29. The Right to Protest Under Human Rights Law The right to peaceful protest is protected under international human rights law, including under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR); Türkiye is party to both. The right to peaceful assembly is closely linked to the right to freedom of expression. While the rights to freedom of assembly and expression are not absolute and can be subject to restrictions, both the ECHR and ICCPR require that any restriction must be prescribed by law to pursue a legitimate aim and to be necessary and proportionate to that aim. Blanket bans on protests are disproportionate and unjustifiable. The UN Human Rights Committee, which oversees compliance with the ICCPR, in its General Comment No. 37 (2020) stipulates that peaceful assemblies should not be criminalized, and that states must facilitate and protect such gatherings. The European Court of Human Rights has repeatedly found that Turkish authorities’ use of powers under the Law on Meetings and Demonstrations (Law no. 2911) to ban or disperse protests and punish protestors violated the right of assembly. The right to peaceful protest is also protected under the article 34 of the Turkish constitution, which guarantees the right to organize peaceful, unarmed demonstrations and marches without prior permission.

India: End Crackdown on Protesters, Arbitrary Detentions. Click to expand Image Police detain protesters during a demonstration demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner, in New Delhi, India, October 10, 2026. © 2026 AP Photo/Manish Swarup (New York) – Indian authorities are using abusive methods to crack down on thousands of peaceful protesters in New Delhi and other Indian cities, Human Rights Watch said today. The protests, led by the Gen Z Cockroach Janta Party, opposition parties, student organizations, and civil society groups, have demanded the resignation of the country’s top election official over alleged wrongdoing and the scrapping of a contentious voter list revision process. As the protests grew in October 2026, the police have beat protesters, forcibly dragged them on the streets and stuffed them into vans and buses, arbitrarily detained them, imposed excessive restrictions on movement, and suspended mobile internet services. The authorities have also harassed and arbitrarily detained journalists covering the protests. “Police in Delhi are responding to peaceful protests with seemingly unnecessary or excessive force and have wrongfully detained thousands of people,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The Modi government should stop throwing young protesters in jail and instead engage with them to address concerns over the right to vote and fairness of elections.” Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration should stop the ill-treatment and arbitrary detention of protesters, allow people to protest peacefully, and restore mobile internet services and freedom of movement, Human Rights Watch said. Since June 2025, the Election Commission of India has carried out a nationwide Special Intensive Revision (SIR) to clean electoral rolls, ostensibly to remove any dead, duplicate, or ineligible voters. But the process, which has deleted more than 130 million names so far, has been arbitrary and opaque, prompting fears of mass disenfranchisement, and is disproportionately affecting Muslims and other religious minorities, women, and people living in poverty. Protest leaders and opposition parties allege that the commission has manipulated the lists to benefit Prime Minister Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The protests began on September 25, soon after the Indian Express published its investigation into alleged irregularities in the revision process. The newspaper found that the Election Commission’s two commissioners had raised multiple objections against decisions by the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. Petitions challenging the revision process and seeking Kumar’s removal are before the Supreme Court. As protests in Delhi grew in October, security forces arbitrarily arrested and assaulted numerous protesters each day, and took them to undisclosed locations, later releasing many of them. Those detained included journalists and political opposition leaders, including four former chief ministers and Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition. When the protests began, Delhi Police released a set of “guidelines,” instructing journalists to “carry valid identity cards” that are “visibly displayed,” to “not obstruct police operations,” and to “maintain a reasonable and safe distance.” On October 11, the Supreme Court directed that lawyers and journalists “should not be impeded from carrying out their professional duties.” On October 10 and 11, officials arbitrarily detained at least 30 journalists who were covering the protests. Four journalists’ organizations condemned the police actions, saying that journalists were “bundled into buses” used to detain protesters, and that police seized some of their phones and equipment. Three female journalists alleged that Delhi police officers sexually harassed them during the protests. A journalist from the magazine Caravan said that on October 11, police officers in Delhi hit him on the head several times, slapped him, and assaulted him with a rifle butt while he recorded them detaining a protester. “My press card was hanging by my neck but they still dragged me into the bus, ripping my shirt buttons,” a 31-year-old journalist told Human Rights Watch. Police detained him in a bus on October 10, and he was released only after the bus overheated and caught fire. “We could smell the fumes and had to shout at them to get us out,” he said. “The police personnel assaulted me and pinned me to the seat,” said John Brittas, a member of parliament participating in the protests, in a letter to the chief justice of India. The Cockroach Janta Party called for a protest on October 10 at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in Delhi. In response the authorities deployed over 40,000 security forces, canceled trains, shut down 43 metro stations, and suspended mobile internet services. Police took three Cockroach Janta Party leaders into custody aboard an airplane after it landed in Delhi, dragged several protesters from trains and buses who were traveling to Delhi, and put some youth leaders under house arrest. Air India has sought a response from the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security on how security forces entered its aircraft without prior authorization. On October 9, a police officer entered a Delhi mosque during Friday prayers to warn Muslims against participating in any “unnecessary protests.” The next day, police officials entered a Sikh temple in central Delhi to detain protesters who sought refuge there. Citizens for Fraternity-Bharat (CFF-Bharat), a civil society group that includes former government officials, has questioned why police entered religious premises and called for an independent inquiry. On October 11, India’s Supreme Court directed the authorities to ensure that people gathering peacefully are not illegally detained, internet services are restored, and people and traffic are allowed to move freely, subject to lawful restrictions. Thus far, the authorities appear to have ignored the directions. A journalist, 26, told Human Rights Watch he witnessed at least three instances in which BJP supporters and police chased protesters together. “It is collaborative,” said the journalist, who covered the protests on October 10. “The police looked on and did not stop the violence.” A female journalist, 27, said a group of about five men, some of them wearing saffron scarves, were beating protesters and targeting female journalists. “They were shouting at us, mocking us, and showing us the middle finger,” she said. “I saw two policemen laughing while the right-wing goons were kicking and beating protesters.” The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights expressed concerns over the mass detention of demonstrators and said that the government should engage in meaningful dialogue. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs called the statement “unwarranted” and “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of India.” The Indian government should publicly direct security forces to respond to protests in accordance with international standards, notably the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials, Human Rights Watch said. “Indian authorities should allow people to protest peacefully by resuming transport services, removing unnecessary barricades, restoring the internet, and ensuring media freedom,” Pearson said. “Peaceful protest and freedom of expression are fundamental rights protected under the international human rights law that India’s leaders claim to uphold.”

Japan’s Commitment to Sport Needs to Include Athlete Protection. Click to expand Image Photo montage of the Tokyo Olympic Stadium and youth in Japan training and playing popular sports. © 2019 imagenavi/Aflo; 2005 Doable/a.collectionRF/amanaimages; 2020 Human Rights Watch; 2015 Satoru Kobayashi/a.collectionRF/amanaimages; 2016 RYO/amanaimages; Trevor Williams/Getty Images; 2020 Human Rights Watch; 2016 Matsuo/Aflo; AdobeStock Every October, Japan celebrates Sports Day, a public holiday established to commemorate the 1964 Tokyo Olympic Games and Japan's longstanding commitment to sport as a national priority. There has been much to celebrate in recent years. For more than six decades, Japan has had dedicated legislation – now known as the Basic Act on Sports – to advance sports on a national level. By investing in facilities, athletes’ development, and public participation—and hosting mega-events like the 2020 Olympics—Japan has become a leading sports nation. Yet, one critical issue has received too little attention: protecting athletes and children from sports-related abuse. Human Rights Watch has documented the widespread physical, sexual, and verbal abuse many Japanese children and athletes experience when they participate in sports. A professional athlete described suffering abuses from his coach: “I was hit so many times, I can’t count ... the coach … hit [me] in the face in front of everyone. I was bleeding, but he did not stop.” Under public pressure from athletes and survivors to reform, the Japanese parliament passed in 2025 amendments to the Basic Act on Sport requiring the national government to prevent abuse in sport. So far, however, the government has not adequately implemented the law—largely relying, instead, on individual sports federations and organizations to handle complaints of abuse. But, as Human Rights Watch has reported, athletes and children are often hesitant to report abuse to these institutions because they fear retaliation and because federations often protect their leaders rather than athletes. Reporting mechanisms also vary widely by sport, creating unequal access to protection. The Japan Sports Agency is now drafting the government's five-year blueprint for sports policy, which will be implemented in 2027. This plan should better address abuse in sport, including by establishing an independent Safe Sport Center to receive complaints, investigate abuse allegations, and support those who have been harmed. Sport Day should be an opportunity not only to celebrate Japan’s athletes but to make them safer. Japan’s government should ensure that everyone can participate in sport safely, without abuse, and can report harm through a trusted system.

France Shouldn’t Return Afghans to Taliban Rule. Click to expand Image Afghan refugees board a truck with their belongings as they await deportation at the Pakistan-Afghanistan border in Chaman on October 19, 2025. © 2025 Abdul Basil/AFP via Getty Images France has confirmed that it has opened a “technical dialogue” with the Taliban authorities regarding forced returns to Afghanistan. The announcement marks a dangerous shift in policy that places Afghans in France at risk of persecution, torture and other grave abuses in contravention of France’s international human rights obligations. The “technical dialogue” follows in the wake of a Taliban delegation to Brussels in June in which migration and return policies were discussed with European Union officials. Germany has already deported 263 Afghans since last year. The French Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the talks aim “to facilitate the removal of Afghan nationals who are illegally on the national territory and who represent a national security risk.” French officials say the dialogue is narrowly focused but have not set out any guarantees that those at particular risk, including women, would be protected. Since taking power in August 2021, the Taliban have issued decrees and enacted laws that have deprived Afghans of their fundamental rights. Women and girls are restricted from exercising their rights to education, freedom of movement, and expression. There is also compelling evidence that Taliban forces have detained and tortured people who have been forcibly returned to the country. French cooperation with the Taliban on a returns process would be with full knowledge of the Taliban’s responsibility for grave human rights violations and systematic oppression. Earlier this month, the International Criminal Court publicly announced the arrest warrants for Taliban Supreme Leader Haibatullah Akhundzada and three other senior officials for the crime against humanity of persecution on gender and political grounds. The warrants, issued in 2025, relate to the persecution of women, girls, and people who do not conform to the Taliban’s expectations of gender, and the political persecution of those viewed as “allies of girls and women.” No country should be forcing refugees to return to Afghanistan so long as the Taliban continues to commit widespread human rights abuses. France should suspend any plan for deportations, and any cooperation on migration control should not be used as a vehicle for sending people back to a country where they would face a real risk of persecution or worse.

Saudi Arabia: Death Penalty for Facebook Comment. Click to expand Image Anojan Sivarasa. © Private (Beirut) – A Saudi court has sentenced a Sri Lankan migrant worker to death over a Facebook comment that was deemed blasphemous, Human Rights Watch said today. Saudi authorities should reverse the judgment and release him immediately. The Saudi Court of Appeal in the Eastern Region handed down the death sentence to Anojan Sivarasa, 24, on September 17, 2026, after two court sessions. An initial ruling had sentenced him to five years in prison. “Sentencing a migrant worker to death over a Facebook comment that he has publicly apologized for is an outrageous overreaction from Saudi authorities amid a surge in executions,” said Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “No one should face execution for a comment on religion.” On June 28, Sivarasa replied to a video circulating on Facebook with a comment in Tamil deemed offensive to the Prophet Muhammad by some viewers. The comment quickly gained attention, and a screenshot was apparently sent to Saudi authorities and Sivarasa’s employer, a family member of Sivarasa’s told Human Rights Watch. Sivarasa deleted the comment and uploaded an apology video to his Facebook account. Sivarasa’s employer held him in its office for at least 24 hours and then took him to the Dammam police station, where he was arrested on July 1, the family member said. Sivarasa was working in construction and had arrived in Saudi Arabia just 10 months earlier. He is the sole breadwinner for his family in Sri Lanka, the family member said.
